data.title: Johnson & Johnson offers £4.1bn to settle talcum powder cancer claims
data.description:
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5bn (£4.1bn) to resolve tens of thousands of claims that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer.

The pharmaceutical giant’s offer of a settlement could end a decade-long legal battle that has dogged the company.

Erik Haas, vice-president of litigation at J&J, said the claims that its talcum powder products caused cancer were “meritless” ‌but said the company was willing ⁠to settle to get closure.

The settlement covers around 76,000 claims and must be accepted by 95pc of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.

J&J previously settled the majority of cases alleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma, a rare but aggressive cancer affected the lungs, abdomen or heart.

Mr Haas said: “While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save ⁠lives.”

J&J expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028.

More than 3,000 people filed lawsuits at Britain’s High Court last year alleging that either they or a family member developed ovarian cancer or mesothelioma as a result of using Johnson’s Baby Powder between 1965 and 2023.

The settlements announced on Monday included groups who filed claims in federal and state courts.

J&J ended global sales of baby powder containing the mineral talc in 2023, switching to a formulation based on corn starch.

The settlements come after cases were put on hold for more than three years after a series of bankruptcy filings by J&J.

It filed three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ‌effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal and the litigation resumed in March 2025.

Chris Seeger, an attorney who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, said J&J could ultimately pay $7bn or more.

The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap J&J’s total payout.

He said: “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”

data.title: British baked beans ‘under threat from Burnham tariffs’
data.description:
British baked beans are under threat from Andy Burnham’s decision to cut tariffs on imported food, manufacturers have warned.

On Tuesday, the Government announced the suspension of tariffs on more than 100 food products, including cutting the 16 per cent levy on tinned beans.

The move was part of a package of measures the Chancellor announced in his Budget to give families “breathing space” amid the cost of living crisis.

However, British food bosses have warned that cheap exports from the US and China could undermine the country’s major bean processing industry.

The Heinz baked bean plant in Wigan, Greater Manchester, employs up to 850 people and produces 1.5 million tins a day. The Princes Group, which makes Branston baked beans, is owned by Italian food conglomerate Newlat and is one of Britain’s biggest food manufacturers with around 2,000 UK staff.

Karen Betts, chief executive of the Food and Drink Federation (FDF), said Mr Healey’s Budget had done “nothing to ease the pressures food and drink manufacturers are under”.

“One of the Chancellor’s flagship announcements, removing tariffs from some food and drink products, will have no meaningful impact on consumer prices,” she said.

“But it will undermine British factories and their workers, grappling with much higher costs, producing the same products.”

A spokesman for the Princes Group said: “Based on our understanding of the proposals so far, removing tariffs on imported finished baked beans is unlikely to have a meaningful impact on prices, particularly as there are currently no tariffs on the imported haricot beans used by UK manufacturers and no tariffs on EU imports.

“We believe measures that help address the higher costs of manufacturing food in the UK, particularly energy costs, would have a greater impact for both consumers and British businesses.”

The tariff announcement was made days after the Prime Minister said he would put the British family favourite in his emergency box in case of a national disaster. Asked what items he would stockpile, he picked baked beans, soup and Twiglets.

The FDF said it was also concerned about the lifting of tariffs on boiled sweets, toffees and caramels and pressed sweets like Love Hearts and Parma Violets, as well as chocolate.

Last year, the UK and US both applied a tariff of up to a 10 per cent on chocolate imports from the other country. Since then, the US has increased its tariff to 20 per cent and the UK has just removed it for most products.

In addition, the FDF said there were concerns around jams, marmalades and purees, tomato ketchup, tomato sauces, soups and broths.

“Food and drink manufacturing should be central to the Government’s growth and reindustrialisation agenda,” said Ms Betts. “But time and again, we are treated as an afterthought.

“The Treasury, in particular, has persistently failed to recognise the importance of food and drink manufacturing to jobs and prosperity across the length and breadth of the UK.”

The FDF said that particular companies that could be affected, including confectioners Nestle in York and Halifax, Haribo in Bradford, and Cadbury in Bourneville and Tiptree jam in Colchester.

The Government says the tariff suspensions, taken together with others announced earlier this year, will reduce consumer costs by up to £595m a year, saving households up to £21 on their annual food shop.

In its response to a consultation on the changes, the Government said it recognised there “may be some limited impacts on domestic producers of goods”, but said it “considers the benefits of this to consumers, through reduced costs, outweigh those risks”.

data.title: Channel 4 chief: Handling of Russell Brand complaints ‘almost unforgivable’
data.description:
Channel 4’s handling of complaints about Russell Brand was “almost unforgivable”, its chief executive has said.

Addressing MPs on Tuesday, Priya Dogra apologised to one of Brand’s victims who complained to the broadcaster about his behaviour in both 2009 and 2023.

In a victim statement read out in court ahead of Brand’s conviction for rape and sexual assault on Nov 5, the woman, who was referred to as Bella in The Times’s investigation, said her complaint had been “brushed under the carpet” by Channel 4 bosses.

Ms Dogra told the digital, media, culture and sport select committee on Tuesday that she was “horrified” to learn that other people had made complaints they felt were not dealt with properly.

She said: “That is not acceptable. It shouldn’t be. And in the instance of Bella, I’m not sure we can apologise enough as an organisation for putting her through that twice.”

The Channel 4 boss added: “I want to express my dismay and frustration that we end up in these cycles as a media industry. This is not what we want to be known [for] as an industry.”

Brand, who has begun a decade-long prison sentence, was convicted of sexually assaulting Bella in 2009 by demanding a massage and placing his head in her groin without her consent.

Bella, who has lifelong anonymity, reported the incident to Channel 4 the day after it happened but no action was taken.

Following the release of its Dispatches investigation into Brand in 2023, the broadcaster commissioned an internal inquiry into the disgraced comedian, who worked on programmes including Big Brother.

Alex Mahon, Channel 4’s chief executive at the time, apologised to Bella for failing to investigate her complaint.

But the former employee described the company’s inquiry as “shambolic” and described its report as a “whitewash”.

Ms Dogra said Channel 4 would not open another investigation into its handling of complaints, but insisted the broadcaster had strengthened its protections for staff.

She said the company had expanded its anonymous whistleblowing service, while it will now require all production companies it partners with to sign up to the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority (CIISA), an industry-funded body aimed at cracking down on misconduct.

Geoff Cooper, Channel 4’s chairman, added that a change in culture was now a priority for the broadcaster’s board.

It comes after Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, summoned TV bosses on Monday to call for an end to the culture of abuse across the media industry.

She has threatened to introduce tougher regulation if bosses fail to protect people from workplace abusers.

Ms Dogra acknowledged that the industry had a problem with power imbalances between stars and crew and said broadcasters would have to prove that commercial interests did not override their principles.

The Channel 4 boss pointed to her decision to axe Married at First Sight, which she described as a “very profitable show”, following allegations of rape on the reality show.

Ms Dogra, who took up the role in March, also defended Channel 4 and news producer ITN against criticisms about the widespread use of non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) to silence former employees.

She said: “We do have clauses, but they are not intended to be gagging orders in any way. If somebody has seen misconduct or misbehaviour, they are open to report that.”

The Commons committee will grill TV bosses next month about whether NDAs are preventing people from reporting abuse and inappropriate behaviour in the media and entertainment industries.

data.title: Housebuilder shares slump as surging mortgage costs put off buyers
data.description:
Shares in one of Britain’s biggest housebuilders slumped after it warned that higher mortgage rates were putting off buyers.

Taylor Wimpey, which is listed on the FTSE 100, saw up to £130m wiped off its shares on Wednesday.

It now expects to sell 10,500 homes this year, down from July’s forecast of up to 10,800.

The group warned the housing market had been “challenging” during the autumn, with higher building costs combining with weaker house prices and rising interest rates for buyers.

This month, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years after warning inflation would rise close to 5pc in early 2027 as a result of the Iran war.

Jennie Daly, the chief executive of Taylor Wimpey, said: “The autumn selling season has been more subdued, as higher mortgage rates and living costs continue to reduce customer affordability.”

The housebuilder warned shareholders that it expected its adjusted operating profit to come in at the bottom of a range estimated by analysts at between £262m and £299m.

House prices rose at their slowest pace in nearly three years during October, according to a closely watched index from Nationwide.

Property values have been hit by higher mortgage rates, which have put strain on buyers.

The average five-year fixed deal with lenders stood at just under 6pc on Tuesday, up from just under 5pc on the eve of the Iran war outbreak, according to Moneyfacts.

In a further blow to the housing market, traders expect the Bank may raise interest rates again to 4.25pc in December.

Money markets suggest rates will rise to 4.75pc by July next year.

Anthony Codling, an analyst at RBC Capital Markets, said Taylor Wimpey had cut its sales forecasts as “higher mortgage rates continue to squeeze affordability”.

He added: “Pricing continues to reflect subdued market conditions.”

The company said it welcomed the Government’s Your First Home Scheme announced in the Budget last month.

The programme, expected to open for applications in February, aims to help first-time buyers purchase a new-build home with deposits as low as 2.5pc and a 20pc equity loan.

Ms Daly added: “We welcome the Government’s Your First Home Scheme to support getting people on to the property ladder.

“Our strong first-time buyer proposition and growing outlet base position us well as the scheme develops.”

Shares fell up to 5pc before recovering to be down 3pc.

data.title: GB News launches British-only rival to Amazon
data.description:
GB News has launched an Amazon rival that will only sell products from British businesses.

The online marketplace, called Shop GB, will allow shoppers to browse and purchase thousands of products, ranging from food and drink to clothing, jewellery and electronics.

While the items can be sourced from anywhere, every seller on the site must be registered and based in the UK.

Shop GB is launching before Black Friday, the major retail event that kicks off the Christmas shopping season.

The site is offering discounts on a range of gaming chairs, while a large blanket printed with black-and-white images of Diana, Princess of Wales, is listed at 41pc off.

Shop GB will sell items from both independent sellers and established national brands.

Fashion retailer 80s Casual Classics, which specialises in retro sportswear popularised by films such as This Is England and The Business, is among the first businesses to go live on the website.

Steve Smith, the founder of Poundland, who is backing the launch, said: “Having spent much of my career building British businesses, I know first-hand the hard work, commitment and determination it takes to succeed.

“British entrepreneurs and business owners are an incredible asset to this country. They create jobs, generate wealth and give people opportunities and we should never underestimate the importance of supporting them.”

Tim Dray, of Shop GB, said: “Shoppers increasingly want to know who they are buying from.

“Every business on Shop GB is a verified British company, so people can shop with confidence and know their money is supporting UK firms and the jobs that depend on them.”

It marks GB News’s latest foray into new areas as the broadcaster seeks to celebrate Britain’s economic and cultural contributions.

The channel last month launched an “all-British” radio station that promises a soundtrack dedicated exclusively to artists from the UK, with programmes including Great British Party Night every Saturday.

But the launch of Shop GB signals that the company – which is owned by Sir Paul Marshall, the hedge fund tycoon, and Dubai investment firm Legatum – is pushing further beyond broadcasting.

A new division, called GB Media, has been launched to lead the expansion plan.

GB News, which launched in 2021, has fended off competition from Rupert Murdoch’s media empire to establish itself as a new player in Britain’s broadcasting market.

But the channel has been beset with controversies over its opinion-led programming and has been hit with an advertising boycott. It has racked up £140m in losses since its launch five years ago.

GB News is facing a fresh challenge from Reform UK, which is using major donations from two crypto billionaires to build its own YouTube-based TV channel.

The venture raises the prospect of a new rival to GB News, though insiders have played down the threat, insisting that the channel is not reliant on one presenter or political party.

data.title: Lime bike jousters defy warnings from company to stop
data.description:
“Joust, joust, joust,” the crowds jeered, as two knights charged towards one another, lances raised.

You might be forgiven for thinking the scene had been lifted from medieval Camelot.

But, atop a neon-green steed, the “knights” in question were taking part in a new phenomenon called “Lime bike jousting”, which sees riders on the rental e-bikes charge at one another brandishing striped poles.

Jack Carden, an artist, and actor Camtholomew the First, whose real name is Cameron Carnegie-Brown, staged their first duel earlier this month, drawing hundreds of spectators to London Fields, east London.

Footage of the first duel showed the pair charging towards one another on the e-bikes, dressed in chainmail, red and black cloaks and full suits of armour.

Each wielded a striped lance as they attempted to knock their opponent from his saddle.

But their medieval enthusiasm was not shared by Lime.

The company said in a statement: “While we appreciate the medieval spirit, safety must always come first. Lime bikes are designed for getting around the city, not for jousting.”

The company also discouraged riders from “attempting similar events”.

The men defied the warnings to stop and took part in another event on Saturday, called Lime bike Jousting 2: No Horses, No Mercy.

More than 5,000 people had registered their interest within a day of the invitation going online.

The organisers received police approval for the mass gathering and dropped the exact location coordinates just an hour and a half before the duel.

Hundreds of spectators descended on the park in an assortment of medieval finery and Hallowe’en fancy dress, transforming the east London park into a makeshift jousting arena.

Mr Carden said before the contest began: “This is a very special moment, not just for us, but for London... this is the most viewed joust of the modern era.”

The combatants were helped into their armour by their entourage before mounting their electric steeds, decorated for the occasion. “Ring maidens” in medieval dress set out the various rounds.

The pair battled through five rounds, with Mr Carnegie-Brown eventually claiming victory after landing the decisive blow.

Both Mr Carden and Mr Carnegie-Brown said that crowd safety was their “biggest priority” at the event. There were organising stewards to help with crowd control and health professionals on hand.

Hackney council said it did not give permission for the event to be held in the borough, but organisers claimed that they had informed the council that the event was going ahead with a full safety team.

The two “knights” competed in the duel for charity, raising more than £1,200.

The charities include The Bike Project, which fixes second-hand bikes and gives them to refugees, Honour Thy Woman Group, a domestic abuse charity, and the Mental Health Foundation.

There was even a seal of approval from the world of traditional jousting.

Andy Deane, the captain of the Royal Armouries jousting team in Leeds, said it was a “joy” to see the bike jousting “capturing the spectacle” of the medieval sport.

“This is absolutely a legitimate form of jousting,” he said following the first joust.

Mr Carden told The Telegraph: “We informed the council it was going ahead. We had a full safety team with first aiders, safety stewards, clean up crew, and had a chat with police before going ahead to ensure everything would be safe.

“We have been in touch with Lime from the first joust and they have at no point told us not to go ahead, merely to reinforce safety messages.”

Lime has been contacted for comment.

data.title: Buses to be driven by teenagers as operators face staff shortages
data.description:
Teenagers will be allowed to drive buses for school trips and weddings as part of a government shake-up to tackle shortages.

Ministers confirmed on Friday they were exploring changes to licensing rules that currently stop 18 and 19-year-olds from undertaking certain kinds of journeys.

Currently, they can qualify as bus and coach drivers, but operators can only assign them regular routes of less than 50 kilometres (31 miles).

The Department for Transport (DfT) wants to give teenagers the right to take on longer journeys and “non-regular” jobs as well, such as school trips, weddings, transport for football matches and holiday tours.

As well as tackling driver shortages, the DfT said the shake-up would provide more opportunities for young people at a time when around one million aged 16 to 24 are not in education, employment or training – also known as Neets.

However, the Government said it was also considering potential safety issues with young drivers more prone to being in accidents than their elders.

It acknowledged that only limited data were available on young bus drivers, but pointed to wider road transport data showing that nearly a quarter of collisions resulting in deaths last year involved drivers aged 17 to 24.

Simon Lightwood, the minister for buses and local transport, said: “We want to clear the roadblocks that have been preventing too many young people from getting behind the wheel of a rewarding career.

“The proposed changes will help more 18 and 19-year-olds get into the bus and coach sector, giving them the opportunity to build skills, earn a living and develop a rewarding career, while maintaining the highest standards of road safety.”

This came after ministers separately lowered the minimum age for train drivers in Britain from 20 to 18 earlier this year amid a youth worklessness crisis.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, has described the current number of jobless young people as an “economic catastrophe and moral failure”.

In consultation documents published on Friday, the DfT said there were an estimated 113,900 bus and coach drivers in the UK but only around 500 were aged 18 or 19.

Keith McNally, of the Confederation of Passenger Transport, which represents bus and coach operators, said the sector had also been battling a recruitment crisis since the Covid pandemic, which prompted some older drivers to retire while problems securing tests stopped new ones from qualifying.

“We’ve had shortages, so we think the opportunity to bring in more young people and let them experience what our industry has to offer is very positive,” he said.

The current rules “have some inconsistencies”, Mr McNally added, with teenage lorry-drivers not facing equivalent curbs.

At the moment, 18 and 19-year-olds can qualify as bus and coach drivers, but they are restricted to driving regular scheduled services of less than 31 miles.

This effectively means they can take on most local bus routes, school bus work and some inter-city services run by the likes of National Express and Flixbus.

However, it excludes them from school field-trips, football-team transport, weddings and other private-hire contracts.

Such non-regular services make up the majority of trips carried out by the coach sector, Mr McNally said.

He also sought to ease safety concerns by claiming that young drivers of buses and heavy goods vehicles are “just as safe as people who are older than them”.

“We don’t believe there are legitimate safety issues here, not least because of the training and selection processes that companies have got in place,” he said.

The Government’s consultation closes on Dec 18.

data.title: Former WH Smith chain TG Jones put up for sale
data.description:
Hundreds of shops once known as WH Smith have been put up for sale after its new owner rebranded them as TG Jones.

Modella Capital, which acquired the company last year for £42m, has appointed financial advisers from Teneo to handle the sale after receiving unsolicited approaches from potential buyers.

WH Smith was one of the best-known names on the high street for more than two centuries until it decided to split in two. Its bricks-and-mortar stores were sold to Modella, while WH Smith concentrated on its travel outlets at railway stations and airports.

However, rebranded as TG Jones, the old stores ran into tough trading with double-digit falls in sales as consumers reacted negatively to the newly invented brand.

Modella, which also owns the Hobbycraft and Flying Tiger brands, sought court permission for a sweeping restructuring plan to put the business on a sustainable footing that was approved in July.

This involved 150 store closures, rent cuts and holidays and a £15m cash injection from the owner. The chain now has around 350 outlets and employs around 3,500 people. The fall in sales is said to have stabilised.

A formal auction of the TG Jones business will not start until next year to avoid disruption during the crucial Christmas trading period, according to Sky News, which first reported the news.

The latest twist comes as another familiar high street name owned by private investors, Poundland, fights for survival.

The discount chain, controlled by US firm Gordon Brothers, won a 10-day stay of execution last week from an administration that could put more than 10,000 jobs at risk.

Around 200 Poundland stores have already closed in a restructuring.

TG Jones and Modella Capital said in a joint statement: “High-street retailer TG Jones has received unsolicited offers for the business; management and owner Modella Capital have jointly agreed to instruct Teneo corporate finance to review these offers and undertake a market-testing exercise.”

Alex Willson, the chief executive of TG Jones, said: “As ever, our focus is on providing a great experience for customers, especially with the critical Christmas period coming up.

“We continue to execute our turnaround plan, which is improving our performance month by month.

“We’re grateful to our fantastic colleagues for their commitment and to our suppliers, our owner and other stakeholders for their continued support.”

Joe Price, the managing director of Modella Capital, said: “When TG Jones was acquired in 2025, it was a loss-making business with an uncertain future.

“Turning it around meant taking some hard decisions, including closing stores through a court-approved restructuring plan.

“We are extremely grateful to our colleagues from across the business for their continued support.

“The turnaround is starting to deliver and we are seeing improved trading results.”

data.title: Burnham’s devolution drive to cost bus operator £260m
data.description:
One of Britain’s biggest bus operators stands to lose £260m from Andy Burnham’s move to hand increased powers to local mayors.

FirstGroup, which runs routes across the UK, said the figure represented lost revenue from services it operates in Wales and Yorkshire that are set to come under municipal control as part of the Prime Minister’s local transport crusade.

The UK is set to move away from privatisation to a bus franchising model whereby local authorities take over fleets and depots and then hire firms to operate them.

Graham Sutherland, FirstGroup’s chief executive, said a franchising model set to be rolled out would deliver lower margins, prompting the group to invest in more dependable markets such as coaches and London buses.

FirstGroup’s switch away from the regions highlights the risks of the Prime Minister’s decision to place buses at the heart of his devolution drive.

It was revealed in August that the West Midlands had been hit with a £30m bill after National Express chose to exit local buses completely in response to franchising, forcing the combined authority to buy out 1,400 vehicles and a network of depots.

FirstGroup’s renewed focus on London comes after it quit the capital in 2013 amid a clampdown by Transport for London (TfL) on the value of contracts.

It reversed the move in December 2024 – less than six months after Labour came to power – with the £90m takeover of RATP London, followed last year by the purchase of the Tootbus sightseeing fleet.

The firm now has more than 1,000 buses in London, with revenue this year expected to rise to £350m, an increase of 13pc.

Mr Sutherland said the franchising of buses in West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire and Wales would deprive FirstGroup of around 30pc of its £890m a year in regional bus revenue.

Industry-wide, he said firms faced a slump of £1.5bn a year in revenue in regions that had already announced their intention to move to franchising.

“We will have materially less regional buses in operation. We’ve diversified on the basis that these policy changes were going to impact our regional bus business,” he said.

“We’re still confident that over the next period of tranches we can continue to grow our bus business.”

FirstGroup said it would monitor plans announced by Lord Khan of Tooting for a new public company – Buses for London – which would compete in the capital, where a franchising model already operates but private firms are allowed to operate their own bus fleets and depots.

Mr Sutherland said: “It’s a handful of routes and a small part of the London network at this point. We don’t think it changes much in the short term and we’re confident that the costs and value we provide will stand up in comparison against any operator.”

Industry sources have called the proposals “mad” and “a Sadiq Khan vanity project” that would heap costs on TfL, which is £14bn in debt.

data.title: Burnham accused of dodging scrutiny after ditching press pack
data.description:
Andy Burnham has been accused of avoiding media scrutiny for not taking a full press contingent to two international conferences.

In an unusual move, the Prime Minister chose not to take the normal “press pack” to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda earlier this month, or to Cop31 in Turkey on Thursday.

Guto Harri, the former No 10 director of communications for Boris Johnson, said he had seen travelling to CHOGM with the pack as “loading the plane with a bunch of assassins determined to take out the PM I worked for, but that’s the deal”.

At the last CHOGM in 2024, Sir Keir Starmer took a full press contingent nearly 10,000 miles across the world to Samoa, and held both a press conference and an on-the-record grilling by journalists on the government plane.

Mr Harri said: “You sign up for scrutiny. You agree to be accountable. It’s at the heart of our democracy, and for someone as articulate as Andy Burnham to avoid the press on such an important occasion is not only a sign of weakness but concern.

“I appreciate he does a lot of communication, he does quite a lot of decent interviews, but his modus operandi seems increasingly to be to provide reasons for not answering, not to mention, more importantly, addressing the big questions that a leader needs to tackle, and that’s the one to watch.”

A government source said Mr Burnham had taken part in two pool interviews on Thursday, one in Turkey for COP31 and one in Dublin, as well as a huddle in Dublin where the Prime Minister took 16 questions, including one from The Telegraph.

CHOGM ended up dominating headlines, as the Prime Minister became embroiled in diplomatic clashes over the Commonwealth’s future relevance and slavery reparations.

It is not the first time Mr Burnham has appeared to avoid the press.

In June, the morning after Mr Burnham’s Makerfield by-election victory, he rallied supporters at Ashton Town football club’s ground but did not take questions from the press, nor did he at his scene-setting speech at the People’s History Museum in Manchester just over a week later.

The day he took office, Mr Burnham managed just four questions in seven minutes in an informal, unfilmed huddle with political editors in Downing Street’s Rose Garden before being ushered away for his first call with Donald Trump.

No 10 said it would rearrange the event, but did not, The Telegraph understands.

Government sources said Mr Burnham’s huddle on the first day showed that the Prime Minister’s first instinct was to speak to lobby journalists.

In a similar way to his predecessors, Mr Burnham was interviewed by broadcasters in the run-up to the Labour Party conference in September.

In an interview with ITV at the start of the month, he was asked whether he cared less than his predecessors about what the traditional media said about him. Mr Burnham replied: “Oh, definitely. Well, you see, I left Westminster for a reason.

“I got fed up with commentators deciding things down there, and then the whole world meant to believe what they believe. Well, sorry, the world’s not like that any more.”

Mr Burnham has been interviewed by TikTok and Instagram influencers. However, critics said he was “running away from being asked questions” by traditional journalists by choosing his own interviewers on social media.

Two weeks before he entered No 10, the future Prime Minister took to Reddit for an “Ask Me Anything” session, inviting users to send in their questions.

However, Mr Burnham chose to avoid queries on why the Government was “unable to do major infrastructure projects in this country” or whether he had plans to unfreeze income tax thresholds.

One Reddit user, after his question on “scandalous” student loans was left unanswered, wrote: “Oh Andy, you bottled it. At least we know what the next prime minister’s favourite films are I suppose.”

After his first Prime Minister’s Questions (PMQs), Mr Burnham took to answering social media questions for “People’s Major Questions”, which he called “the real PMQs”.

At the time, Kemi Badenoch, the Tory leader, told journalists: “I don’t need to use Reddit because I’m happy to take questions from the media.

“Andy Burnham, I’m amazed, was running away from being asked questions. Reddit is easy.”

Matt Vickers, the deputy chairman of the Conservative Party, told The Telegraph: “As mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham never met a camera he didn’t like. Now he’s Prime Minister, he’s gone into hiding.

“The Prime Minister has questions to answer about the tax rises and broken promises piling up on his watch. Social media skits are no substitute for serious scrutiny.

“If he cannot face a room of journalists, how on earth can he face the country?”

Industry sources also warned against the Government’s increasing use of so-called “vanity photographers”, who are employed by No 10 and instructed to take carefully staged photographs of politicians.

Sources told The Telegraph that greater use of internal photographers meant the public only saw a glimpse into the side of politics the Government wanted them to see, in contrast to the images typically taken by the traditional news media.

Some of the most widely distributed photographs surrounding the Budget were taken by No 10 PR photographers, including a prominently used photograph of John Healey’s selfie with his Treasury team.

Sir John Whittingdale, the chairman of the all-party parliamentary group on media freedom, told The Telegraph: “At a time of growing disinformation and social media influence, it is even more important to support professional journalism and mainstream media who can properly hold government to account.

“Access to the Prime Minister is an essential part of that and I hope Andy Burnham will follow the example of his predecessors in regularly making himself available.”

data.title: Nine steps to protect your money from a cyber attack
data.description:
From high street shops and online marketplaces to supermarket fridges, hackers have exposed how fragile our companies and systems are in a wide-ranging wave of recent cyber attacks.

While much of this is out of your control, you can at least take action to protect your money and personal information – and you don’t have to be particularly tech-savvy to do it.

Kiran Fothergill, of Sapphire Security Services, explained: “Think of it like securing your home. You wouldn’t leave your front door unlocked, hand your keys to a stranger or ignore a broken window. The same common sense should apply online.”

We’ve spoken to cyber security experts to explain the simple steps you can take today to make yourself a harder target for criminals.

1. Lock down your most important accounts

One of the first steps you should take is ensuring your most important accounts are secure.

Zain Javed, of cyber security platform Citation Cyber, said: “If you only make one change today, turn on two-factor authentication, particularly for your email, banking and social media accounts.

“This adds an extra layer of security, so even if a criminal steals your password, they will usually need another form of verification to access your account.”

With two-factor authentication, you’ll usually be asked for a second proof of identity when you sign in, such as a code sent to your phone or generated by an authenticator app.

Free authenticator apps include Duo Mobile, Microsoft Authenticator and Google Authenticator. Where available, using an app rather than receiving codes by text message is generally more secure, as text messages can be intercepted or diverted.

2. Don’t reuse passwords

Remembering umpteen different passwords across various websites isn’t easy. But resist the temptation to use the same password across multiple sites.

Doing so means that if one website has a data breach, criminals could try using your stolen login details to access your other accounts.

Instead, you could use a password manager, such as 1Password or Bitwarden, to generate and securely store unique passwords for different accounts.

Jonathan Lee, of cybersecurity platform TrendAI, said: “Pay particular attention to your personal email account. It can be the front door to much of your digital life, because access to your email may allow someone to reset passwords for other critical services you rely on.”

If passkeys are available on websites, these can be even better than traditional passwords. They let you sign in using your fingerprint, facial recognition or your screen lock PIN.

3. Protect your identity

Your personal information is valuable to criminals, so it’s worth taking steps to protect it.

Mr Fothergill said: “Identity protection services can help you monitor your personal information and identify potential exposure or suspicious activity.

“They aren’t a guarantee against identity theft, but they can provide an additional early warning and help you respond more quickly.”

However, you might not need to pay for a specialist service.

Paul Bischoff, of research company Comparitech, said: “Identity protection apps don’t do much that you can’t do yourself, such as monitoring bank accounts and credit. For most of us, these apps are mainly a convenience.”

Instead, you can take some simple steps such as regularly checking your bank and credit card statements for unfamiliar transactions, checking your free credit report for accounts you don’t recognise, and being alert to unexpected password reset emails.

4. Don’t give personal details to AI

With increasing numbers of people turning to AI to ask for advice on everything from medical issues to personal finance, you need to think carefully about the information you share.

Tom Vazdar, of Open Institute of Technology, said: “Treat an AI chatbot like a stranger with a very good memory. Conversations may be stored, read by reviewers or leaked. Don’t type in passwords, bank details, ID documents, medical records or work files.”

Also check your provider’s privacy settings as not all AI platforms handle data in the same way.

Charles Radclyffe, of EA Global AI, said: “Consumer AI tools may use user interactions to help improve and train their models, so users should think carefully before sharing personal information.”

5. Don’t ignore app and device updates

Another simple but important step is to ensure you have turned on automatic updates on your phone, laptop, web browser and apps. It can pay to keep the built-in security features on your devices switched on, too.

Mr Javed said: “Those software update notifications we all put off are actually one of the simplest ways to protect ourselves.

“Cybercriminals regularly exploit known weaknesses in outdated software. Manufacturers release updates to fix these vulnerabilities, but those fixes only protect you once they’re installed.”

6. Guard your bank account

Scammers are finding ever more convincing ways to part people from their cash, which makes it even more important to be on your guard.

Mr Javed said: “The days of spotting a scam because of poor spelling or bad grammar are disappearing. AI means criminals can now write convincing messages and even imitate familiar voices.”

To protect yourself, agree a family code word and ask for it if someone calls asking for money.

Mr Fothergill added: “Criminals are very good at creating a sense of urgency. You might receive a text claiming there’s suspicious activity on your bank account or a telephone call warning that your money is at risk. The golden rule is never to act under pressure.”

This means never clicking on links in unexpected messages or sharing passwords, Pins or security codes with someone who contacts you. If you’re unsure, always hang up and contact your bank directly using the number on the website or through the official app.

Remember, your bank will never ask for your Pin or account details or request you transfer money into a so-called “safe account”.

7. Stick to familiar websites

When shopping online, stick to trusted websites you’ve used before. Criminals can create convincing copies of genuine websites, so check the web address carefully before entering any personal or payment details.

Even if the website has a padlock symbol or “https” address, this doesn’t mean the website is safe.

You should also be wary of adverts and offers that seem too good to be true.

Jamie Akhtar, of cybersecurity platform CyberSmart, said: “Cybercriminals are quick to exploit trending topics, using the excitement surrounding popular games, new film releases and other cultural moments to trick unsuspecting users into clicking malicious links or downloading harmful content.

“If you receive a message promising exclusive access, early releases or special offers, take a moment to verify that it comes from a legitimate source before clicking any links or sharing personal information.”

8. Delete apps you don’t use

Most of us have far too many apps on our phones, so it’s worth having a digital clear out every so often.

The more apps and services you give access to your personal information, the more potential ways there are for it to be exposed if an account or company is compromised.

Art Gilliland, of cyber firm Delinea, said: “Check which apps you’ve allowed to read your emails, see your contacts or access your files. Remove connections you no longer use. Don’t forget that deleting an app from your phone doesn’t necessarily cancel its access.”

It’s also worth reviewing the permissions of the apps you keep and switching off access to your camera, microphone, location or contacts if they don’t need it.

9. Regularly back-up files

Finally, don’t forget to back-up files on your phone or laptop. Doing this means you’ll still have access to important information if your device is damaged, lost or compromised in a cyber attack.

You can do this using a trusted cloud service or an external drive that isn’t permanently connected to your computer.

Mr Fothergill said: “Cyber attacks aren’t always about stealing money. Ransomware and malicious software can also lock you out of family photographs, important documents and personal records.”

Try to back-up your files regularly and check you can restore them if needed.

data.title: Fraud office brings charges over ‘Britain’s biggest Ponzi scheme’
data.description:
Britain’s fraud squad has brought charges against an investment scam believed to be the country’s biggest Ponzi scheme.

The Serious Fraud Office (SFO) has charged eight individuals in connection with the 2019 collapse of London Capital & Finance (LCF), which led to an estimated £251m in losses for 11,200 investors.

They include Michael Thomson, LCF’s former chief executive, and Simon Hume-Kendall, the former chairman of London Oil & Gas – the main company that LCF lent money to before its collapse – who have been charged with conspiracy to defraud.

Four other executives – Elten Barker, Paul Careless, Robert Sedgwick and John Russell-Murphy – have been hit with the same charge, while Helen Hume-Kendall, Simon’s wife, has been charged with concealing criminal property.

An eighth defendant has been charged with conspiracy to defraud and acting in contravention of a director disqualification undertaking. It is understood that this individual’s legal team will make an application for anonymity at the first court hearing.

All eight defendants are set to appear before Westminster magistrates’ court on Dec 7.

The High Court in 2024 ruled that LCF amounted to a Ponzi scheme after executives fraudulently collected hundreds of millions of pounds from retail investors through “widespread, fundamental and systematic” misrepresentations.

Bosses were found to have spent investors’ cash on lavish purchases, including helicopters, diamond earrings, horses, shotguns and membership of Annabel’s nightclub.

LCF, which was based in Tunbridge Wells, raised money by selling mini-bonds to retail investors with the promise of high returns.

The High Court previously found that LCF presented itself as a commercial lender to borrowers in the small and medium-sized business sector.

In reality, however, it had no independent source of income and relied “almost entirely” on bringing in new investors.

The court heard that one of the executives compared another to Bernie Madoff, the disgraced Wall Street financier who led the largest Ponzi scheme in history, defrauding investors of an estimated $65bn (£49.3bn).

A Ponzi scheme, named after con artist Charles Ponzi, is a scam where an operator pays apparent profits to earlier investors using funds from new investors.

The City watchdog has since banned the mass marketing of speculative, illiquid securities – including mini-bonds – to retail investors.

Emma Isaac at the SFO said: “Thousands of investors believed backing London Capital & Finance would yield high returns. Instead, they lost over £250m.

“Today’s charges mark a significant step forward in our investigation into the collapse of the firm and [in] ensuring those responsible are held to account.”

data.title: FTSE energy giant quits North Sea over tax raids
data.description:
A British energy giant has quit the North Sea after Labour’s windfall taxes and drilling bans made its operations unviable.

EnQuest, which is listed on the London stock market, said on Wednesday that it had sold its entire UK operation to Neo Next+, a relative newcomer to the North Sea, for a knock-down price of $960m (£730m).

It plans to move its investments to south-east Asia after quitting British waters.

The FTSE 250 company’s UK operations include the giant Magnus and Kraken fields, 1,000 km of key subsea pipelines and the Sullom Voe terminal in Shetland.

EnQuest’s decision follows an industry backlash against John Healey’s decision to keep a windfall tax on North Sea oil and gas profits in place until 2030 despite pressure to scrap it.

Labour’s initial extension of the windfall tax from 2028 to 2030 under Ed Miliband left EnQuest facing a $124m bill, it revealed on Wednesday, pushing the company into a $2m loss for the year.

This was in addition to an $84m bill it paid in 2025, which was much higher than expected after Labour abolished some tax allowances. The windfall tax added another $24m to its tax bill in the first half of this year, alongside $28m in other levies.

Amjad Bseisu, EnQuest’s chief executive, blamed an “uncertain investment environment within the UK”.

The company said it would instead focus on its operations in south-east Asia, aiming to recycle “invested capital from a high-tax, low-return basin into a high-growth region that is structurally short on energy”.

EnQuest’s decision means Neo Next+ will consolidate its position as the North Sea’s largest oil and gas producer.

John Knight, the founder and executive chair of the private equity firm, said: “The addition of EnQuest’s UK oil and gas business further strengthens our scale and resilience in the UK North Sea, while adding production, reserves and cash flow to our portfolio.”

EnQuest is among the UK’s top producers of oil and gas, producing the equivalent of 31,000 barrels of oil a day last year with reserves approaching another 500 million barrels.

Its untapped Bressay and Bentley fields are among the largest in UK waters, capable of producing up to 600 million barrels of oil.

Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, said: “The devastating news that EnQuest is withdrawing from the UK is the latest sign that this Government’s policies on oil and gas are hanging a ‘closed for business’ sign over the North Sea.

“We are in the midst of an energy crisis but Labour is still banning licences and maintaining windfall taxes. We need to open the North Sea, abolish the windfall tax and get Britain drilling.”

EnQuest is is the latest energy firm to leave UK waters over Labour’s windfall tax. BP has also announced plans to sell all its UK offshore assets, with the final date for bids due in early December.

Meg O’Neill, BP’s boss, linked the decision to the UK tax regime.

data.title: Nscale investigates ties to blacklisted tech companies
data.description:
The British AI company Nscale is investigating links to a company on a US blacklist after a trade crackdown by Donald Trump.

Nscale said in stock market filings that it was examining a supplier’s ties to the entity list, which bars companies considered a national security risk from accessing US technology.

Separate disclosures show the company’s flagship data centre in Norway is furnished with equipment from Aivres and Kaytus, two companies owned by a blacklisted Chinese tech conglomerate.

The disclosures come as the Nvidia spying scandal prompts calls for new measures to restrict China from obtaining US technology.

The two suppliers, based in the US and Singapore respectively, have been accused of supplying Megaspeed, the Singaporean company at the centre of the Jensen Huang row, with billions of dollars of Nvidia chips.

They are subsidiaries of Inspur, a tech company majority owned by the Chinese state that was placed on the US entity list in 2023. The scandal has led to calls for Aivres to be shut off from acquiring American technology.

Nscale is spending billions of dollars to build data centres providing AI chips to the likes of Microsoft and Anthropic. It disclosed the potential link to a blacklisted company in US filings before a potential $35bn (£27bn) stock market debut.

The company, whose directors include Sir Nick Clegg, the former deputy prime minister, warned that a US trade crackdown could affect supplies of computing equipment needed for a substantial data-centre building spree.

The entity list, operated by the US commerce department’s bureau of industry and security (BIS), is designed to prevent companies from obtaining sensitive US technology such as advanced microchips.

Inspur was put on the entity list in 2023 for seeking to acquire US technology to aid the Chinese military. IEIT, an associated company listed as Aivres’ parent, was put on the list in 2025 for developing supercomputers with the goal of helping China’s military.

Inspur rebranded its US business as Aivres shortly after being added to the list, allowing it to continue acquiring Nvidia chips and other US technology.

The White House last year introduced an “affiliate rule” extending the crackdown to foreign subsidiary companies, but recently delayed enforcement of the rule until January.

Purchases from the two companies are not illegal and Nscale obtained the equipment through an IT reseller, rather than through a direct relationship with the companies, filings show.

Aivres has been accused of sending billions in Nvidia chips to Megaspeed. Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy with whom Mr Huang reportedly had an affair, was an executive at Megaspeed, which is under investigation over concerns it was used to smuggle chips to China.

There is no suggestion of a link between Megaspeed and Nscale.

Aivres, which has been a key Nvidia partner, has also supplied large numbers of AI servers to Singapore-based Aolani, which intends to rent them to Chinese AI company ByteDance, according to reports.

ByteDance was also Nscale’s biggest customer last year, although deals with Microsoft and Anthropic have since surpassed the Chinese company.

US senators Lisa Blunt Rochester, a Democrat, and John Curtis, a Republican, last week urged the commerce department to cut off Aivres from buying US technology.

In US filings, Nscale said: “We have identified potential exposure within our OEM supply chain involving a supplier with reported ownership links to entities on the BIS Entity List.

“We are continuing to assess the relevant ownership structure and potential implications of reinstatement of the affiliates rule, including whether any additional licensing obligations could arise in respect of future transactions or affect procurement and supply-chain continuity.”

It said application of the affiliates rule could mean “requiring us to modify or terminate contractual arrangements, delay or cancel projects, or decline new business in order to remain compliant”. It did not name the supplier it was examining.

Nscale is considering whether to press ahead with a New York Stock Exchange listing that could be one of the biggest ever involving a UK tech company. However, it has been buffeted by a market sell-off exacerbated by the departure of Mr Huang from Nvidia, and is considering delaying the listing.

It recently warned that it needed to raise more cash to fulfil promises made to major customers. Microsoft also cancelled a deal for Nscale’s UK data centre, The Telegraph revealed last month.

Nscale declined to comment. Aivres did not respond to a request for comment.

data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.title: AstraZeneca dumped by investors over £300bn US merger talks
data.description:
AstraZeneca shares have taken an £18bn hit after investors baulked at reports it was plotting a mega-merger with a US rival.

Shares in Britain’s second-most valuable company slumped on Monday after it emerged that AstraZeneca had held talks about a potential $400bn (£300bn) tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb.

If completed, the merger would create one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical businesses. The potential deal would also raise fears that AstraZeneca could shift its business to the US in a blow to Britain.

However, analysts said it was a high-risk deal that risked destroying more value than it created. It would be one of the biggest mergers of all time, meaning any missteps could prove hugely costly, and would be likely to draw the attention of competition regulators and politicians.

News of the talks, first reported by the Financial Times, sent AstraZeneca’s shares plunging 9pc on Monday to their lowest level since September 2025.

Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Union Investment and an ‌AstraZeneca ⁠shareholder, told Reuters: “A combination with Bristol ​does not make strategic or financial sense.

“Many past mega-mergers have destroyed value and there is no apparent need for Astra to do it.”

Jefferies analysts said in a note: “If there is ​one company that doesn’t need financial engineering, it’s AstraZeneca.”

Michael Leuchten, an analyst at Jefferies, said he was “perplexed” by the potential takeover. He said investors backed the company because of its consistent sales growth, not because management “go out and do big deals”.

AstraZeneca is worth around £184bn on the London Stock Exchange, while New York-listed Bristol Myers Squibb has a market value of $133bn.

Bristol Myers Squibb shares surged as much as 3.8pc on Wall Street on Monday.

Analysts said competition concerns would be the biggest hurdle to a deal as both companies have large cancer treatment businesses.

The potential deal could also trigger a political backlash from Donald Trump’s administration, Jefferies warned.

Mr Leuchten added: “AstraZeneca would effectively be a UK-based acquirer of one of America’s large Pharmas, at a time when US policymakers are focused on domestic manufacturing and strategic industries.”

The deal would raise questions about AstraZeneca’s continued links to Britain as Sir Pascal Soriot, its chief executive, pushes ahead with a pivot towards the US.

AstraZeneca upgraded its listing on the New York Stock Exchange last September to let American investors buy its shares directly, while keeping its listing in London.

The move put AstraZeneca’s New York listing on a par with that of London, in what was seen as a blow to the UK’s struggling stock market.

AstraZeneca subsequently struck a $50bn deal with the Trump administration to invest in US manufacturing and transatlantic research facilities.

At the time, Sir Pascal described the drugmaker as a “very American company”.

The business subsequently agreed to sell some medicines at a discount to the US Medicaid programme to avoid being hit with tariffs.

Despite this, Britain’s biggest drugmaker has insisted that it intends to remain headquartered in Cambridge and retain its listing on the London Stock Exchange.

Mr Leuchten said buying Bristol Myers Squibb as a way to shift permanently to the US would be “a fairly drastic way to go about it”.

However, Neil Birrell, the chief investment officer at Premier Miton, an AstraZeneca shareholder, said the likelihood of the pharmaceutical business shifting its shares to the US would increase if the Bristol Myers Squibb deal went ahead.

Mr Birrell added: “There hasn’t been a huge amount that I’ve seen coming out from any of the authorities – whether it be the Government or the London Stock Exchange – of any great substance to try and keep these sort of companies here.”

The Prime Minister said the talks were “a private matter for the companies involved”.

A No 10 spokesman said: “More broadly, the UK life sciences sector is one of our greatest national assets, driving innovation, skilled employment and investment across the country while developing medicines that improve health outcomes and save lives.”

AstraZeneca has around 10,000 staff at five UK sites, including 4,000 at its main facilities in Cambridge and Macclesfield and another 2,000 in London and Luton.

Steve Boden, a regional organiser at GMB Union, said he was seeking urgent assurances from AstraZeneca that jobs would be protected.

“These reports of a merger are causing great concern amongst AstraZeneca’s loyal workers. While no deal has been formally announced, mergers can create pressure to cut costs, so staff are understandably worrying about what this could mean for them.”

The proposed mega-merger will evoke memories of Pfizer’s attempts to take over AstraZeneca a decade ago.

The US company’s acquisition ultimately collapsed after a wave of resistance from the board and politicians alike.

Ed Miliband, then Labour leader, said at the time that Pfizer’s assurances about protecting research and saving jobs were “worthless”.

Bristol Myers Squibb is headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and was started in 1858, making it one of the US’s oldest pharmaceutical companies.

data.title: Deutsche handled almost $600m of suspicious payments linked to Epstein
data.description:
Germany’s largest bank handled nearly $600m (£455m) of suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein, a figure far higher than previously thought.

Epstein was a long-standing client of Deutsche Bank, the country’s largest and best-known lender, after the bank took him on in 2013, despite his 2008 conviction for soliciting prostitution from a minor.

Internal documents show that Deutsche filed suspicious activity reports (SARs) in the US in 2019 identifying $582m of money transfers – more than double the amount previously known.

SARs are confidential alerts that banks must file with the authorities when they suspect a payment or customer could be linked to money laundering, fraud or other financial crime.

The SARs covered payments to women and suspected misuse of charitable donations, the Financial Times (FT) reported.

The value of the transfers is substantially higher than the sum disclosed in August after an investigation by the US Senate finance committee.

Investigators for US Senator Ron Wyden, who wrote the committee’s report, said at the time that Deutsche had flagged more than $250m in suspicious wire transfers flowing in and out of Epstein’s accounts.

The difference could reflect the wider scope of Deutsche’s investigation, which covered about 3,200 payments, the FT said.

The revelations emerged on Tuesday following the leak by whistleblowers of about 15 million internal files from Deutsche.

After he was forced out by JPMorgan Chase in 2013, Epstein followed his long-standing banker to Deutsche Bank.

The paedophile financier’s banker estimated that the relationship could eventually generate $2m to $4m a year from cash transfers of $100m to $300m or more, the FT said, but in reality it was worth far less.

The lender decided to terminate its relationship with Epstein only at the end of 2018, when renewed media coverage drew attention to his sexual abuse of girls and young women.

Epstein was found dead in his US jail cell in 2019.

Shares in Deutsche fell 6pc on Tuesday after the FT’s revelations from the whistleblower leak.

Deutsche has paid more than $200m in fines and settlements for its past dealings with Epstein without admitting wrongdoing.

The anonymous whistleblowers said in a statement that they were motivated by the “public interest”, adding that the bank needed a “complete overhaul in management and culture”.

A spokesman for Deutsche said: “As we said in 2020, the bank acknowledges its error of onboarding Epstein in 2013 and regrets our historical connection with him.

“We have cooperated with regulatory and law enforcement agencies and the US Congress regarding their investigations, and have been transparent in addressing these matters in parallel.”

data.title: Hundreds of pharmacies face closure from Labour tax raid
data.description:
Hundreds of pharmacies are facing closure because of soaring business rates, with owners warning that high taxes are forcing them to cut services for vulnerable patients.

Almost half of the 420 pharmacy owners surveyed by the National Pharmacy Association (NPA) said they were considering shutting down their practices because of higher business rates bills.

The trade body warned that pharmacies, many of which are family-run businesses, are unable to offset the higher tax burden by raising prices, which are fixed by the NHS.

The NPA found 55pc of pharmacy operators were considering moving to cheaper premises, raising fears that some rural and coastal communities could be left without a local branch.

Andy Burnham has made lowering business rates for high-street businesses a key pillar of his summer policy blitz, announcing a 20pc reduction for pubs, clubs and live music venues from April next year.

However, pharmacies have been excluded from the relief.

The tax squeeze has intensified since business rates were increased for many properties after Rachel Reeves’s second Budget. Bills have also been affected by the latest revaluation of commercial property.

GPs and NHS dentists, meanwhile, have their business rates reimbursed.

Pharmacies are particularly exposed because most of their income comes from the NHS, meaning they cannot simply raise prices to cover higher costs. Roughly 90pc of pharmacies’ income comes from the health service, the NPA said.

Onkar Singh, who runs 20 pharmacies across the Black Country, Staffordshire, Herefordshire and Worcestershire, has seen his business rates bill rise by roughly 20pc to 30pc in the past year. His total bill is now about £250,000.

He has closed two of his pharmacies in the past two years and reduced opening hours across virtually his entire estate. He has also been forced to cut back services, such as offering free medicine deliveries to elderly patients.

Mr Singh said: “The last three years have been the worst period in my 30 years of pharmacy.

“People are having to close a lifetime’s worth of work and effort, and having to close or reduce hours or dip into their pension pot just to keep going for their communities.”

The NPA survey found that 92pc of pharmacies said their rates bill was preventing them from investing in their workforce or renovations. Some pharmacists have warned that their bills have tripled.

Mr Singh said the impact was particularly painful because pharmacies were often being asked to fill gaps elsewhere in the NHS.

He said: “It is frustrating that pubs and restaurants get the headlines, but pharmacies are actually delivering care.

“The NHS accepted that pharmacy did an exceptional job, but in terms of funding and support with business rates we seem to be forgotten.”

The NPA said 44 pharmacies had already closed this year, leaving the national network at its smallest since 2006.

Nine in 10 council areas have lost at least one pharmacy since 2022.

Olivier Picard, the chairman of the trade group, said pharmacies should receive the same rates treatment as GPs and dentists, arguing that they provide an essential health service.

A government spokesperson said: “Pharmacies already benefit from our wider business rates reforms, including permanently lower multipliers and our £4.3bn package to support ratepayers – and the government has increased funding for the sector by £340m this year as part of our shift to bring care closer to home.”
