data.title: The West is hooked on Chinese drugs but they could save your life
data.description:
Sir Keir Starmer’s decision to invite Sir Pascal Soriot, AstraZeneca’s chief executive, to Beijing at the beginning of the year was a textbook piece of modern diplomacy.

The then-prime minister’s attempt to revive economic cooperation rested on a knockout deal that went beyond the usual warm words. Sir Pascal, a sworn Sinophile and one of the biggest cheerleaders of Chinese innovation, was only too happy to oblige.

Within hours of Sir Keir’s arrival, AstraZeneca had unveiled a plan to invest $15bn (£11bn) in China, building on its existing medical manufacturing and research capabilities in Beijing, Shanghai, Wuxi, Taizhou and Qingdao.

AstraZeneca’s pledge was the marquee announcement of Sir Keir’s trip. Sir Pascal said the “landmark investment” marked the next chapter for the company in China. For the politburo, it was further proof that their plan to turn China into a global pharmaceuticals leader has worked.

In the West, China has long been dismissed as little more than a dealer in cheap copycat medicines – both legal and illegal – and increasingly knockoffs too, such as unlicensed GLP-1 weight loss medication.

This portrayal no longer bears scrutiny, however. In recent years, the Chinese pharmaceutical industry has undergone a remarkable reinvention. Western industry leaders view it as a bona fide drug superpower at the forefront of discovery.

China controls an exciting pipeline of groundbreaking medicines and occupies a growing role as a globally important venue for clinical trials.

But for now, cooperation between East and West suits both sides. European and American drugmakers have rushed to embrace Chinese research, forging multi-billion licensing deals. Those with the appetite have opened their own labs and even set up manufacturing outposts.

Chinese science is now “the best in the world” and ignoring it is not an option, says one European pharmaceuticals chairman.

Few have led the charge as enthusiastically as Sir Pascal, AstraZeneca’s swashbuckling French boss. China is now its second-biggest market. Meanwhile GSK, the UK’s other national drug champion, has struck a series of partnerships with Chinese labs to licence promising drugs outside the country.

These relationships are critical for China’s pharmaceuticals industry, providing access to the lucrative markets that fund innovation. At home, their only customer is Xi Jinping, and he sets the price.

Yet this partnership is fragile. Amid growing concern in the US about the threat China’s new scientific prowess poses to drug supplies, innovation and even national security, industry executives fear an iron curtain will be drawn.

Drugs may be the next front in the superpower trade war that has already drawn in telecoms equipment, semiconductors, electric vehicles, rare earth minerals and solar panels.

For Europe, including Britain’s pharmaceutical giants AstraZeneca and GSK, the looming nightmare is that an American administration will sooner or later use its economic muscle to effectively outlaw their cooperation with China.

One senior figure says the possibility of a sweeping American crackdown is “probably the one question that keeps me awake at night”.

China’s rapid scientific progress

Dr Zhao Hong, a renowned Chinese cancer specialist, shocked thousands of Communist Party delegates in March last year: a Guangzhou-based biotech firm had developed a cancer drug that had outperformed the world’s bestselling equivalent in clinical trials.

The work of China’s Akeso Biopharma, lung cancer drug ivonescimab had shown that it could delay non-small-cell lung cancer progression for five months longer than US giant Merck’s Keytruda treatment – the world’s bestselling prescription drug in 2025.

The success of ivonescimab was hailed as a breakthrough moment for China’s pharmaceutical industry.

“China is at the best time of its biopharmaceutical sector’s development,” Hong told state media at the annual Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference.

The speed with which China is catching up in pharmaceuticals and biotech is astonishing.

By 2024, China had 1,255 drugs at the research stage, a nearly eight-fold jump in less than a decade. America had 1,441 – a 15pc rise – while the total in Europe had shrunk slightly to 400.

Experts attribute the leap to a fundamental shift in how the industry was perceived by the Chinese regime.

One veteran UK executive recalls how when he first used to visit China in the late 1990s, it was to complain about “counterfeits and pharmaceuticals that were really dangerous”. Today, China is seen as “a golden opportunity”, he says.

“They have moved deliberately to be at the leading edge of science,” he adds.

Beijing has provided vast support in the form of scores of state-financed biotechnology parks equipped with advanced laboratories and heavily subsidised hardware, together with a sweeping overhaul of the regulatory system beginning in 2015.

A study by Prof Yimin Cui, of Peking University, and colleagues found that the time taken to approve a drug for human trials fell to 87 days after the reforms, from 501 days previously.

Chinese researchers are helped by the sheer size of the country’s population – last counted at more than 1.4 billion – says Freddy Yip, a corporate lawyer at Cooley.

“In the US, it may take a long time to recruit sufficient patients, but in China, you have access to lots of different patients with different kinds of diseases, including many rare diseases,” Yip says.

Sir Pascal has said this combination of scientific capability and rapid execution – “China speed”, as he has called it – can help to dramatically accelerate drug development.

One of China’s leading biotech venture capitalists estimates clinical trials are “two thirds cheaper and half as quick in China”.

Progress has been spurred by a massive increase in spending on research and development – leaping from $35m in 2015 to $15bn in 2023 – and a “reverse brain drain” in which thousands of foreign-educated Chinese scientists and entrepreneurs have returned home, according to Porsche Consulting.

Chinese scientists are now at the vanguard of treatment for cardiovascular diseases and cancer, as well as spearheading drug development for metabolic conditions and neurological disorders, such as Parkinson’s, among many others.

Alarm bells in Washington

Mere months before Sir Pascal was lending heft to Sir Keir’s Beijing bridge-building mission, the Frenchman was being warmly welcomed at the Oval Office by Donald Trump.

Thanking the US president for welcoming him “in this beautiful office”, Sir Pascal was armed with another crowd-pleasing announcement: a pledge to cut drug prescription prices in the US, after Trump had accused other countries of “freeloading” at the expense of Americans.

Sir Pascal went further as well, unveiling a $50bn plan to expand the company’s existing operations in the US. In return, AstraZeneca received a three-year exemption from tariffs.

Privately, AstraZeneca executives acknowledge it was also an attempt to ward off growing concern in the White House about the deepening of ties with China.

“We are cognisant of some of the more hawkish commentary [from US politicians]. It is a delicate balancing act, and we are treading a fine line by recognising what the US is trying to achieve,” an insider says.

Yet, for all Washington’s alarm, dependency has become more pronounced, not less. Western companies have piled into the country, hoovering up clinical trial data and striking licensing deals to develop Chinese medicines outside the mainland, which they hope can then be used to treat patients across the developed world.

“This is the golden age of science and China is white-hot right now,” an industry source says.

Deal activity is being driven by anxiety among European and US companies as their pipeline of drugs peters out.

America’s biotech industry faces the alarming prospect of an estimated $350bn worth of medicines – equivalent to roughly one fifth of projected global prescription-drug revenue – losing patent protection by the end of the decade.

When patents run out, generic rivals are allowed to gatecrash the market, jeopardising sales.

Few have led the way with the verve that AstraZeneca has demonstrated.

Sir Pascal’s Beijing announcement was accompanied by a boast that it had signed 16 global licensing agreements with 15 Chinese partners since 2023 alone – thought to be the most of any overseas pharmaceuticals multi-national.

GSK hasn’t been far behind. Last year, the company struck an alliance with local giant Hengrui Pharma to develop a dozen new medicines outside the mainland. The value of the deal could eventually total $12bn.

The agreements are part of an industry-wide surge in deals totalling $138bn last year – a nearly tenfold jump since 2021 – according to data provider PharmCube. 2026 is expected to be another record.

Deal flow shows little sign of slowing.

A fortnight ago, GSK unveiled a $1.3bn pact with Hutchmed, a Hong Kong-based biopharmaceuticals company with research facilities in Shanghai, for the bulk of the licensing rights to what it called “first in-class” cancer treatments.

Brewing geopolitical storm

Amid the feeding frenzy, concern in Washington has turned to outright hostility in some quarters.

In December last year, Trump signed into law the Biosecure Act, a move widely seen as a sharp escalation in tensions and the moment the longstanding strategic rivalry between the US and China spilt into the biotechnology arena.

The act prevents US companies reliant on federal contracts and funding from working with Chinese biotech firms with ties to the Chinese military and any deemed to pose a national security risk. It also bars Chinese companies from accessing US government funding themselves.

US biotechnology companies with federal contracts are now engaged in a mad dash to purge their supply chains of equipment obtained from any Chinese biotechnology firms on the banned list.

Next up is the Biotech Investment National Security Act. Though not yet signed into law, it will subject licensing deals involving Chinese companies to national security reviews.

Though technically a screening mechanism rather than a ban on licensing Chinese drugs, it will effectively function as one, says Craig Garthwaite, a professor at Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management.

There is also pressure to bar the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) from accepting Chinese trial data, amid concerns about their reliability. The FDA has repeatedly rejected one of Hengrui’s cancer drugs, citing questions about quality control at its manufacturing sites.

As one senior City figure puts it: the White House has conjured up other reasons to “erect a wall around China”.

AstraZeneca’s attempt to navigate this geopolitical storm by investing in both China and the US divides opinion. Some see it as an inspired way to keep both Washington and Beijing happy at the same time.

“I think Pascal has been very smart in not allowing anybody to question his US credentials. He’s playing his cards very wisely,” the boss of a rival company says.

Others see it as a high-stakes gamble from a company that is more exposed than most of its competitors and has learnt the hard way the risks that come from operating in China.

Leon Wang, the former head of its Chinese operations, is awaiting trial on charges of illegal trading, unlawful collection of personal information and medical insurance fraud, alongside another former employee, having been arrested in 2024.

If the saga made Sir Pascal reconsider his appetite for doing business in China, there is little sign of it.

Alongside licensing deals potentially worth tens of billions of dollars, it has around 17,000 employees in China, two “global strategic” research and development centres in Beijing and Shanghai, and four advanced manufacturing sites in Wuxi, Taizhou, Qingdao and Beijing.

China is now AstraZeneca’s second-largest market after the US, accounting for roughly 12pc of the company’s global turnover, and its Chinese facilities supply more than 70 markets worldwide.

In a written submission to the Commons business and trade select committee in July, AstraZeneca described co-operation with China as a “win-win”.

But as one investor with extensive interests in China points out: “If you’re a big pharma company with a significant proportion of your licensing spend coming from China and the tap suddenly gets turned off, that’s obviously a problem.”

Europe’s wary response

Despite sharply rising tensions, there are concerns that European policymakers are still a long way off from having a coherent industrial strategy that addresses the China question.

Having been slow to react to the threat that cheap Chinese manufacturing poses to the continent’s steelmakers, solar panel producers and its car industry, the risk is that the pendulum swings too far the other way and Brussels takes a similarly antagonistic approach in trying to shut China out of other sectors, such as pharmaceuticals.

Calls by Oliver Blume, the chief executive of Volkswagen, for tougher trade measures against Beijing have been interpreted in some circles as a signal that EU-China relations are close to a tipping point after years of resistance to anti-Chinese duties from the continent’s car giants.

Yet, a senior industrialist says Europe lacks the “economic counterweight to be able to exclude China”.

“I don’t necessarily think it’s good in the long term for the US to do so, but I think it’s very dangerous for Europe,” he adds.

“We need a more nuanced industrial strategy that seeks Chinese expertise and cost effectiveness, and to somehow bring some of the economic benefit of that into Europe,” he says.

Such sentiment echoes a growing willingness among car manufacturers to partner with Chinese counterparts amid an onslaught of imports. Nissan’s decision to share its Sunderland plant with Chery, one of China’s largest car exporters, is expected to be among the first of many similar tie-ups.

Some believe the growing divide between Washington and Beijing because of pharmaceuticals may even present an opportunity for Europe.

“I’m sure Europe would be more than happy to take Chinese-developed products that are sold to them at a lower price than what they might otherwise get from the United States,” Garthwaite says.

As Brussels bureaucrats try to agree on a co-ordinated approach, the rhetoric, particularly among some influential Republicans, continues to harden.

Chris Klomp, a top lieutenant of Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, has likened the situation to “a war”.

Anxiety has been heightened by a so-called “hot mic” incident at a Beijing military parade late last year, in which Vladimir Putin and Xi were overheard discussing the possibility that humans could live to 150 years old, thanks to advances in biotechnology.

Some China hawks saw it as further evidence that the US risked falling behind in the global race for domination in advanced science.

The Council on Foreign Relations, an influential American think tank, has called for reliance on China’s biotech know-how to be treated as a strategic vulnerability akin to critical minerals.

“The US (and just about every other nation) faces a growing risk that China will deliberately withhold essential pharmaceutical inputs as a tool of economic or political coercion … as China has done with rare-earth critical minerals,” it warned in June.

The Atlantic Council, another US think tank with a history of shaping American foreign policy, points out that the US is reliant on China for three quarters of some imported drugs and as much as 99pc of some raw materials that are critical to the production of certain key medicines.

What’s more, China’s 2020 export control law and 2021 biosecurity law “grant broad authority to weaponise pharmaceutical exports”, it said recently.

‘All in or all out’

AstraZeneca declined to comment on its position, but there are signs it is more nervous than it is willing to acknowledge.

It emerged in August that the company had held detailed discussions with American rival Bristol Myers Squibb about a potential £300bn mega-merger.

In seeking to substantially deepen its US footprint, AstraZeneca may have concluded that the best chance it has of escaping any crackdown is if the company can demonstrate it is willing to take action to address Trump’s demands for the “reshoring” of pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Radical corporate restructuring plans have also been explored in China. AstraZeneca previously looked at the possibility of carving out its Chinese business into a separate legal entity and listing it on the Shanghai stock exchange. Though nothing came of those plans, they were seen as an attempt to insulate it from mounting geopolitical tensions.

GSK, meanwhile, sees no reason for such drastic action. Publicly, all a spokesman is willing to say is that it has “a longstanding presence in China, to make sure patients can access our medicines and vaccines”.

“China is also increasingly a source of cutting-edge biopharma innovation, and we have established several important collaborations for potential new treatments in oncology, respiratory, immunology and inflammation,” the spokesman adds.

However, like AstraZeneca, it too has fallen foul of Beijing after the company was engulfed in a bribery scandal in 2014.

GSK was found guilty of bribing Chinese doctors and hospitals to prescribe its medical products and was forced to pay a record $490m fine.

That ordeal prompted GSK bosses to take a much more cautious approach in which its activities were limited to strict licensing deals rather than the asset-heavy approach of others, such as AstraZeneca.

“It [GSK] went through a very difficult time in China. The experience damaged the company immeasurably in terms of its willingness to take risks,” a City source says.

By focusing on developing local collaborations, GSK believes it can still capitalise on the opportunities in China while being “less vulnerable” than rivals who are more “asset-exposed”, an insider explains.

Yet, the same person admits it ultimately boils down to one question: “Are they [China] helping us long-term or are they harming us? And I can’t answer that, which is why we can’t afford to be all in or all out.”

Industry figures hope common sense prevails between the two superpowers.

Garthwaite acknowledges deals that come with potential national security risk should be scrutinised, while attempts to reduce American over-dependence on Chinese antibiotics are also to be applauded.

However, he says the White House needs to distinguish between drug production and drug development, which “shouldn’t be too hard”.

Another investor says patients don’t really care where the drugs come from, “as long as they’re subjected to the same trials”.

In response to a recent US ban on imports of humanoid robots, China’s foreign ministry said: “Protectionism does not make the US more competitive … it will only hurt the interests of US companies and consumers.”﻿

Yet, nor is it in China’s interests to actively undermine American science. Chinese drugmakers simply cannot afford to be shut out of Western markets, particularly the US, experts say.

“China is really vulnerable too. It has to rely on its export machine because it doesn’t have sufficient levels of internal consumption,” one analyst says.

Ultimately, industry sources admit they are at the mercy of an unpredictable Trump administration whose appetite for trade wars shows little sign of waning.

As one boardroom veteran puts it: “It’s akin to walking a tightrope – we’ll continue trying to walk it and hope we stay on.”

data.title: Labour meddling ‘scaring off Poundland suitors’
data.description:
The Danish supermarket giant behind discount chain Netto has walked away from a potential rescue bid for Poundland, blaming a growing political backlash over the sales process.

The Salling Group pulled out of the bidding process earlier this month as Gordon Brothers, the American restructuring firm, came under fire from Westminster over its ownership of Poundland.

Representatives for Salling Group told Poundland’s advisers that the company was withdrawing as a result of the “political risk and inflammatory commentary” surrounding the situation, according to a City source. Several other unnamed parties had also been scared away by the publicity, the same source said.

Gordon Brothers has been the subject of fierce criticism from Labour and Reform UK MPs amid accusations it has deliberately pushed Poundland towards administration.

A source close to the negotiations said some of the censure “was very unhelpful” because it risked “damaging the process and the outcome”. Some of Gordon Brothers’ most vocal detractors were in danger of “grandstanding”, the source said.

Liam Byrne, chairman of the Commons business committee, accused the American outfit last week of behaving “almost like a wolf on Wall Street, ravaging the British high street”.

Mr Byrne was speaking just minutes after Mark Newton-Jones, boss of Gordon Brothers Europe, was summoned to appear before the committee to answer for its actions.

The Prime Minister, Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, and Reform’s Robert Jenrick and Richard Tice have also weighed in.

Andy Burnham has said the Government was “prepared to find what we can do” to help save the chain, comments that prompted speculation about the possibility of temporary nationalisation for Poundland. Mr Burnham later clarified there was a limit to what ministers could do.

However, Mr Byrne rejected suggestions the scrutiny had been counterproductive.

He told The Telegraph: “Everyone from the Prime Minister to UK Private Capital [the private equity industry body] has urged Gordon Brothers to do the right thing and do what’s right to save a business that employs 30,000 people in the firm and the wider supply chain.

“Anyone who knows anything about retail knows that a successful next step for Poundland depends on the numbers. Recent scrutiny hasn’t changed Poundland’s numbers nor revealed anything commercially confidential.”

A separate Westminster source said the scrutiny had had the desired effect, pressuring Gordon Brothers to release funds and helping to identify several more potential rescue bids. “It has forced them [Gordon Brothers] to behave in a different way,” the source said.

Following the committee hearing, Mr Byrne also accused Gordon Brothers of “extracting millions” from Poundland at the same time as restricting cash and credit access – a decision that risked forcing the retailer into insolvency.

The session was held behind closed doors because the firm had complained about the prospect of it becoming a “show trial”. It denied restricting funding but Mr Byrne said its evidence had been directly contradicted by Poundland’s management.

Mr Newton-Jones told the hearing that Gordon Brothers supported extending the administration deadline to allow several live rescue bids to progress. The next day, Poundland applied for a further 10-day moratorium from creditors so it could pursue talks with those parties.

It is understood Salling could yet return to cherry pick some of Poundland’s shops if its bid for survival is unsuccessful. Close to 20 rival retailers and supermarket chains have expressed interest in buying parcels of stores. Poundland has almost 600 across the UK and Ireland. 

Founded as a small draper’s shop in Aarhus, central Denmark, the Salling Group is now the country’s largest retailer. It operates more than 2,100 stores across six European countries and employs nearly 70,000 staff.

It serves roughly 15 million customers every week and generated turnover of more than 83bn Danish Kroner (€11bn) in 2025. Any profits that are not reinvested in the business are handed to charity.

The group’s Netto brand has hundreds of stores in Germany and Poland. However, it has been less successful in attempts to crack the UK market, exiting in 2010 with a sale of its 700-strong business to Asda. In 2014, Netto returned via a joint venture with Sainsbury’s, but the partnership was scrapped just two years later.

The Salling Group was approached for comment.

A government spokesman said: “Thousands of Poundland workers have their livelihoods on the line, and everyone involved must use this extra time to secure a deal that protects jobs and keeps shops open.

“We will continue to closely monitor developments - our priority will always be protecting workers.”

data.title: Production at Jackdaw in North Sea to start within days
data.description:
The controversial Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea is set to start production within days, an energy minister has said.

Michael Shanks, who is deputy to Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, said gas from the site would start flowing into UK pipes shortly to help meet winter household energy demand.

He said: “We expect that in the coming days gas will start to flow from the field to meet demand right across Britain.”

Industry sources confirmed the timeline, although the exact date of “first gas” remains uncertain.

Adura, the joint venture between Shell and Equinor that owns Jackdaw, has repeatedly suggested production could ramp up from mid-November.

The gas from Jackdaw will travel through a 20-mile subsea pipeline to the Shearwater processing hub before coming ashore. Adura staff on Shearwater are said to be ready to open the taps.

It also emerged this week that offshore drilling rigs needed to prepare the platform for production have finished their work and departed, leaving the facility in apparent readiness. 

However, industry insiders suggest the switch-on may be delayed because of the COP31 climate conference in Turkey, where Ms Fahnbulleh is leading the UK delegation.

The arrival of Jackdaw’s gas in UK pipes will mark the culmination of a 21-year battle to get the field into production.

Discovered in 2005 in the central North Sea, Jackdaw used to belong to Shell, but after corporate restructuring it is now operated by the joint venture Adura.

It was granted a licence by ministers in June 2022 amid the European energy crisis triggered by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

However, the decision prompted a landmark legal case when Greenpeace successfully petitioned Scotland’s Court of Session, arguing that the Government had unlawfully ignored the climate impacts of burning Jackdaw’s gas.

Ms Fahnbulleh approved a fresh licence application last month.

The Government’s decision to approve Jackdaw has been controversial – flying in the face of Labour’s previous climate commitments and drawing criticism from Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary.

Mr Shanks, however, defended it strongly in a recent Westminster debate.

“The Jackdaw decision will support the country’s energy security, protecting hundreds of jobs and adding an estimated £2.9bn to the UK economy,” he said. “That decision was fully in line with our climate commitments.”

However, data have cast doubt on Mr Shanks’s claims.

At its peak, Jackdaw is projected to boost UK domestic gas production by approximately 6pc.

However, the North Sea accounts for only about 42pc of the UK’s gas needs, so Jackdaw’s contribution will be around 2.5pc of total UK gas supply – compensating for some of the decline in other fields.

The Jackdaw development coincides with new government data that show UK gas production fell by 7pc in the three months to June, hitting a near-record low, while net imports rose by 15pc.

Gas prices remain elevated at 230p per therm, compared with 82p a year ago.

An Adura spokesman said: “Jackdaw will provide an estimated 6pc of projected UK North Sea gas production – enough to heat the equivalent of 1.4 million homes – at peak production. This is a material contribution to Britain’s domestic energy supply and UK energy security.”

Adura is still awaiting a decision from Ms Fahnbulleh on the equally controversial Rosebank project west of Shetland, where it has invested £2bn in opening the UK’s largest remaining oil field.

data.title: Only 500 shoplifters behind more than 22,000 thefts
data.description:
The 500 most prolific shoplifters were behind more than 22,000 store thefts recorded by retailers, research has shown.

Each of the criminals was linked to at least 27 shoplifting incidents – and 140 of them had notched up more than 50, according to the analysis.

The most prolific of the 500 offenders was associated with more than 265 shoplifting incidents across several retailers.

Some seven in 10 of the prolific shoplifters were violent towards staff or customers, while targeting everything from alcohol, energy drinks and chocolate to high-value meat and skincare products.

The data have been revealed by Auror, a company that provides police forces and retailers including Marks & Spencer, Tesco and Boots with a data-sharing system that enables them to identify prolific offenders.

Last week, the Home Office said that as many as 16 police forces would target their most prolific shoplifters with city-centre bans and GPS tagging to track their movements.

The data also show that many of the shoplifters operate as gangs and target stores in several towns and cities.

The analysis showed that more than 7,000 offenders had hit stores in more than one city or town.

Repeat offenders, who were linked to more than 21 shoplifting incidents, were recorded alongside more than four other co-offenders on average. One shoplifter was associated with 42 other offenders.

Mark Gleeson, general manager for Auror in Britain and Europe, said: “These top offenders are overwhelmingly violent and organised.

“They offend across brands, are connected with other associates to carry out their offending and target products that carry high resale value such as alcohol, energy drinks and skincare products.”

Examples included one violent offender who was connected to more than 60 thefts in Manchester, London and Norwich comprising £50,000 in stolen products.

In London, retailers helped identify a multi-million-pound organised crime group in July who had stolen £500,000 worth of goods.

In Glasgow, seven separate large retailers linked a known violent offender to more than 70 thefts across 19 different stores from Clydebank, to Rutherglen, to Cadder – and in central Glasgow.

In the Home Office crackdown, the 16 police forces will use criminal behaviour orders to curb repeat offences by prolific shoplifters.

The court orders enable police to apply for restrictions banning convicted thieves from the specific areas in which they have focused their shoplifting.

Officers can impose electronic tags to enforce the bans, as well as curfews and requirements to undergo treatment for drug or drink addiction.

The criminal behaviour orders can also be used to ban offenders from meeting or gathering with named individuals, possessing alcohol in public, using social media or digital contact and carrying or using certain articles such as e-bikes, tools or spray paint cans.

Breaches of the orders carry a maximum penalty of five years in jail.

Retail chiefs say thieves have become “more brazen, more organised and more aggressive” amid a fourfold increase in shoplifting since the Covid pandemic.

It has risen to record highs of more than 500,000 offences a year in England and Wales, although the British Retail Consortium estimates under-reporting means there are in reality some 5.5 million store thefts in a year, resulting in direct losses of £2.2bn.

However, thefts have started to plateau, with data published by Auror showing that violence by shoplifters in stores has fallen by up to 20 per cent since police and shops started targeting prolific offenders.

Zia Yusuf, Reform UK’s home affairs spokesman, said: “Tory and Labour governments have allowed criminals to dominate Britain. The Tories imported five million net new people and built just 455 net new prison places to cope. Reform UK will deport all 10,000 foreigners in our jails to make space so we can jail these shoplifters. We will restore order on our high streets.”

data.title: David Beckham sues after fragrance found on sale in Poundland
data.description:
Sir David Beckham has launched a lawsuit against the company distributing his branded fragrances, claiming they have been found for sale in Poundland.

The former England and Manchester United footballer, who sells Eau de Toilette and Eau de Parfum, filed court papers that detailed his “shock and dismay” at finding them in discount stores and petrol stations.

DB Ventures, the firm set up to manage his businesses, brands and commercial rights has begun legal action against the perfume company, Coty.

The legal team for Sir David, 51, claims Coty has sold about £18m ($24m) worth of stock through “unapproved distribution channels”. The lawsuit, filed in New York, said: “How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”

According to the Daily Mail, the legal document continues: “Coty distributed David Beckham fragrances through the budget retailers Poundland, allowing the product to be sold for dollar store prices and associating the David Beckham brand with cheap, discount products.”

Sir David’s legal team is seeking compensation and damages totalling around £31m ($41m) as a result. They argue that he is “one of the most iconic and influential figures in sports fashion and business”, and note the knighthood he received in 2025 in efforts to assert his “global icon” status.

His legal team added that his “world-renowned global brand is synonymous with excellence” and that he has “carefully cultivated” his “luxury image ... for decades”.

An agreement has been in place between DB Ventures and Coty for several years, with the company producing 45 David Beckham fragrances, all selling for about £20 a bottle.

However, last year the company that owns the Beckham name, Authentic Brands Group, contacted Coty’s rivals at Interparfums to sell the licence to them instead, and a deal was announced in January – with the partnership expected to start in 2028.

In legal papers, Coty has also been accused of under-reporting sales by $123m (£93m), meaning that DB Ventures has missed out on $6m (£4.5m) in owed royalties.

Coty has filed its defence, asking for the case to be dismissed.

It argues the case is not about Poundland or petrol stations, but is an attempt to ditch it early and begin its partnership with its rivals – via a “transparent effort to manufacture a pretextual basis”. The firm’s lawyers added: “This is not about protecting the David Beckham brand.”

Coty denies that the fragrances were ever sold in Poundland but says that it has the right to decide where it wants to sell its David Beckham range.

data.title: ‘Ozempic face’ powers revival of a fading British giant
data.description:
A surprise discovery may have saved one of Britain’s oldest chemical companies from sliding into irrelevance.

Croda, founded more than 100 years ago, was once known as the “mini ICI”, a powerhouse industrial giant with 70 factories in Lancashire and Yorkshire.

But like so much of Britain’s chemical industry, its star has been fading in recent years.

A share price rally during Covid – after it teamed up with Pfizer to produce one of the first vaccines – has been fizzling out, with its stock declining for four consecutive years.

Now, however, a surprise discovery is reversing Croda’s fortunes, giving the biotech-to-chemicals group a new lease of life as a beauty giant.

Croda recently discovered that one of its old chemicals can be used to treat “Ozempic face”, the often alarming facial transformation associated with the fat-jab craze.

For about a decade, Croda had been producing a skin-plumping chemical derived from the root of the plant anemarrhena to limited sale success.

Known as Volufiline, the agent swells the skin by chemically expanding fat cells and is used mostly in body creams.

But after users of GLP-1 drugs complained of hollow cheeks and sunken eyes, doctors discovered that Volufiline can combat the gaunt features associated with rapid weight loss.

The discovery has led to an explosion of sales for Croda, turning Volufiline into a TikTok sensation, in demand from the French and South Korean cosmetics industry.

Steve Foots, Croda’s chief executive, said the success of Volufiline had taken everybody by surprise.

“It had been in our portfolio for a decade,” he admits. “Ozempic coming on the market has created a big opportunity, which we’re capitalising on. It can lead to facial hollowing, but we can innovate around that by plumping your skin.”

Revenue from Volufiline sales jumped 270pc in the first half as more than 150 companies signed up to use it in their products.

Videos tagged #Volufiline have also generated 200 million views on the US TikTok Shop app in 12 months.

It has prompted Croda to lean into its new profile as a key force in the burgeoning TikTok influencer economy, helping send shares up 25pc from their August 2025 nadir.

Unlike Botox, Volufiline is applied as a face cream or in a lipstick-style tube.

Estée Lauder, the cosmetics giant, is hooked and has started selling a 92pc concentrate version of Croda’s agent under the Volufiline name.

Croda has even managed to sell it to the Korean “K-beauty” industry, which pioneered the skin-transforming agents and exports $11bn (£8.3bn) every year.

Foots said that while the fat-jabs windfall was unexpected, it had resulted from a decades-long repositioning of Croda from traditional chemicals into a supplier to customers, including L’Oréal, Procter & Gamble and Unilever, as well as Estée Lauder.

Next up is hair care. Alongside Volufiline, Croda is pushing KeraBio, a synthetic form of biotech-derived keratin, as its next miracle product.

While Volufiline was an existing ingredient that found a new use, Foots said KeraBio – developed at Croda’s research facility in Daresbury, Cheshire – will be its “first big product launch in the beauty industry”.

A similar serum from an American rival sells for £80 a shot.

“It’s solving the problem of repairing hair that’s been damaged through combing and heating and colouring, which breaks the keratin bonds,” Foots said.

“It strengthens your hair in a chemical way by creating new bonds, and stops it from ageing, which is a bit of a holy grail in the industry.”

For Croda’s proud British roots, its re-emergence as a cosmetics force is a major boost for the nation’s chemicals sector.

Foots said that while Croda’s business was driven by breakthroughs made at a plant in Daresbury and a second research lab at its headquarters near Goole, East Yorkshire, still not enough was being done to make the UK a chemical powerhouse.

Only 950 of Croda’s 5,500 employees are UK based, and while it has three British plants, most production takes place at factories scattered around Europe, the United States and Asia.

While the beauty industry may be Croda’s new frontier, the firm is also expanding the plant in Leek, Staffordshire, that was so critical in producing lipids used to deliver the Pfizer jab.

A recent breakthrough by Moderna and Merck in developing a melanoma vaccine that uses the same mRNA gene therapy principles shows the potential of the sector, Foots said.

He said: “We were prominent in solving the biggest medical crisis of a generation with the biggest innovation of its time, which was gene therapy drugs. And it’s still advancing.

“Flu vaccines, cancer treatments. The science is there. It will take time to get to market, but we’re excited because Croda is provital in many of these programmes.”

Croda may be one of the few independent British chemicals groups still standing, but its Ozempic discovery proves there’s life in the old dog yet.

data.title: Two-tier safety regulations are strangling Britain’s housebuilding
data.description:
The Canada Water redevelopment plan is perhaps the most ambitious construction project in London. The first new London town in 50 years, it promises thousands of homes, millions of square feet of retail and office space, new streets and a town square.

The capital and the economy desperately need this sort of shot in the arm. But the scheme is now in deep trouble.

Rising costs, high inflation and interest rates, and weakening demand have put the second phase of the plans on hold, throwing the £3.6bn development into chaos.

You’ll see plenty of headlines blaming the economic weather, but there’s a truth that nobody wants to confront. The Canada Water scheme didn’t die by accident: it was killed off by government regulation.

The worsening housing market that dealt the coup de grâce was only the last of a series of blows, many of them dealt by government policy.

British Land has been trying to break ground in Canada Water since 2005, only for the financial crisis to hit the pause button. It was restarted in 2014, but it took six years for Phase 1 to begin. Such things take time, but lengthy consultation processes and wrangling held up the project until it had been shaken down for a massive 35pc “affordable housing” target.

Finally ready to go in 2020, Covid lockdowns caused matters to be delayed once again. And just as things went back to normal, in 2023, the Government brought in stringent new fire safety requirements that required the entire development to be redesigned.

The result was to further delay and reduce the viability of the project, leading the affordable housing target to be lowered to 9pc in a desperate last-ditch attempt to save the project.

Some of the new measures were sensible, but the most costly – and least rational – was the requirement for two stairwells in every structure above 18m.

This requirement made Britain an international outlier. In Europe and Asia, mid-rise apartments commonly have a single stairwell, and in France, Germany, Singapore, China and Sweden, the requirements only come in for buildings of around 50-60m, which would have covered a building the height of Grenfell in any case.

Indeed, we know that three central problematic features of the Grenfell disaster were nothing to do with the stairwell. The flammable cladding, of course, which is now rightly banned, allowed a fire to spread that would not have otherwise. A modern sprinkler system would have put out the fire in the first place but was absent. The fire doors would have given residents time to evacuate, but these failed because of poor maintenance by the council.

Beyond some minor adjustments to the cladding, none of these issues would have applied to Canada Water’s apartments, which, like all new high-rises, would have been equipped with sprinklers and brand new fire doors. A failure born entirely of the negligence of the state, and the age of Grenfell, is now being offloaded on to private developments.

In the US, there is emerging research which suggests that restrictive second stairwell requirements there have made construction more expensive and reduced floorspace, without demonstrably improving safety.

In fact, the British Government has done nothing to require existing high-rises to implement the most effective fire safety system – a sprinkler system (estimated to be 99pc effective by the London Fire Brigade) – while making it harder and more expensive to build the modern apartment blocks that would have them by default.

We’ve made new housing too safe to build. By loading excessive safety requirements on to new builds, we are slowing the roll-out of modern fire safety systems and trapping millions of people in unsafe, ageing buildings. It’s estimated that more than a million people live in apartments at risk of fire and as many as eight million live in homes that are in some way dangerous.

When we make it too costly to build safer homes by adding redundant safety measures, it’s those lives that we’re putting at risk.

data.title: Italy puts Revolut under supervision after mobsters move millions
data.description:
Revolut has been placed under supervision by an Italian court after prosecutors discovered that convicted mobsters and money launderers had funnelled cash through the bank.

The digital-only lender, which is based in London, was found by a court in Milan to have “serious deficiencies” in its anti-money-laundering controls in Europe, allowing 24 convicted or suspected criminals to conceal transactions worth nearly €42m (£35m).

The court has put the fintech’s Italian operations under “judicial administration” for one year, a ruling that gives authorities greater oversight of how Revolut operates in Italy.

The issue stemmed from problems at the fintech’s Lithuania-based Revolut Bank UAB, which runs its business in Italy.

A spokesman for Revolut said the company had acknowledged the court’s decision and would co-operate fully with the Italian authorities, adding that its banking services in Italy continued to function normally with no disruption to customers.

The bank is not under criminal investigation, and the supervision process does not amount to an indictment or penalty.

However, the ruling could have broader consequences overseas, with Cetin Duransoy, Revolut’s US chief executive, warning on Monday that the Italian action could harm the group’s American business.

“If you ⁠would have a massive hiccup somewhere, it’s going to have an impact ‌in other places,” he said. Revolut is in the process of obtaining a full US banking licence.

The Milan court said that shortcomings in controls were not isolated incidents but “embedded in a stable management model, repeatedly applied over time”, preventing authorities from freezing illicit funds, according to a 39-page ruling seen by Reuters.

The court has appointed two judicial administrators with oversight and inspection authority, and their powers could be expanded if Revolut does not co-operate fully or if further issues emerge.

Under the ruling, Revolut must execute a 15-point remediation programme and has 60 days to submit an action plan addressing its compliance failures.

The fintech has grown rapidly in the past decade and recently reached a valuation of $115bn (£91bn).

It has faced problems with its internal controls before.

It took Revolut roughly four years to acquire a banking licence in the UK because of concerns about governance. Lenders are usually granted a full licence within 12 months.

Between 2021 and 2026, rival banks reported 256 suspicious transactions involving the suspects, while Revolut filed none.

It was reported in 2024 that the European Central Bank had, after a review, been pressing Revolut to improve the financial crime controls and governance of its EU unit.

The digital-only lender was founded by Nik Storonsky and Vlad Yatsenko in 2015, focusing on prepaid travel cards for spending abroad.

It has since expanded to become one of the world’s biggest fintechs, offering financial products ranging from stocks and shares Isas to crypto trading. The digital-only lender says it has more than 80 million retail customers globally.

The Revolut spokesman also said: “We take our regulatory obligations and anti-money-laundering controls extremely seriously, and we continuously invest in strengthening our financial crime systems, transaction monitoring models and dedicated compliance teams across all markets.”

data.title: Energy bills expected to jump by £443 in January
data.description:
Annual household energy bills will jump by £443 in January to their highest level since 2023, according to a new forecast.

It means the average household’s annual gas and electricity costs would hit £2,166 at the start of next year, Cornwall Insight said on Wednesday. That is 26pc higher than the current level of £1,723, announced in October.

The energy consultancy blamed the painful midwinter hit on the Iran war keeping wholesale gas prices high.

Difficulties getting liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments through the Strait of Hormuz has left European storage tanks at record early-winter lows, prompting a scramble for higher-priced supplies.

Craig Lowrey, an analyst at Cornwall Insight, said: “Events beyond our control have a very real impact on our energy bills.”

Cornwall has raised its forecast from an earlier prediction of a 16pc increase in the January cap, which would have kept the average bill just below £2,000.

Although exporters have found ways to shift crude oil out of the Gulf, there is no alternative for LNG exports – and Iran is still attacking vessels as they pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

European gas prices have dropped to €83 (£69) per megawatt hour from more than €100 in late October but are still more than 160pc higher than before the war.

The hefty increase is a setback for John Healey, the Chancellor, after he vowed to get energy costs down last month.

Mr Lowrey said government initiatives, such as a £100 household energy payment and the removal of VAT from electricity charges “can only chip away at the edges of a bill that continues to be pushed up by events in the Middle East”.

He urged the Government to look for ways to “control how exposed we are to these shocks in the future”, especially by decoupling energy costs from global gas prices.

Ofgem, the energy regulator, is poised to unveil its price cap next Wednesday.

The higher price cap is likely to be a double-blow for poorer households: it will also power even faster inflation, putting pressure on interest rates.

Inflation hit a one-year high of 3.6pc in October, driven by higher petrol prices and a 4pc increase in the energy price cap last month.

data.title: China blamed for loss of half a million German factory jobs
data.description:
China has been blamed for the loss of half a million German factory jobs since 2019, as experts have warned that Europe’s manufacturing engine is losing momentum.

German industry shed 496,000 jobs between 2019 and 2025, according to the Ifo Institute in Dresden, representing a drop of 7.1pc.

Joachim Ragnitz, the managing director at Ifo Dresden, said: “Employment is shrinking in almost all industrial sectors, which is likely a result of declining competitiveness, particularly vis-à-vis China.

“Traditional German core sectors, such as the automotive industry and mechanical engineering, are particularly hard hit.”

The figures follow warnings of a “China shock 2.0” as the world’s second-largest economy pumps out cheap advanced-manufacturing exports that threaten to crush Western industry. China’s trade surplus with Germany has doubled in the last year.

It brings back painful memories of the first shock in the early 2000s, when China unleashed a wave of cheap toys, clothes and manufactured goods into Western economies.

In addition to growing competition from China, the Ifo Institute also blamed vanishing factory jobs on a fresh wave of de-industrialisation triggered by high energy prices and changing demographics.

Europe’s biggest economy has suffered several shocks in recent years, reeling in particular from losing access to cheap Russian gas after the Ukraine war.

As factory jobs have disappeared, hiring in less productive sectors has risen significantly.

The services sector employs 2.2 million more people than in 2019, mainly in health and social care and public administration.

Mr Ragnitz warned that this would spell trouble for the future, as these jobs were unlikely to provide a significant boost to growth.

He said: “The new jobs are for the most part not being created where Germany is especially productive and innovative. That may slow down our growth potential in the future.”

Car manufacturers and their suppliers have cut 123,500 jobs since 2019, a plunge of 13pc. Meanwhile, metal products manufacturers cut 115,600 jobs, and mechanical engineering another 64,500.

These three sectors account for 60pc of the job losses.

By contrast, service providers saw strong growth with 391,000 new jobs in healthcare and 357,000 in social services, including nursing homes.

Mr Ragnitz said the country’s ageing population was the key driver of this trend.

Germany has for years had a relatively low fertility rate. It improved briefly for a few years before and during Covid, before plunging again to its current level of 1.3 children per woman.

A fierce backlash against immigration means politicians may struggle to offset such demographic pressures.

Industrial decline has caused job losses in every part of Germany apart from Hamburg. Jobs are also falling faster in the east than in the west, at 8.4pc vs 6.8pc. In Thuringia and Saxony-Anhalt, overall employment has even declined.

These are both states where the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is popular, with the hard-Right party winning the largest vote share in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt last month. It also won the state election in Thuringia in 2024.

data.title: Harvey Nichols’ former owner to sell London mansion for £40m
data.description:
The Hong Kong tycoon who formerly owned Harvey Nichols is to sell his London mansion for £40m to a parrot-fancying hedge fund boss.

Sir Dickson Poon, 70, has exchanged contracts for the sale of his Georgian townhouse in Belgrave Square, which sits in one of London’s most exclusive postcodes just a few hundred feet away from the grounds of Buckingham Palace.

It was bought by hedge fund manager Hamza Lemssouguer, according to the Financial Times.

The townhouse, which was sold off-market, was previously home to Queen Victoria’s grandson, Prince Arthur of Connaught, and was later used as the residence for East Africa’s high commissioner. The property’s current neighbours include the embassies of Germany and Norway.

Mr Lemssouguer is a former Credit Suisse trader who now runs his own firm, Arini Capital Management, which has made a name for itself by betting on distressed corporate debt.

He came to prominence after providing a loan to the Barclay family’s Very Group last year.

Away from finance, the Moroccan-born banker breeds parrots at his farm in Surrey, and has said that parrots are his passion.

Sir Dickson’s decision to sell comes as his empire is navigating a rough patch.

The Chinese magnate has been an influential figure in British retail since his company, Dickson Concepts, acquired Harvey Nichols from Burton Group in 1991 for £53m.

Nicknamed “Harvey Nicks”, and popularised in the television sitcom Absolutely Fabulous, the luxury London department store business expanded to other cities under Sir Dickson’s ownership and opened restaurants.

It now carries more than 800 premium and luxury brands and has more than 1,000 employees, with stores in Knightsbridge, Manchester, Birmingham, Bristol, Leeds and Edinburgh.

However, Sir Dickson put the chain up for sale earlier this year amid mounting pressure on his business empire, with Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group acquiring it for an undisclosed sum.

Frasers said the brand was “a British institution with significant potential”, but faced “tough choices” to become sustainable again.

The deal includes the Harvey Nichols physical stores in the UK, international franchise partnerships and the company’s online presence.

Sir Dickson has stepped back from his former executive chairman duties after Dickson Concepts, which trades on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, warned that sales and profits were not likely to return to their historic growth rates.

Dickson Concepts has said the chain’s Hong Kong stores are unaffected.

Knight Frank, which was involved in the deal, was approached but declined to comment.

data.title: Janet Malcolm, the finest – and most hated – journalist in town
data.description:
Among discerning members of the literati, Janet Malcolm is treated with reverence. A long-time New Yorker journalist, serving for 58 years until her death in 2021, she’s admired for her exacting prose and her shrewd analysis. Yet her aversion to the cult-of-personality style of journalism, which put the writer at the centre, meant she was never quite a celebrity.

I came to know Malcolm’s work after I’d been working as a journalist for a few years. Other writers, a bit older and much cleverer than me, recommended her. I was so taken with the combination of her subjects and her meticulous style – never dry, never florid – that I soon arranged a weekend break in a coastal B&B, taking nothing but all of her books.

Why is Malcolm so intriguing? Firstly, her work. She wrote for The New Yorker first as a lifestyle journalist, then a photography critic, and eventually as a general staff writer. In the last of those roles, she undertook in-depth profiles, literary criticism and longer-form investigations on a sequence of related subjects: psychoanalysis, a heated dispute about Freud’s legacy, the moral question of what journalists should disclose to their subjects, the ethics of biography as seen through Sylvia Plath’s story, a murder-for-hire case in a religious community and plenty more.

One of Malcolm’s great gifts was to be constantly and curiously aware of what her presence as a journalist was doing to the subject and the situation. She never, though, clumsily foregrounded her own experience. Each subject she took on was interesting not only in its own right but in a second light: how does this subject morph under my gaze? I have no especial interest in photography or visual art, but I read her writing on those topics with as much thirst as I did that on subjects more in my wheelhouse (psychoanalysis, Sylvia Plath).

Secondly, the woman herself. She defied aestheticisation, as many of her peers did not. At the opening of The Absent Woman, a nimble and tender new biography of Malcolm, Eve Sneider tells us that in 2014, when both Malcolm and her fellow essayist Joan Didion were turning 80, New York magazine asked to run a joint feature in tribute. Malcolm declined. Her work is light on emotional or personal news. (Didion, by contrast, modelled for Celine in her latter years, and never shied away from the impulse among some of her fans to enshrine her as a cultural icon.) There’s something valuable in Malcolm’s caution against being too personally available: something always tantalisingly withheld. She reminds us, I think, of the pleasure of ephemera, especially in an age when it’s becoming extinct.

She was born Jana Klara Wienerová in 1934, in Prague, to a family of Jewish intellectuals. In 1939, they fled to America to avoid Nazi persecution, and settled in Manhattan, in a heavily Central and Eastern European neighbourhood. Their Jewishness was, understandably, a matter of anxiety. Janet’s father, Joseph, changed the family name to “Winn”; he and his wife, Hanna, decided not to disclose their religion to the children.

The family assimilated well, though complicatedly so: both Jewishness and European identity would remain sensitive for Malcolm’s sense of self. While she would wrestle with and to some degree bury her heritage, she would also end up surrounded in her adult life by people who had the same sensibilities. “A select few called her ‘Jana’, including Philip Roth,” Sneider writes. “They traded notes on each other’s writing, they gossiped, they cracked jokes.” (At one point, when a Malcolm essay was being praised from all quarters, he wrote a note to her: “There is a devil in you called Jana and she should be encouraged, prodded, rewarded, at every turn.”)

Malcolm was among the first generation of writers who grew up reading The New Yorker. She attended the University of Michigan, graduated in 1955 and – following her husband Donald, who’d been hired already – was taken on by the magazine. Her beginnings were in gift guides, then photography columns, but in 1978 she published her first piece on psychoanalysis, a subject that would become the undercurrent of her career.

First came Psychoanalysis: The Impossible Profession in 1981, a book widely feted both in literary circles and among the profession she sought to illuminate. Analysis was, back then, in a slump, fearful of its dwindling cultural significance; here was a sharp reinvigoration. Malcolm is unmistakably everywhere, through the mordant wit of her observation. She tells one loquacious analyst that she gets sick of listening to him talk without being able to respond. Doesn’t he get sick of listening to his patients? “And how!” he responds with glee.

After the success of that book came In the Freud Archives in 1984, equally brilliant and riveting – but also the genesis of a traumatic, lengthy legal battle with one of its subjects. Malcolm depicts a power struggle between the analysts Jeffrey Masson and Kurt Eissler over Freud’s legacy and who would be granted access to the archive of the great man. It’s a moreish tale of competing egos and ideas, of men of a certain stature who pride themselves on having insights into the human condition yet can’t see their own silliness. As Sneider reports, one admiring reader told Malcolm: “You are, if I may say, an inspired gossip.”

This book and its aftermath would prove a fulcrum for Malcolm’s career. Masson, in particular, had been an incautious and flamboyant respondent, bragging about his womanising proclivities as well as his analytic genius, and he now took Malcolm to court alleging defamation, citing several remarks attributed to him that Malcolm didn’t have on tape. Sneider’s account of the trial is absorbing. As Malcolm herself knew, there’s nothing like a trial to distil vast, abstract questions in compellingly strange and human ways. She was cleared in 1994 – after a jury found that she’d intended no malice, even if the quotes had been fabricated – but the ordeal had roused plenty of professional animosity among fellow journalists, who disdained what they perceived as Malcolm’s hubris and hypocrisy.

The lengthy legal battle had flown under the radar for some years, but as it rumbled on Malcolm had published another pair of New Yorker pieces in 1989 that would become a classic book: The Journalist and the Murderer. That story took as its subject a lawsuit between a non-fiction writer named Joe McGinniss and a man convicted of murder, Jeffrey Macdonald. McGinniss had been hired to write about Macdonald’s trial. He had feigned sympathy and belief in Macdonald’s innocence to gain his trust and proximity, before publishing a book that portrayed the other man as an egotistical killer. An appalled Macdonald sued, accusing McGinniss of fraud; they eventually reached a financial settlement. It was an almost too perfect iteration of the questions about loyalty and disclosure with which Malcolm was obsessed.

But the book functioned, in many ways, as a brutal criticism of the profession of journalism itself. Her colleagues in the industry were furious. She didn’t mention her own ongoing legal troubles – she was herself, after all, a journalist accused of defamation – even as she pored over the alleged offences of others. This was too much for some to take. In New York magazine, John Taylor wrote a feature titled Holier Than Thou: The Curious Case of the Ferocious New Yorker Article, in which he and various subjects of Malcolm’s theorised that The Journalist and the Murderer served as a way for Malcolm to launder guilt about her own misdoings. Sneider is excellent at conveying the hubbub of Malcolm’s salivating colleagues, eager to decry her throughout these years.

The New York Times and New York, in particular, showed Malcolm open contempt. Today, it’s shocking to read: much of their disgust was over her appearance and demeanour. In the Times: “Ms Malcolm’s severe bearing and slight accent hark back to her European childhood.” In New York: “Her dark, lank hair is parted in the center… which has the effect, along with her owlishly oversized glasses, of emphasising her broad Slavic cheeks.” She was held up as smug and superior, and The New Yorker was implicated alongside her.

But, as widely reviled as she was in that period, Malcolm has come to be known, 30 years on, as a journalist’s journalist. Her most famous line, the beginning of The Journalist and the Murderer, is: “Every journalist who is not too stupid or too full of himself to notice what is going on knows that what he does is morally indefensible.” My boyfriend, who works as an editor on The New Yorker, winces when this line arises in conversation, the gist of his objection being: great line, obviously untrue exaggeration. I was pleased to show him a passage from Sneider’s book, showing that some of Malcolm’s other drafts had the journalist “aware” rather than “know”-ing, and not judged as “morally indefensible” but the more nuanced “obscurely shameful”. Part of the pleasure in reading Sneider’s biography is in having these famous sentences revealed in the fullness of their process: the care and time from which they benefitted.

Malcolm reverted to her original, sturdier proclamation upon her daughter’s advice. Again, it provoked her peers. One has to admire Malcolm’s willingness to be an irritant even as she fought legal battles and professional eschewment. Today, her line is quoted admiringly, the book taught in journalism schools. And Malcolm’s not-niceness is seen now for what it always was: a restless genius for observation, for being precise.

★★★★★

The Absent Woman is published by Atlantic at £18.99. To order your copy, call 0330 173 0523 or visit Telegraph Books

data.title: Rick Stein blames Labour tax raid as losses double
data.description:
Rick Stein’s restaurant empire has blamed Labour’s tax raid for an “exceptionally challenging” year in which losses almost doubled.

The TV chef’s Cornwall restaurants suffered a £600,000 hit last year as the group grappled with a combination of the rising minimum wage, lower business rates relief and the National Insurance raid.

This meant pre-tax losses jumped to £814,000 from £459,000 a year earlier. Sales were flat at £18.9m, the company said.

The group responded by raising prices, changing menus and tightening control of staffing costs.

Mr Stein’s group is one of the largest private-sector employers in Cornwall, with 329 staff at the end of 2025.

However, the latest accounts filed for Mr Stein’s company, The Seafood Restaurant (Padstow), showed it was forced to lay off 22 staff during the year as it struggled to offset additional costs from Labour policies.

It comes just a day after a review into youth unemployment by Alan Milburn, the former Labour health secretary, blamed government tax raids for making it more difficult for companies to hire younger workers.

Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, increased the rate of employer National Insurance contributions in her first Budget and lowered the threshold at which companies begin to pay the levy.

Mr Milburn has called for the National Insurance threshold for workers aged 21 to 24 to be doubled from £5,000 to £10,000 over five years, starting with hospitality and retail.

Kathy Coxhead, a director at Mr Stein’s company, said: “In 2025, our sector faced some of its most financially challenging legislative changes.

“Despite disciplined action on pricing, menus, purchasing and labour management, we could not fully offset substantial government-led cost increases.”

Mr Stein, 79, has spent more than half a century building his restaurant empire from a single seafood restaurant in Padstow, Cornwall, which he opened with his former wife Jill.

His success helped turn the fishing town into a culinary destination nicknamed “Padstein” with the business expanding into hotels, shops and a cookery school.

Mr Stein has previously criticised Labour’s tax increases, warning that they were discouraging restaurants from taking on staff.

He told the Evening Standard last year that increasing National Insurance had “just stopped growth”.

He added: “You’re certainly not going to hire people unless you absolutely need to.”

data.title: Labour’s defence spending delays blamed as BAE cuts more than 1,000 jobs
data.description:
Defence spending delays have been blamed for more than 1,000 job cuts at Britain’s biggest weapons maker.

Unite, Labour’s leading union backer, has criticised a lack of urgency in Government after BAE Systems announced 1,070 redundancies across its air division and in head office.

Union chiefs said “delays in defence spending” had resulted in the cuts, referring to the Government’s failure to set out how it will hit its target of spending 3pc of GDP on defence by 2030.

Sharon Graham, Unite’s general secretary, said: “For months Unite has been warning that delays in defence spending are driving companies in the sector to make negative decisions impacting British jobs.

“We won’t have a manufacturing industry left if the Government doesn’t start making critical decisions.”

BAE’s proposals will see staff made redundant primarily in its Air division, which makes the Typhoon fighter jets used by the Royal Air Force (RAF).

Bosses said the move had been made to increase “speed and efficiency”.

However, Ms Graham blamed the Government’s failure to invest more in domestic defence manufacturing.

She said: “In order to stop the erosion of defence jobs and get the growth we need, the Government needs to announce contracts for British built Typhoons and Collaborative Combat Aircraft immediately.”

BAE employs 50,000 staff across Britain, including 1,000 at its head office in London and a further 18,500 workers in its air division.

Staff were informed of the job cuts via an email sent this afternoon and BAE has entered talks with unions to cut the jobs through a voluntary redundancy scheme.

BAE says the lay-offs are intended to streamline decision-making by cutting bureaucracy, in line with wider plans to overhaul its processes using new technology and digital tools.

The job cuts will exclude shop-floor manufacturing workers and maintenance staff on RAF bases.

Unite warned that more redundancies could follow across British manufacturing if defence spending plans continue to be delayed.

Under Sir Keir Starmer, Labour announced plans to increase the UK’s defence spending to 2.5pc of GDP by the financial year 2027-28, in response to the growing threat from Russia.

However, long-term ambitions to increase Britain’s defence budget to rates of 3pc of GDP by 2030 have since suffered a series of delays.

John Healey resigned as defence secretary this year over Sir Keir’s refusal to commit to lifting spending to 3pc of GDP.

However, Mr Healey, now Chancellor under Andy Burnham, has since admitted that the plan to hit 3pc was only a “target” rather than a full commitment.

In his maiden Budget, Mr Healey confirmed that he would wait until next year’s spending review to set out how the Government would hit its Nato commitment to spend 3.5pc by 2035.

A report from the House of Lords’ industry and regulators committee has since raised concerns about the speed with which spending pledges will be turned into contracts, because of slow procurement processes inside the Ministry of Defence.

The lack of commitment has since caused a slump in the shares of some of Britain’s biggest weapons makers, including BAE Systems and Rolls-Royce.

In March, Turkey signed a $10.7bn (£8bn) deal to buy 20 Eurofighter Typhoon jets from BAE, which will be delivered in 2030.

Unite also raised concerns about possible job cuts at Airbus amid concern that the Government could hand a £2bn military satellites deal to America’s Lockheed Martin.

The European aerospace giant has made previous generations of Skynet satellites at facilities in Stevenage, Hertfordshire, and Portsmouth, where it collectively employs thousands of staff.

Ms Graham said: “Unite has also warned that these problems are not limited solely to BAE. For instance the government must now award the Skynet 6 contract to Airbus protecting thousands of highly skilled jobs in Portsmouth and Stevenage.”

A BAE spokesman said: “We recognise that this news may be unsettling for our people and we’re focused on achieving potential workforce reductions through a voluntary process.

“We’re committed to working closely with our trade unions and employee representatives and to keeping our employees informed and supported throughout.”
