data.title: The renovation decisions that cause the biggest arguments (and how to avoid them)
data.description:
Renovating a property together should be a unique bonding experience, but anyone who’s ever bickered over a Farrow & Ball colour chart might understand why it can break even the strongest of relationships.

Alarmingly, a recent study by finance company Novuna found that almost one in five couples (19 per cent) seriously considered splitting up – or ended their relationship entirely – amid a home improvement project, while more than half (57 per cent) admitted to fighting over key decisions.

So why can a property makeover cause so much friction? “A home is not only our most expensive possession, but there’s huge emotional investment, too,” explains interior designer Piers Thurston. “Renovation choices are very subjective, and everyone’s vision is different. It’s also much more complicated than many realise, from red tape to liaising with trades, and costs that only emerge once work begins. People often sign up without really knowing what they’re getting into.”

For Valerie Couillard, a renovation project manager who is also trained in mediation, keeping the peace between clients is all in a day’s work. “My role is a bit like that of a couples’ counsellor,” she says. “It can get heated, but I use conflict resolution skills to make sure everyone is heard and brings their ideas to the table. The trick is to work out what really matters to each party and find solutions that tick as many boxes as possible.”

Here we reveal which décor dilemmas are most likely to spark full-scale domestic warfare – and how to navigate them without ending up in the divorce courts…

Paint colours

According to a 2025 study by Houzz, paint shades are the single biggest source of DIY discord, as cited by 51 per cent of respondents. “Colour is so personal,” says Couillard, who founded the Place Between to guide couples through challenging refurbs. “People often get cold feet about bold shades, but using mood boards and Pinterest can increase their confidence, or help them decide if the black ceiling one of them is keen on would look ridiculous or not.”

In moments of tension – or indeed, imminent marital collapse – she says there is usually a way through, with more daring shades reserved for smaller and less-prominent rooms. “Most people are willing to be flexible, so there’s usually a middle ground. With so many thousands of colour options, it doesn’t have to be a deal breaker.”

Thurston says he often looks beyond the paint itself. “I worked with a couple in Surrey on a TV snug, and while the husband preferred plain neutrals, his wife wanted more colour. To meet both their needs, we went for a very understated base colour, and created layering with different textures in subtle sage greens, which pulled in the colours of the beautiful countryside around them.”

Flooring

A close second in the Houzz study, 47 per cent of survey participants admitted clashing over the bewildering choice of carpeting, floorboards, stone and everything in between.

“Flooring is a real Pandora’s box,” says Couillard. “Clients may have their heart set on a type of tile, only to discover that excavation or other alterations are needed, which all add to the cost. There are also technical considerations like thickness, humidity and longevity.”

If squabbles arise, she says one solution is to identify what matters most to each partner and find a meeting point. “Hardwood floors are durable and easy to maintain, for example, but if the other person wants something cosier, you can add rugs.”

While a good designer will never try to sway a couple, Thurston says it is essential they warn them of potential pitfalls. “The most beautiful option is unfortunately not always the most practical,” he says. “If I point out issues like durability and maintenance, and whether someone wants to be sealing a natural stone floor every few years, opinions can change pretty quickly.”

Wall coverings

Wall materials caused rifts for 37 per cent of respondents in the Houzz study, showing that one person’s enthusiasm for flamboyant patterned wallpaper or elaborate tiling can be another’s design nightmare.

“Feature walls can look wonderful, but there’s a risk they’ll end up looking dated,” Thurston says. “I always recommend leaning towards who actually uses the room most, so for instance, if we’re looking at the kitchen, who does most of the cooking or entertaining? It’s really worth considering what the space is used for.”

Couillard says most bust-ups can be avoided if three-dimensional visualisation software is used. “It lets you see how a room would look with wallpaper on every wall, or just one,” she says. “If there’s disagreement over something like a botanical print, the answer might be to use it in a downstairs cloakroom. In my experience, the person who was originally unsure not only accepts it, but comes to love it.”

Appliances

With 22 per cent of couples confessing to feuds over appliances according to Houzz, gadgets such as bespoke wine fridges, built-in audio systems and integrated coffee machines can tip the already-frazzled over the edge.

“One partner is often far more interested in luxury appliances,” says Couillard. “If they really have their heart set on something, let them run with it – the other person can have final say on something else.” She adds that tussles over eye-watering price tags can be averted with a little forward planning. “I always start by asking for a wish list of everything they want if money was no object,” she says. “We work through that and gradually make compromises.”

Thurston agrees that determining which extras are non-negotiable before work begins is vital to prevent future hostilities. “Identify these things early, because when you get to the end of a project, there’s rarely any budget left.”

Worktops

When it comes to doing up a kitchen, few issues generate as much heat as the all-important worktop.

“Marble or natural stone can look amazing, but you have to factor in things like staining and sealing,” says Thurston. “I advise clients to consider overall kitchen design, which means getting samples and looking at them against the rest of the cabinetry, hardware, flooring and even the windows. A lot of the time, any issues are resolved based on what works with the rest of the scheme.”

In her role as a project mediator, Couillard believes in being armed with practical questions: “Who is cooking? Will you want to put hot pans on a wooden counter top, and what’s the risk of burning it?” she says. “I’ll also ask clients if they really want to replace existing marble or granite tops. Changing the cupboard fronts instead can save a lot of money and unnecessary waste,” she says.

Lighting

Even basic decisions over lighting can trigger flashpoints, which Thurston tackles with good old-fashioned compromise. “I’m working with a couple on a country house in Hampshire, and though the husband loves high-tech LEDs, his wife wants a more traditional feel,” he says. “So we’ve incorporated discreet LEDs into Shaker-style joinery around the fireplace and TV that give the look he wants, but still feel appropriate for the property.”

Battles over one-of-a-kind statement lights can be trickier to solve, however. “I’ve had a case where one person wanted a glamorous glass chandelier like you might see in a hotel, but their partner was quite bohemian and very against it,” says Couillard. “So we went for a big rattan pendant instead. That still looks great without being as blingy.”

Budgets

Finally, the thorny issue of money lies at the core of many renovation projects – backed up by Houzz’s findings that 37 per cent of couples lock horns over budgets.

“Usually clients take on good cop, bad cop roles,” says Thurston. “One wants to splash out, while the other is more insistent there’s a finite amount of money.” His solution is a high/low approach. “Some things are absolutely worth the investment, like a sofa which is a strong focal point. But we balance that by going for more cost-effective furniture elsewhere, like in a guest room which isn’t used as much.”

He advocates a healthy contingency pot for unexpected costs, while Couillard – who suggests allowing up to 25 per cent – says extinguishing financial flare-ups is a crucial part of her job. “I bring money up a lot, even though it can be boring,” she admits. “Different levels of finish can mean huge variations in budget, and sometimes I have to ask, ‘Can you afford that?’ I don’t necessarily want the answer. I want them to ask themselves.”

And if those conversations turn ugly? “That’s where the therapy element comes in,” she says. “I take it as a compliment when couples argue in front of me, because they’re not waiting for me to leave before they have a row. They bring it to the table and we deal with it together.”

data.title: Boots to sell medicinal cannabis
data.description:
Boots is to start prescribing medicinal cannabis in a first for a UK high street pharmacy chain.

The retailer, which operates more than 1,800 stores across the country, will offer the drug to patients suffering from chronic pain, anxiety or insomnia as part of a new online cannabis service known as SureLeaf.

The move will make Boots the first UK pharmacy chain to offer medical cannabis, which was legalised in Britain eight years ago but has been tightly restricted by the NHS since then.

Patients aged 25 and over will be eligible for a prescription but only after they have completed an online assessment and video consultation with a registered doctor.

The new service will operate privately, rather than through the NHS, which rarely prescribes the drug and offers it only to people with cancer, severe forms of epilepsy or multiple sclerosis.

Boots’ service is likely to significantly expand the availability of the drug to patients, with people suffering from conditions including arthritis, sciatica, chronic back pain, migraines and endometriosis-related pain all eligible for a prescription.

However, they must first have tried conventional medicines without obtaining adequate relief.

Jamie Kerruish, Boots’ chief healthcare officer, said millions of people were living with pain that conventional treatments had failed to relieve.

He said: “Medical cannabis is a specialist area of healthcare and, through SureLeaf, we’re giving eligible patients another treatment option to consider, supported by clinical expertise and robust ongoing care.”

Dr David Gwynne, the medical director of Boots Online Doctor, said: “Medical cannabis is not appropriate for everyone and prescribing decisions need to be made carefully on an individual patient basis.”

Founded in 1849, Boots is one of Britain’s best-known high-street retailers. Last month it was sold to the billionaire Weston family from Canada for £6.7bn.

Under the scheme, patients will complete an online assessment before attending a video consultation with a specialist doctor.

Any proposed prescription must then be approved by a separate medical team, including a second consultant, before treatment begins.

Patients will also be monitored regularly, with an initial review after 28 days and further appointments at least every three months.

Medicinal cannabis was legalised in Britain in 2018 following campaigns by families of children suffering from severe epilepsy.

However, patients were only able to obtain supplies via prescription from a specialist doctor.

Recreational cannabis remains illegal and is classified as a Class B drug, with possession carrying a maximum sentence of five years in prison.

However, Britain’s approach to cannabis has looked increasingly out of step with the US, where nearly half of states have legalised recreational cannabis for use by consumers.

The effectiveness of cannabis-based treatments for some conditions also remains disputed, with official NHS guidance advising against their routine use for chronic pain.

Boots is also exploring a research partnership with the University of Nottingham to investigate how medicinal cannabis affects patients with chronic pain.

The research would look at how well cannabis works for patients with chronic pain and how doctors prescribe it.

data.title: How much cash should I have at home – and where should I keep it?
data.description:
The UK Government is urging households to stock up on basic supplies in case of emergencies such as cyber attacks, flooding, fire or power cuts.

Alongside practical items such as bottled water, a wind-up torch, a first aid kit and a portable power bank, the advice includes keeping some cash at home to provide essential backup if card payments or banking apps stop working.

Here, Telegraph Money explains how much cash is safe to keep at home, and the best way to store it.

  • Is it a good idea to keep cash at home?
  • How much cash is safe to keep at home?
  • Where should you store cash at home?
  • How else can I protect my access to money?

Is it a good idea to keep cash at home?

Although cash usage is on the decline in the UK, keeping a small amount of cash at home can be a practical safety net. Recent global events, from cyber attacks and data breaches to widespread power outages, have shown how quickly modern payment systems can break down.

Simon Phillips, a retail and foreign exchange business leader, said: “Most of us take card and contactless payments for granted, and the technology is great – right up until the moment it stops working.”

Last month, a Google system failure caused several banking apps to crash, which resulted in millions of Revolut customers being unable to access their money or use their bank cards, while users of Lloyds Bank, HSBC, Barclays, Bank of Scotland, Natwest, Halifax, Nationwide, Royal Mail and DPD also reported issues.

Keeping some cash at home can therefore be a sensible precaution to ensure you could still pay for essentials, such as food and fuel, in an emergency.

How much cash is safe to keep at home?

As a rule of thumb, you should have enough cash to cover essential spending for two to three days. For smaller households, this might be around £100, while larger households or those living in rural areas might prefer to keep up to £300 at home.

You might be tempted to keep even more, but Harriet Guevara, the chief savings officer at Nottingham Building Society, warned against going overboard.

“Beyond concerns like loss or theft, cash held outside the banking system loses any potential for interest, isn’t protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) and is often not covered in full by home insurance policies,” she said.

Most home insurance policies only cover cash up to a limit, usually between £200 and £500, so check your policy to be sure. Anything beyond that won’t be covered in the event of theft, fire or flood.

Sarah Coles, the head of personal finance at AJ Bell, also suggested having a broader backup plan.

She said: “If you’re worried about having access to your bank, it can make sense to have an arrangement with someone you are close to (and you trust) that you can call on in an emergency, and vice versa. In some cases, if you can’t withdraw money, you can still transfer it.”

Where should you store cash at home?

Cash at home should be kept securely. Yet research from security site Safe.co.uk found that more than two-thirds (67pc) of people keep valuables, including cash, in storage that is not locked.

Anthony Neary, the company’s security expert, said: “Far too often, people are relying on obvious hiding places, such as inside drawers or cupboards, or even out on shelves, which offer little to no protection against opportunistic theft.

“Instead, use a secure storage solution such as a compact home locker or cash box with a lock.”

Storage should be fireproof, as well as heavy or bolted to a wall so that it would be difficult to remove if someone broke into your home. It should also be stored out of sight, away from windows and doors, according to Vlatka Lake, of self-storage operator Space Station.

She said: “Lofts are ideal because they are hard to reach and sometimes require ladder access. If you do go for this option, make sure to store the cash in a sealed container to avoid it getting damaged or mouldy. It should be stored in a dry but well-ventilated area.”

Whatever you do, don’t keep your cash in a bedside drawer or under your pillows or mattress, as these are the first places intruders will check.

Ms Coles added: “There are some traditional hiding spots where burglars will look first, like the freezer, the sock drawer and biscuit tins, so they’re worth avoiding. If you have a lot of books, one option is to choose a book to hide it in. A burglar will run out of time looking for it.”

How else can I protect my access to money?

In addition to keeping some cash in hand, it may also be sensible to be prepared in case your bank experiences an outage.

Ms Coles said that some people will hold two current accounts for this reason, so that if one is inaccessible, they can still get hold of money deposited with a different bank.

Furthermore, the FSCS only guarantees your money up to £120,000 per person, per firm. So if your deposits are likely to go over the threshold, you should spread your money between accounts to ensure that you’re protected.

Similarly, it is considered good practice to keep some of your savings in an easy-access account so it is on hand in case of emergencies. However, this money will not generate the same level of interest as accounts that require notice, so it’s important to only keep what you need there.

data.title: Volvo loses £1bn in value as it slashes 2,500 jobs
data.description:
Volvo has announced plans to slash 2,500 jobs after a sharp fall in sales triggered a share price slump that has wiped £1bn from its value.

Shares in the company, which is owned by Chinese group Geely, plunged as much as 31pc after it revealed revenues fell by 23pc in the third quarter.

Volvo announced a 5bn Swedish kronor (£376.4m) cost-cutting plan that will result in around 2,000 job cuts in Sweden and another 500 globally “through natural attrition and by targeted exit packages to employees”.

The car manufacturer warned it may have to take “additional actions” after revenues in China fell by almost 50pc and it was hit by the loss of electric car subsidies in the US.

Volvo issued a profit warning and pulled its annual guidance earlier this month as sales declined.

Hakan Samuelsson, Volvo’s chief executive, said on Friday: “We continue to operate in a very tough environment with strong external challenges: de-globalisation, hypercompetition and climate change.

“The third quarter of 2026 was very disappointing and reflects a year that has become far more challenging than originally anticipated. Our ongoing turnaround plan therefore needs ​a decisive reinforcement.”

Volvo is the latest European car manufacturer to announce sweeping job losses. In July, BMW revealed it would cut 8,000 jobs in an attempt to reduce costs. Earlier this year, Volkswagen said it would cut as many as 100,000 roles out of a total workforce of 650,000. The move is expected to result in the closure of four factories.

Jaguar Land Rover, Britain’s largest car manufacturer, said in September that it would cut 4,000 jobs over the next two years.

Volvo’s revenues in the three months to the end of September slumped to 66.9bn Swedish kronor (£5bn), a 23pc decline from the same period a year earlier.

The car manufacturer also fell to a net loss of 5.7bn kronor (£429.2m) in the third quarter, down from a net profit of 4.5bn kronor (£338.8m) a year earlier.

Volvo, which had bet heavily on electric vehicle sales, said the axing of customer incentives in the US under Donald Trump had dented its revenue.

In 2024, the carmaker scrapped a target of transitioning to selling only electric cars by the end of the decade.

Last month, Volvo said that Mr Samuelsson would leave as chief executive next year, with Klaus Zellmer, the boss of Skoda Auto, due to take up the Volvo chief executive of the Swedish car manufacturer “no later” than October next year.

data.title: The 33-year-old at the forefront of Britain’s defence revolution
data.description:
To see the future of Britain’s defence industry, you have to visit a four-storey building found on what used to be a car park off Old Kent Road. This clean and functional edifice is the biggest new factory in London since the Second World War.

A Union Flag overlooks the factory floor, where 12 machines are silently engaged in turning steel, aluminium and titanium into precision components for jet engines, drones, robots and much more.

Presiding over them is Alexander Fitzgerald, the 33-year-old founder and chief executive of the company, Isembard, which he established in late 2024.

Like everyone who creates a successful business, the T-shirt-wearing entrepreneur spotted a problem and proposed a solution. “What’s happening across every single sector right now – from aerospace to defence to robotics to energy to semiconductors – is that demand is massively increasing, but the supply of manufacturing capacity to make those components is reducing,” he says.

Isembard’s driving purpose is to provide some of that desperately needed extra capacity. The opportunity is all the greater because of a revolution sweeping Britain’s defence industry.

For generations, the sector has been dominated by a handful of large “prime contractors”, such as BAE Systems, which specialise in the slow and hugely expensive production of a relative handful of advanced jet fighters, tanks and warships, designed to stay in service for decades.

But the lesson from Ukraine is that there are increasing – and critical – advantages for countries that can speedily produce an abundance of smaller and cheaper systems, such as drones, then constantly improve and redesign them, and turn out new and better models every few months. This requires a multitude of small and medium-sized enterprises that can compete to be the most innovative and efficient by deploying AI to make an ever-changing array of components as quickly and cheaply as possible.

Isembard is already doing exactly that. Companies send 3D designs for the parts they need, and Isembard manufactures them according to those designs. “We build our own software and AI to make setting up our factories and running our factories really efficient,” says Fitzgerald.

At present, about 95 per cent of components for manufacturing are produced by small and medium-scale businesses. It is an extraordinary fact that the average age of the owners of these companies in the UK is 65 – and that no less than 40 per cent of them plan to retire within five years.

At the exact moment when Europe is rearming – with all Nato countries, including Britain, pledging to spend at least 3.5 per cent of GDP on defence by 2035 – the supply chain for new components is contracting.

Hence, Isembard is expanding rapidly to meet pent-up demand. Fitzgerald opened his first factory last year, and today his company has 18 worldwide – eight in Britain, eight in America and one each in France and Germany.

This growth has been accelerated by Isembard’s unique business model, which allows for franchised factories. All but five of the existing plants are not owned by the company, but franchised to individual operators. The newest, in Swindon, took a mere 90 days to set up, and Fitzgerald aims to get this down to one or two weeks.

Speed and agility are everything. Fitzgerald notes that what has allowed Ukraine to resist the Russian invaders is not one kind of exquisitely engineered drone, but rather a vast and constantly changing array of different models. “In Ukraine, it’s not one type of drone – and 10 billion of them,” he says. “It’s a zoo of different types of drones, at all classes and all stages. Then you need to be able to scale up.”

Fitzgerald adds: “You need a manufacturing base, which is fundamentally a question of, ‘Have you got enough stuff that can make stuff? Have you networked them enough to be more efficient?’ That’s really the core of our business.”

Reindustrialising Britain by reshoring production is, he believes, the key to the country’s future prosperity. “The grand theory of everything is manufacturing because it’s the root of our prosperity, security and purpose,” he says. “I subscribe to the manufacturing dream – that means security and prosperity [depend on] your ability to make stuff.”

Nearby, the computer numerical control (CNC) machines – which have affectionate nicknames such as Cathy and Big Bertha – on the factory floor are playing their part in reindustrialising Britain by turning out the precisely shaped objects that will soon be flying at high speed as the components of jet engines or drones.

The factory, which covers three floors and 160,000 square feet, aims to triple its workforce to 200 by the end of next year. Taking delivery of the hulking CNCs required Fitzgerald to install a bigger loading door in the building, which was previously used as a grocery depot. The machines had to arrive in the early hours of the morning, since there are timing restrictions within three miles of Charing Cross for loads of that weight and size.

Fitzgerald emphasises that Isembard is not a “defence tech company”, but rather a “manufacturing company”. About 60 per cent of its customers are in aerospace and defence, while most of the rest are in robotics.

But Russia is unlikely to be interested in that distinction as its intelligence services carry out their escalating campaign of sabotage and subversion across Europe, including in Britain.

Is Fitzgerald concerned about that threat? “Yes, and I think the Government should be concerned,” he replies. “We have good security protections in both the cyber and the physical side. We’ve had a lot of support from the Government, and from the police and other agencies, as well.”

Fitzgerald has personal experience of Whitehall, since he spent three years as a Treasury civil servant after graduating from Nottingham University with a degree in biochemistry. Earlier, he had also tried his hand at journalism as an intern at City AM.

He enjoyed his time working in the Government, but cannot help remembering: “When I thought I had the right answer for something, it still had to go through six pairs of hands to get to someone to make a decision. That frustrated me.”

He left the Treasury to start a broadband company that amassed almost 100,000 customers before he sold it to Octopus Group in 2022. Fitzgerald founded Isembard soon afterwards, and the company now makes components for customers like Anduril, which manufactures drones and autonomous weaponry, and Oxford Space Systems, which produces the antennae for satellites.

In the past, certain British investors and banks had a fastidious disdain for any businesses linked to defence, some of which were denied financial services. Fitzgerald, who is also an Army reservist, has encountered no such difficulties, and he believes that attitudes have changed. “I think Ukraine has changed that,” he says. “Geopolitics has changed that.”

Something else that has changed is the attitude towards manufacturing in general. One of Andy Burnham’s central priorities is “reindustrialisation” and recapturing the dynamism of former years.

In that spirit, Fitzgerald named his company after the great Victorian engineer, Isambard Kingdom Brunel, though he adapted the spelling of his hero’s Christian name because the original domain had already been taken.

Today, he keeps a black top hat on his desk in tribute to the man whose individual drive and genius powered Britain’s first industrial revolution.

His other inspiration is Lord Beaverbrook, the minister for aircraft production in 1940, who galvanised British industry into delivering 100 Spitfires and Hurricanes every week, making him an architect of victory in the Battle of Britain and changing the course of the Second World War.

“The Air Ministry didn’t like him. He was threatening to resign the whole time, but he got the job done,” says Fitzgerald, who notes that Beaverbrook tripled production in a matter of months by distributing the manufacture of Spitfire and Hurricane components between hundreds of superbly innovative and cost-efficient small and medium enterprises across the country.

That formula saved Britain in 1940. It might yet do the same again.

data.title: Elon Musk to kill off Tesla’s Cybertruck
data.description:
Elon Musk is to end production of Tesla’s Cybertruck after sales of the controversial electric pick-up proved a disappointment.

The electric carmaker’s chief executive signalled last night that production of the Cybertruck will wind down in 2027, making way for the business to produce more robotaxis at its Texas Gigafactory.

Posting on social media, Mr Musk said: “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

The announcement comes just three years after the Cybertruck first went on sale.

Mr Musk had hailed the three-ton vehicle as “bulletproof” and “apocalypse-proof”, while the company’s website promotes its “ultra-hard stainless-steel exoskeleton” and a range of up to 325 miles.

However, the truck’s high price dampened demand among motorists.

It was initially set to cost $39,999 (£30,600) but the cheapest version now starts at $60,000 (£45,900).

Tesla sold just 11,586 Cybertrucks in the first nine months of 2026, according to analysts Cox Automotive, far below Mr Musk’s previous predictions of 250,000 sales a year.

While Mr Musk had billed the pick-up as the ultimate off-road electric vehicle, the Cybertruck has suffered from a series of mishaps and faults before and after it went on sale.

When demonstrating the truck’s toughened glass during its 2019 launch event, a Tesla executive threw a ball bearing at its window, causing it to shatter.

Tesla has also been forced to issue recalls of the truck over braking issues and other problems, including the vehicle’s trim falling off.

Several trucks have been involved in accidents where they have burst into fireballs after a crash.

Mr Musk took the decision to end production as he attempts to revive Tesla by focusing on AI, robotics and driverless taxis, increasing production of its Cybercab vehicles and Optimus humanoid robots.

The company has launched ride-hailing services in a handful of US cities, while it is planning to build up to 125,000 autonomous electric cabs per year at its flagship Texas plant.

Shares in Mr Musk’s companies have plunged this week after the Democrats swung to victory in the US midterm elections, taking both the House and the Senate.

Tesla’s stock is down more than 12pc since Tuesday, while SpaceX is down 11pc. Mr Musk’s net worth plummeted by close to $80bn in one day on Thursday to around $785bn, according to Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index.

data.title: ‘Tesla of China’ could make cars in Britain as Burnham considers tariffs
data.description:
A company nicknamed the “Tesla of China” is considering manufacturing its vehicles in Britain as Andy Burnham mulls tariffs on Beijing’s electric car companies.

Brian Gu, the vice-chairman and president of Xpeng, told The Telegraph it would be “natural to think about local manufacturing” if sales in Britain hit a certain level.

The comments came as the Guangzhou-headquartered company this week announced plans to launch five new luxury vehicles aimed at British buyers.

Xpeng has been seen as a potential challenger to Tesla, pursuing a similar strategy of hi-tech vehicles packed with self-driving technology, while it has also developed humanoid robots.

Its sleek coupes, such as the LO3, share similarities with Tesla’s vehicles, pitting the Chinese companies directly against Elon Musk’s car business.

At a launch at the luxury Fairmont Windsor Park Hotel on Thursday, Xpeng unveiled the UK version of its LO3 SUV coupe, which it said would start at £32,990 and feature a range of more than 300 miles.

Speaking to The Telegraph, Mr Gu said the company would consider building vehicles in Britain if its launch in the market is a success.

Mr Gu said: “It depends on the success that we anticipate from these launches. We hope to generate a substantial business. And once we reach a certain volume, then it’s natural to think about local manufacturing.”

It comes as the Prime Minister considers imposing tariffs on Chinese electric cars. The EU has already enforced steep tariffs of up to 35.3pc on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) and the Prime Minister has been seeking closer ties with Europe, raising the prospect the UK will adopt similar rules.

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, has been drafting a tariff blueprint and Anas Sarwar, the trade minister, said last month that Britain and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to combat the flood of Chinese EV imports.

Xpeng’s latest UK vehicles will be built in China and shipped to Britain, meaning they would fall foul of any prospective tariff regime. It also produces cars for Europe out of a factory in Austria, although this plant is already near full capacity.

Xpeng’s launch in Britain follows a flood of other Chinese car brands that have swept across the UK market. The Jaecoo 7, made by China’s Chery, was the UK’s top-selling car in September, while BYD, which makes electric cars such as the Seal, has claimed close to 10pc of EV and hybrid sales so far this year.

The European tariffs have prompted Chinese carmakers to shift more production into the bloc to avoid the levies.

Some are also now exploring similar arrangements in the UK in anticipation of potential tariffs here. Chery, whose Jaecoo 7 is known as the “Temu Range Rover” for its lookalike appearance of the British marque, has sealed a deal with Nissan to explore making its cars in Sunderland.

Mr Gu said Chery’s deal was “very much a validation of their success in the UK market”. “If you want to be a leading player, you have to have more local capabilities,” he said.

The Xpeng boss said the company would have to “react” to any new UK rules on Chinese imports. It previously began making cars with Austrian manufacturer Magna in 2025 after Europe brought in its own tough levies.

Mr Gu said: “We have to react to whatever arrangement or regime there is, just like when we reacted to Europe when they announced EV tariffs on Chinese brands.

“We want to keep the current open, friendly and conductive market environment. But we as a company need to react whenever there is change.”

Xpeng plans to build a network of 100 retail outlets and service stations across the UK by the end of 2027. It is planning to open three flagship stores in London and Manchester in the next six months.

The company also announced plans to explore bringing its robotaxi service, known as Yoyo, to UK roads. “London is a very important, key robotaxi market. We also want to see how Yoyo can be tested,” Mr Gu said.

data.title: How we created a contemporary hobbit home
data.description:
When Gail Pirkis and her husband David spent two years scouring Wiltshire, Dorset, Somerset and Devon for the perfect site, and a house they could demolish and rebuild, they finally found what they were looking for on the edge of Dartmoor: a modest 1930s prefabricated bungalow with an extraordinary view. Now in its place is one of Britain’s most thoughtful contemporary country homes: a grass-roofed, granite-clad house that appears to grow from the landscape itself.

“The minute we saw the site on a beautiful May morning, we knew it was what we wanted. In fact, we bought the house without looking inside it,” recalls Gail, co-editor of the literary quarterly Slightly Foxed. The condition of the existing building was of little consequence; it was the setting that mattered. “It had the sense of being in its own private valley with a wonderful view overlooking both cultivated land and wilderness,” she says.

Gail imagined sheltered land, while David wanted a view and plenty of sky. With hills rising behind the house to protect it from the prevailing westerlies, and the land falling away in front before rising again in the distance, the site offered both. Living in London at the time, they were already thinking about a future in the countryside. “I think we always knew that we would like to end up living rurally, and we wanted a chance to build a house that would still be standing in several hundred years’ time,” she says.

For Gail, the move was also about creating somewhere conducive to her work. “I wanted to live somewhere quiet in which to edit, commission articles, plan which books we might reissue and think about long-term plans for the magazine. Our London office is a hive of activity, but not always the ideal place in which to think.”

Vision and design

Having bought the property in 1994, the couple initially submitted plans for an Arts and Crafts-style house, but their application was rejected by Dartmoor National Park. Undeterred, they appointed a new architect and took a different approach. “We planned a more timeless, contemporary house that would sit comfortably within the landscape and permission was granted.”

Their thinking was influenced by photographs of a house in Ireland that had been published in Perspectives, the then-Prince of Wales’s short-lived architectural magazine. Built into a slope and incorporating natural boulders at one end, the house provided a starting point for their own ideas. Working with architect Peter Hall, the couple developed a design shaped as much by the internal layout as by its relationship with the landscape. “We had a fairly clear idea of the layout we wanted inside, but it was Peter who gave external form to the internal layout,” explains Gail. “Crucially, he understood our wish that the house should feel part of the landscape.”

A key part of the vision was to create an uninterrupted connection between indoors and out. The gentle curve of the house is articulated through a series of right-angled corner windows, where the glass meets glass without the need for mastic or a supporting bar. “The corner windows give us the most glorious views,” says Gail. The result is a softened boundary between interior and landscape – an almost symbiotic relationship between the house and its surroundings.

Built into the hillside over two levels, the house has an unusual arrangement, with the upper storey set back from the floor below, creating what are effectively two ground floors. Every window opens directly onto meadow grass. Its boomerang-like curve changes orientation where the kitchen meets the hall, offering differing views from one end to the other. “We drew some inspiration from a Frank Lloyd Wright house in Manchester, New Hampshire, which has deep eaves and where the rooms flow into one another,” says Gail.

Both levels have green roofs: the lower is planted with crocuses, and the upper undulates like a meadow and is sown with wildflowers. Granite forms the exterior walls, while the windows, some sills and the undersides of the deep eaves are finished in oak.

Gail and David deliberately avoided fashionable features. “We didn’t want acres of glass and steel, and fittings that would soon date. Nor did we want an island in the kitchen, bar stools or a boiling tap,” Gail says. Although happy with the design, she admits that some decisions proved less successful. “We went for the cheapest quotation when choosing a builder and with hindsight the project would have been completed much faster and for the same amount of money had we gone for one of the higher initial quotes.”

Considering the environment

The choice of materials was largely guided by a desire to use local and reclaimed resources. The granite was sourced from the spoil heap of a disused quarry about 10 miles away, while oak from trees felled on the land was planked and seasoned for the outbuilding doors, porch bench and cupboards. Inside, the flooring is reclaimed oak and all the windows are double-glazed.

The house’s energy provision has also evolved. “Initially we had an oil-fired boiler and underfloor heating, but we switched to air source heat pumps about 15 years ago,” explains Gail. They’ve since added a wood burner to the kitchen. Their recent application to install solar panels behind an existing granite wall on the land was refused by Dartmoor National Park.

The landscaping was designed to complement the architecture while providing shelter from Dartmoor’s changeable weather. “Here, one needs protection, so the land around the house was landscaped to include existing granite boulders and a ha-ha that separates the garden area from the field below where sheep graze.” Beyond the house are fields, woodland, a small section of moor and tor and a restored lake. “We’ve planted 2,000 trees and now that these have matured, most local walkers don’t realise the house is here.”

Creating an interior for book lovers

With a burgeoning collection of books to accommodate, generous shelving was an essential part of the design. From a hallway flanked by green shelves – where grandchildren are fond of climbing up and down the two sets of library steps – to a staircase incorporating curved pigeonhole shelving, books are never far from reach. “The staircase was built off site before being dismantled and installed in the house, before which we enjoyed practising walking up and down, pausing at the shelves, imagining them in situ,” says Gail.

As Gail says: “Books really do furnish a house.” The collection now stands at 4,000. Alongside Slightly Foxed-published books such as a beautifully illustrated edition of Charles Phillipson’s Letters to Michael, Ysenda Maxtone Graham’s Love Divine and all the children’s books by Ronald Welch, Rosemary Sutcliff and BB (Denys Watkins-Pitchford) the publisher has reissued are David’s mountaineering books, a complete set of Everyman editions of PG Wodehouse, and Gail’s copies of Arthur Ransome’s books.

Just off the sitting room, an alcove serves as Gail’s home office. Lined with books – no surprise – it has a desk beneath a shallow dome with concealed lighting and a secret door leading to a small music room. “It’s a wonderful spot, somewhat inspired by Sir John Soane’s house in Lincoln’s Inn Fields, London.”

However, Gail doesn’t always stay at her desk. “I tend to migrate to the dining room for good light when checking proofs or to the kitchen table where the wood burner is going on colder days.” If she gets stuck on a difficult article, she heads outside. “I tend to go off to the veg patch to do a bit of weeding or take Stanley, our cocker spaniel, for a walk around the land. That usually clears the mind: this is the magic of living here.”

data.title: Energy giant hit by wind turbine faults at major offshore field
data.description:
Faulty turbines are causing months of delays at a wind farm project off England’s north-east coast.

SSE said problems with equipment were slowing the construction of the Dogger Bank A wind farm, one of the UK’s biggest renewable energy projects.

It came as the energy company reiterated that it was no longer on track to hit its 2030 net zero goal of generating 50 terawatt (TW) hours of green electricity a year – a setback to Labour’s hopes of decarbonising UK power grids by 2030.

Dogger Bank, an offshore field about 100 miles off the coast of Yorkshire, will eventually be the world’s largest wind farm.

Built in three phases, it will be capable of providing 6pc of the UK’s power at peak and once complete. It makes the project vital for Labour’s hopes of decarbonising the grid by 2030.

However, SSE said that “additional work” was required on some already installed Dogger Bank A turbines “to meet the required quality and reliability standards”. As a result, the project will not be ready until next summer.

Dogger Bank A’s turbines are made by US firm GE Vernova, which has suffered recent manufacturing issues on other projects.

In July 2024, a GE Vernova Haliade-X turbine blade suffered a catastrophic failure at the Vineyard Wind 1 project in Massachusetts, sending debris onto Nantucket beaches and prompting a major cleanup operation.

In a subsequent statement, GE Vernova confirmed there had been “manufacturing deviations” and said it was removing or strengthening the blades of other machines in that wind farm.

Around the same time, a turbine at Dogger Bank also suffered a catastrophic blade failure. SSE blamed an entirely separate commissioning problem.

In a statement, the company said the machine had been left locked in a position that made it vulnerable to strong winds, implying the failure was a one-off.

‘Teething problems’

SSE’s latest statement suggests problems are more widespread, delaying the whole installation process.

An SSE spokesman said: “The first phase of Dogger Bank experienced teething problems, and remediation works are well under way to ensure those early turbines meet our required quality and reliability standards.

“Dogger Bank B (the second phase of the project) is going well and we have now reached around 100 turbines commissioned across all phases and generated well over 1 TW hour of power in the first half of the year.”

Dogger Bank is a large sandbank in the North Sea, spanning UK, German, Dutch and Danish waters. Its shallow depths make it ideal for wind turbine developments.

SSE and its partners plan four major developments in the area, of which Dogger Bank A is the first phase. Ninety-five turbines are planned and the wind farm’s eventual output of 1.2 gigawatts – on a windy day – would be on a par with one of the UK’s nuclear power stations.

The company’s separate warning that it will probably miss its green power target of 50 TW hours of clean power by 2030 follows a 2025 decision to cut spending on renewables by £3bn.

data.title: Burnham to halt wind and solar subsidies in net zero climbdown
data.description:
Andy Burnham has ordered a halt to new wind and solar power subsidies in a net zero climbdown aimed at cutting household energy bills.

The Government revealed on Tuesday that next year’s auction of contracts for difference (CfDs) – a form of state support for renewable energy projects – will be paused to ensure it benefits consumers.

This year’s auction, known as auction round eight, is expected to continue as normal in the coming weeks. It is expected to award subsidies that could be worth hundreds of millions of pounds a year, paid for by households and businesses.

But Michael Shanks, the energy minister, told the House of Lords environment committee that next year’s auction was being put on hold so that the CfD programme could be reformed.

It follows concerns that the development of renewable power capacity is moving faster than work to upgrade the electricity grid.

This has resulted in network bottlenecks and vast amounts of power going to waste. It has also led to wind farms being paid hundreds of millions of pounds to switch off, a practice known as “curtailment”.

Mr Shanks told peers that the Government was drawing up a new plan to prevent too much future capacity being built in Scotland, which is behind the biggest bottlenecks. He said the way subsidies are awarded will also change.

CfDs are the UK’s flagship mechanism for supporting renewable energy projects and are ultimately funded through consumer bills.

They ensure generators are always paid a fixed strike price for the electricity they produce, regardless of market prices.

Developers win CfDs by putting forward projects and bidding for fixed prices in auctions, helping to ensure the strike prices are competitive.

Last year’s estimated CfD budget was £1.7bn, covering wind farms, solar farms and other clean technologies.

“The CfD process has been incredibly useful to give investors certainty to build new projects,” Mr Shanks said. But he added that “we do now want to pause” before the next auction round to “look at whether we need some more significant changes to the contracts for difference scheme to make sure they work for the consumers of the country”.

John Healey, the Chancellor, declared in last week’s Budget that Labour’s priority was “first and foremost cheaper energy”.

Whitehall sources told The Telegraph that his remarks signalled a demotion of the 2030 clean power targets championed by Ed Miliband, the Foreign Secretary, when he ran the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.

Dan Tomlinson, a Treasury minister, said after the Budget that Mr Burnham would pursue “a new energy pathway” to “bring energy costs down to help British business to compete and British households to cope”.

Pointing to the rising cost of wasted wind power, Mr Tomlinson said: “With growing constraint and distribution costs, it’s right that the system costs of all new power are considered.”

He added that the UK would “only procure clean power” through auction round eight “if we are confident it will lower bills” and “we will reform the contract for difference [for the next auction] to support building the lowest cost system, fixing market distortions and siting assets in the right place”.

Ministers have also imposed a moratorium on new levies and policy costs being added to bills.

The Government insists that it stands by the 2030 clean power targets, which aim to ensure that 95pc of electricity generated by the end of the decade comes from “clean” sources such as renewables, nuclear or batteries.

However, ministers have sought to downplay the commitment.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, told MPs last month that it would be “pretty hard” to deliver clean power while keeping bills down, having previously said that affordability was her top concern.

She also told a conference that while her department would “play its part” to try and reach Mr Miliband’s target, “the public doesn’t measure the success of our energy system in gigawatts – they measure it in bills”.

James Alexander, chief executive of the UK Sustainable Investment and Finance Association, which represents pension funds and other big financial backers, said: “Investors will be deeply concerned by comments from the energy minister today that cast doubt on next year’s renewable energy auction.”

He added: “The Contracts for Difference model has been a crucial driver of investment in clean power, helping to secure record offshore wind capacity this year and build a world-leading renewables sector.

“But telling markets the Government intends to review this process risks sending a worrying signal about the strength of the UK’s commitment to the energy transition.

“We now need to see urgent clarity on the future of this process, or the Government could put billions of pounds of capital at risk.”

The Government has been approached for comment.

data.title: Workers fear losing jobs over train delays, warn MPs
data.description:
Workers fear losing their jobs because rail services are regularly late, MPs have warned.

A spate of line closures and cancellations during the summer heatwaves made it impossible for thousands of commuters to arrive at the office on time.

MPs at a Westminster Hall debate said workers were increasingly fearful of the lack of reliable train connections and urged the Government to spend more on rail infrastructure to improve punctuality.

Charlotte Cane, the Liberal Democrat MP for Ely and East Cambridgeshire, said: “One [constituent] in particular has written to say that because their train has been so unreliable for getting to their job in London that their employer is now putting them under pressure.

“They are becoming an unreliable member of staff and their employer doesn’t know when they are going to turn up to work.

“They are also having to make up the time at the end of the day, which means they are getting home very late. It makes it a complete nightmare for them.”

Desperate to protect their jobs, some workers were now considering moving house to be closer to stations with more reliable services, MPs said.

Others are considering giving up well-paid positions in London and other major cities for less lucrative roles closer to home.

Among the worst-hit lines this summer was the route between King’s Cross and King’s Lynn via Cambridge and Ely, the later of which lies in Ms Cane’s constituency.

It suffered three months of disruption, including 900 cancellations after normally damp peat beneath the tracks dried out, leading the ground to become uneven.

James Wild, the Conservative MP for North West Norfolk, which includes King’s Lynn, said people from the town who worked in Cambridge and London had found the disruption intolerable.

He told The Telegraph: “I’ve had quite a number of constituents who have said they’re thinking of moving jobs. They’ve been in tears and incredibly stressed.

“One lady said her husband, who commutes and is self-employed, had been driven to depression and was having suicidal thoughts because he was worried that he wouldn’t be able to provide for his family. It’s pushing people to breaking point.”

Mr Wild said some commuters had opted to drive to Peterborough on the East Coast Main Line, or Norwich, which has trains to Liverpool Street – both an hour away by road – to be sure of getting to work.

He said there were concerns that with the line suffering heat-related disruption for the past two summers, people would stop viewing King’s Lynn as a viable commuter town, which could have a knock-on effect on house prices.

Mr Wild questioned Andy Burnham about the matter in September, when the Prime Minister said he would “convene a rail summit soon”.

Richard Foord, the Liberal Democrat MP for Honiton and Sidmouth, said commuters to cities beyond London had also been affected.

He said restrictions imposed between London Waterloo and the West Country had in one case led a dental hygienist to cancel her 9am appointments “indefinitely”.

Simon Lightwood, the minister for local transport, said he could not rule out further weather-related disruption.

He added that while speed restrictions and closures might be frustrating, the railway’s primary duty was to keep passengers safe.

data.title: Protein craze sparks 180pc sales jump for £750m nutrition brand
data.description:
Britain’s growing appetite for protein has helped fuel a surge in sales at sports supplements brand Applied Nutrition.

The Liverpool-based company said sales via UK supermarkets jumped 180pc over the past year as shoppers bought protein powders, energy supplements and hydration tablets.

Thomas Ryder, Applied Nutrition’s chief executive, said even pre-workout supplements, used by gym-goers to boost their performance, were in demand.

He said: “I thought it was too early, but I was proved wrong. It’s performing really, really well.”

The £750m company has benefited from the growing popularity of “protein-maxxing”, which has seen shoppers seek out protein-rich foods in an effort to build muscle and improve their health.

Its annual sales jumped 51pc to £161.6m in the year to July, while pre-tax profits rose 44pc to £41m.

The protein craze has transformed supermarket shelves, with the nutrient now being added to everything from ice cream and pizza to pasta, cheese and bottled water.

Sainsbury’s has introduced dedicated high-protein ranges, while Marks & Spencer sells a 20-product Nutrient Dense line.

According to figures from NIQ, 57pc of British shoppers follow a high-protein diet to some extent.

The boom has been fuelled partly by the popularity of weight-loss jabs such as Mounjaro and Wegovy.

The drugs suppress appetite, meaning patients eat less and risk losing muscle alongside fat. Doctors recommend eating enough protein to help preserve muscle during weight loss.

Robert F Kennedy Jr, Donald Trump’s health secretary, has also championed higher protein consumption, with new US dietary guidelines urging Americans to eat it with every meal.

Applied Nutrition partnered with Morrisons in January to launch 53 high-protein products, including pizzas, ice cream and ready meals aimed at people taking weight-loss drugs.

Mr Ryder said the company was now in talks with other businesses about similar partnerships.

He said: “We’re in aisles now in supermarkets that we might never have been in.”

The company has also launched supplements aimed at people taking weight-loss jabs, including protein powders, collagen gels and digestive capsules, through Holland & Barrett.

However, the rush for protein has pushed up costs for manufacturers, with surging demand driving up the price of whey, a milk-derived ingredient used in protein powders.

European whey protein concentrate prices more than doubled in the year to August, rising from €11,700 (£10,000) to almost €26,000 a tonne, according to commodity data provider Expana.

Mr Ryder said Applied Nutrition increased its prices in August and had reformulated products to reduce its reliance on whey protein concentrate.

He said ingredient prices were now falling, with the company hoping to benefit from cheaper supplies early next year.

Applied Nutrition has also expanded into the US, where its supplements, branded as Sour Patch Kids, have gone on sale in thousands of Walmart stores.

data.title: Swiss face £9bn bill to keep trains running on time
data.description:
Switzerland’s trains are celebrated for their immaculate punctuality. But now the country is facing a £9bn bill to stop its rail services becoming like those in Germany, its erratic neighbour.

The country’s largest railway operator, state-owned SBB, has said its backlog of repairs to tracks and signal boxes rose 12pc last year to 9.5bn Swiss francs (£8.6bn).

If the repairs aren’t carried out, SBB has warned that Switzerland risks “a situation similar to that in other countries” – a reference to Germany, where the formerly clockwork-like train network has become notoriously unreliable.

So far, the Swiss trains are holding the line on their fabled punctuality. This year 94pc of its trains have arrived within three minutes of their scheduled time, about the same rate as the previous two years.

No other major European country gets above 90pc, and many have resorted to using a looser definition of punctuality.

Britain scored 84pc last year. Germany clocked 88pc, but that excludes cancelled trains and defines punctual as within six minutes. Even on that metric, just 60pc of Germany’s long-distance and high-speed trains run on time.

Germany’s decline arose from underinvestment in maintenance. As it tries to play catch-up, large sections of track often have to be closed for repairs, making punctuality even worse.

Switzerland will be keen to avoid that fate.

But SBB is at loggerheads with the Swiss government, which instead wants to spend 20bn Swiss francs (CHF).on expanding and embellishing the rail network.

This could include building a whole new station at Lucerne, at a potential cost of more than CHF 3bn, and a 17-mile tunnel with a potential budget of CHF 800m.

SBB, in a submission to a public consultation, urged the authorities to prioritise fixing the existing network over any major expansion.

Both sides agree, though, that the signalling system also needs a technological overhaul that will cost a further CHF 9bn.

This week SBB kicked off the first CHF 2bn tender for the IT revamp. The full digitalisation of signalling will cost another CHF 7bn by 2045, but so far the government has budgeted just CHF 1bn for this process.

Meanwhile, money is tight for the essential repairs to keep the trains running on time. SBB has said it needs to repair at least 143 miles of track a year, but last year only managed 116 miles.

Funding for its track and signalling work comes from a separate Rail Infrastructure Fund, which is bankrolled by annual contributions from the national and cantonal governments, alongside some hypothecated portions of VAT, income tax and the mineral oil tax. Some of this funding is due to expire in 2030.

data.title: BBC scraps Room on the Broom over Walliams abuse allegations
data.description:
The BBC has removed an adaptation of Dame Julia Donaldson’s children’s book Room On The Broom featuring David Walliams.

The broadcaster withdrew the animated 2012 film from platforms such as iPlayer as part of a review of “all material” featuring and written by the comedian following the publication of sex abuse allegations.

Walliams, 55, a children’s author and former Britain’s Got Talent (BGT) judge, was named as part of an alleged sexual misconduct investigation by The Guardian and ITV News on Tuesday.

One woman described her alleged encounter with Walliams when she was 15 as “sexual assault”, while several women accused him of “grooming” them when they were teenagers. Walliams denies any wrongdoing.

On Friday, the Metropolitan Police said it had received a number of non-recent “serious” sex offence allegations against him “in recent days”.

Earlier in the week, the BBC said it was carrying out a content review on its platforms and was in the process of “removing” some.

In Room On The Broom, Walliams voices a frog, alongside Gillian Anderson as a witch and Simon Pegg as the narrator.

His character has just three lines in the 30-minute film, along with some “ribbits”.

In one line, his character says: “I am a frog, as clean as can be. Is there room on the broom for a frog like me?”

A BBC spokesman said: “These are serious allegations. As such, the BBC is looking carefully at all material featuring and written by David Walliams on our platforms. We are in the process of removing some programmes, including Little Britain, whilst this review is under way.”

Walliams rose to fame working alongside Matt Lucas on the BBC sketch comedy series Little Britain, which ran from 2003 until 2006.

They then created and starred in Come Fly With Me, which aired on the BBC for one season in 2010.

Both shows are currently unavailable on iPlayer, as is a 2020 episode of Who Do You Think You Are? featuring Walliams.

Adaptations of his best-selling children’s books, including Gangsta Granny and Billionaire Boy, are also unavailable on the service.

Channel 4 and Sky also axe Walliams content

Other broadcasters have also removed programming featuring Walliams from their streaming services.

Channel 4 has taken down episodes of 8 Out Of 10 Cats Does Countdown and the 2021 special Chitty Flies Again with Walliams.

Sky also removed Walliams’s work from its platform and dropped the distribution of the upcoming film Fing! based on his 2019 children’s book.

In a statement, a Sky spokesman said: “The allegations made against David Walliams are extremely serious. We have notified the producers of the film of our intention to exit our position as the UK and Ireland licensee of Fing!

“We have already removed content which features him from our platforms.”

Angel Studios confirmed it would still release the film in the US, but a cameo featuring Walliams would be removed and he would not take part in its promotion.

Walliams has not yet responded to Tuesday’s reports in The Guardian or ITV News.

But in a letter understood to have been sent several months ago to journalists working on the investigations, he denied being a “sexual predator”.

Walliams said he recognised he “behaved thoughtlessly” at times, and regretted not taking people’s feelings “properly into account”, but insisted he had not broken the law.

The ITV and The Guardian reports about Walliams followed his unsuccessful attempts to seek an injunction to prevent the media revealing his identity – with his lawyers arguing there was a risk he would take his own life after two previous suicide attempts.

Several sources alleged inappropriate behaviour towards women at the prime-time show BGT, where Walliams served as a judge from 2012 to 2022, and at his publisher HarperCollins, which dropped him last year.

The allegations also led to Walliams being dropped by his literary agency, Independent Talent Group.

Representatives for Dame Julia were contacted for comment.

data.title: What opening a joint bank account taught me about my relationship
data.description:
How do you and your partner deal with joint expenses? Let us know in the comments or email money@telegraph.co.uk*.

If you had told me a year ago that £1 doughnuts would test my relationship with my partner, I wouldn’t have believed it.

My boyfriend Alex and I have been together for two-and-a-half years, yet because work keeps us in separate cities, we have never lived together. Recently, however, we decided to take a different kind of “next step” in our relationship: opening a joint bank account.

There were practical reasons for this, but I was also curious to see how our relationship, as yet untested by more traditional milestones such as marriage, would handle an experiment such as this.

We both thought we knew each other’s attitudes to money, but creating even a relatively small shared pot compels you to turn abstract ideas about fairness, ownership and compromise into actual rules.

We agreed to put the same amount of money into the account as and when it needs topping up. Household items and food we buy when staying together are considered joint expenses, along with train tickets or petrol for travelling to see each other.

Our foray into shared finances was going swimmingly until one day, I got a notification from the bank saying that £1 had just been spent on our joint card. My partner walked in the door a few minutes later, excited because he had just found a pack of five doughnuts on sale for – you guessed it – £1.

This was something that had come up in our relationship before: Alex, a committed saver, is often content to buy or eat whatever is cheapest, while I am more of a food (and everything else) snob who would sooner spend a few extra pounds.

I wasn’t annoyed at the money, but it did puzzle me that he considered this a joint purchase when he was the only one going to be eating them. Fearful of being petty, I decided to let the issue lie.

Yet soon enough, the same question started appearing everywhere. If Alex wants the cheapest toilet paper while I would sooner spring for something softer, should he have to subsidise my preference? If we buy chocolate from the joint account but he eats most of it, is that really a shared expense?

We might have known what we were getting into. Research published by Starling Bank last year found that 76pc of surveyed couples argued about money regardless of how they managed their finances.

Becky Palmano, a 38-year-old production executive based in Jersey, faced similar issues when she first combined finances with her now-husband, Sam, also 38.

Initially, she tells me, they thought they were alike in how they approached money.

Once they began making financial decisions together, this turned out not to be the case: “My attitude is quite ‘live now’, which can occasionally become ‘spend now’, whereas Sam is more inclined to plan ahead, save and deliberate over bigger decisions like trips.”

The couple have devised a strategy for dealing with financial “missteps”, which they call “idiot tax”. The couple keep a shared savings pot of around £5,000 to cover the financial consequences of either of them doing something stupid.

“Recently, I booked Sam on to entirely the wrong flight. Idiot tax,” says Palmano. “The basic rule is that if it’s a genuine mistake, you’re allowed to be annoyed, but you don’t get to turn it into a huge argument about the money. Whoever has messed up has to hold their hands up, admit they’ve been an idiot and, ideally, not do it again.”

She also spoke of an incident early on in their relationship where a disastrous weekend away resulted in a series of costly financial blunders, including a last-minute hire car (which then got damaged) and a speeding fine.

Ultimately, they decided to split the damage 50-50 after realising that sometimes, trying to establish exactly whose expense something is “becomes more ridiculous than the expense itself”.

This was a trap I had already fallen into with my partner. After an absurd discussion where we tried to calculate who was subsidising more of the other’s spending, we resolved to continue splitting things equally and save ourselves the trouble of accounting for every difference in consumption and salary.

Admittedly, this isn’t something I usually agree with. I have always felt that it is best to split things equitably, so if your partner earns more than you, then what they pay in terms of rent and household expenses should reflect that gap.

Yet the difference between our salaries is small – I would estimate that Alex earns £5,000 more than me annually, although it’s difficult to know for certain as we both take on ad-hoc work.

We agreed that for the time being, our relationship would be best served by letting the little things go.

Tom Desborough, a financial planner at Paradigm Life, suggests that those with different attitudes to spending are not inherently incompatible. He finds most couples are willing to compromise a bit because it’s part of being in a loving relationship.

If you want to avoid being blindsided by your partner’s spending habits, however, he recommends asking more holistic questions early on in the relationship. For example, where do you see your life in 10 or 20 years’ time, or if you won the lottery, what would you do?

You may already know that you are both savers, but what you are saving your money for is just as important.

Desborough also recommends a “yours, mine and ours” approach, rather than pooling everything. It is a system Eduardo Gomes, 38, and his wife Carla, 44, eventually arrived at, although it took an expensive accidental purchase to get them there.

When they moved from Brazil to London, they combined their finances to cover rent and household costs, using a single credit card.

During Covid, Eduardo found an auction website and placed bids on five coffee machines, unexpectedly winning all five at a cost of around £1,000. Understandably, his wife wasn’t pleased. He managed to sell four of the machines for a profit, but they have since switched to having both joint and separate accounts.

Now, Gomes says, they have learned from each other’s attitudes; Carla has taught him the importance of having a savings buffer, especially as she now works part-time to spend more time with their young daughter, and he has encouraged her to be more adventurous.

“Ultimately, we complement each other’s spending behaviours,” he says.

This was another lesson Alex and I learned. We could have gone back and forth for hours over whose attitude to money was better, but ultimately, if we wanted to move forward, we needed to accept that there wasn’t going to be an outcome where either of us “wins”.

In that sense, combining even a small part of our finances became a useful trial run for the long-term relationship we hope to have. We might have spent ages debating fairness and compromise in the abstract, but we needed to put those ideas into practice to see how we would build a financial life together.

Of course, compromising over £1 doughnuts is one thing. Making bigger decisions down the line will be considerably harder. The important thing is that we understand each other’s respective money attitudes before we try.

data.title: Burnham to make new North Sea drilling illegal
data.description:
Andy Burnham is poised to ban drilling for new oil and gas in the UK to end exploration in the North Sea.

The Prime Minister has backed an energy bill that would put into law a permanent prohibition on new drilling, a move to make it harder for ministers to reverse the ban in future.

Energy exploration in the UK is subject to the temporary moratorium originally imposed by Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary, but this could be lifted by a future energy secretary.

Mr Burnham is now supporting new laws being introduced by Mr Miliband’s successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh, that would make it harder to reopen the North Sea.

Repealing the proposed new law would need a parliamentary majority.

The Government said the energy independence bill would deliver on its “pragmatic approach to the North Sea, by ending new licences to explore new oil and gas fields while supporting continued production from existing licensed areas”.

If approved by Parliament, the new laws would allow oil companies to keep operating existing licensed oil and gas fields until they are depleted.

But they would be able to drill new wells only if they could be connected to existing infrastructure by subsea pipelines known as tiebacks.

The move follows the approval last month of the Jackdaw gas field, which operates under an existing licence and uses a tieback to pump gas into established pipelines.

Labour is yet to make a decision on the giant Rosebank oil field, west of Shetland, which also has an existing licence.

Both the Conservatives and Reform UK have pledged to restart North Sea exploration and drilling were they to win power.

Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, criticised Mr Burnham’s plans warning: “Labour’s so-called energy independence bill will only make Britain more dependent on oil and gas imports. Labour might as well hang a ‘closed for business’ sign over our North Sea.”

The legislation honours Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledge, which stated: “We will not issue new licences to explore new fields because they will not take a penny off bills, cannot make us energy secure and will only accelerate the worsening climate crisis. In addition, we will not grant new coal licences and will ban fracking for good.”

Some energy insiders and investors disagree, including Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos group.

David Bucknall, the head of subsidiary Ineos Energy, which has a raft of North Sea assets, said: “The Government’s legislation to ban new drilling in the North Sea would actively decrease energy security in the UK.

“Leaving existing resources in the ground at home while we import the same resources from abroad makes our energy autonomy a victim of global instability.”

Analyst Ashley Kelty, from Panmure Liberum, said: “This bill just highlights the lunacy of net zero dogma.

“It’s risible that they try to say that it’s pragmatic to stop the UK producing more oil and gas. It’s clearly a reaction to poor polling against the Greens. I see this as more vibe driven policy making as opposed to ‘pragmatic’ policy making.”

Dan Slater, from Zeus Capital, said: “While banning new exploration licences via legislation makes resumption a more circuitous process, the logic for new licences is inescapable, and parliament is sovereign and fully has the power to reverse the new ban.”

David Whitehouse, the chief executive of Offshore Energies UK, a trade body for Britain’s oil and gas producers, said the planned bill would simply make the UK more dependent on imported oil and gas.

“This will leave households and businesses exposed in an increasingly volatile world. We should be making the most of the energy we produce here at home rather than relying on imports.”

data.title: Financier caught up in row with neighbours over basement golf simulator
data.description:
A financier has won planning permission to dig 4m under his driveway to build a golf simulator and games room, despite objections from neighbours.

Tim Woolford secured permission to install a basement below the drive of his modern home. The underground room will be 13ft 1in deep and have a simulator, bar area and pool table.

Neighbours in Winchester, Hampshire, where homes are worth an average of £1m, say they have environmental concerns about the project and that the works will affect their lives for months.

Residents have referred to Mr Woolford’s home as the “Lego house”, because of its striking modern design, and say it is not in keeping with traditional properties in the area.

Winchester City Council has approved the plans with conditions, despite a planning officer recommending it be refused.

Mr Woolford, his wife and their two children have lived in the house since the coronavirus pandemic and, in drawing up an underground extension, had sought to create an extension plan that would have the least impact on neighbours.

He said: “Our view was that we wanted to do something that would impact people the absolute least as possible. Some of the people that objected misunderstood what would be here when the builders were done.”

Mr Woolford, who is managing director of a finance-management company in London, said he and his wife would still be able to park on the driveway when the building work was completed, so this would not affect the on-street parking.

He said he wanted to build the space for his two sons, who are aged seven and eight, and wanted to install a golf simulator, because they were interested in the sport.

Mr Woolford said: “We have kids that are growing, and it is good for them. We didn’t actually think there would be any discussions about the plans. We did quite a few developments to the house a few years ago, and arguably this has been more contentious.”

He said one of his sons played the guitar and he thought it would be less disruptive to allow him to play in the basement extension – sometimes referred to as an iceberg basement.

Mr Woolford said: “People go into their lofts and convert garages, and I didn’t want to go into the loft and put big windows, and I don’t have a garage to convert.”

He said the process should be reasonably quick and should not cause very much disruption to the neighbours.

He said: “It is actually a quick build. The soil can be taken out within a week. We should be done in about 10 to 12 weeks, so much more minimal than people expect.”

Mr Woolford said the complaints were a “group effort” and they came from houses further down the street, who were not as affected by the works. As well as being 4m deep, the new basement will be 9.5m in width, and 10.9m in length.

Hazel Agombar, who has lived in the street for 20 years, said the house was already referred to as the “Lego house” and she did not think more work should be done to it.

She said: “I didn’t want it to set a precedent of people applying for basement extensions because of the disruption. We have people who are wheelchair users regularly using this street. There is limited parking up the top.

“This is a lovely street, people get on. It’s very green and leafy, and I just thought it was a poor reason to try to change the character of it and try to navigate that disruption.”

Mrs Agombar said that she thought the decision contravened the council’s local plan to make Winchester more environmentally friendly. She said: “It seems to go against the new local plan. It is only one development but it seems like it is starting a precedent. It is for a golf simulation room.

“This is crazy. They have this massive house with a cinema room and garden. If you want a bigger house, maybe you should move if you want to dig up a conservation area.

“The council has allowed a highly intensive carbon footprint development. Digging up that drive is going to be hugely carbon intensive.”

Another objector is Keith Hatter, 79, who is blind and has lived on the street for the last 14 years.

He said: “The main reason was that it involves digging out to about 2.5m of the ground in front of the house, and I am slightly worried that this might have an effect on the soil structure.”

Mr Hatter added: “The second objection I have come to second-hand – because I am totally blind – is that it might interfere with the character. It would involve the trees and general flora in front of the house being removed and have a slightly detrimental environmental effect.”
