data.title: The Walliams case shows why the rich must not be allowed to muzzle the press
data.description:
In the US, the counterproductive result of seeking an injunction is called “the Streisand effect”. In Britain, the effect is usually related to the massive sales of Spycatcher after Margaret Thatcher’s futile attempt to impose a worldwide ban on the book.

As David Walliams must recognise, if he glumly contemplates Wednesday’s newspapers and the many pages they devote to his obnoxious behaviour, any attempt to injunct the media gives the story more publicity than it would otherwise have received.

Barbra Streisand tried to injunct scientific photos of coastal erosion at her edge-of-cliff mansion in Malibu – only four had been downloaded before she brought the action but hundreds of thousands were after it failed. Spycatcher, a badly written conspiracy theory, sold more than a million copies worldwide on the strength of the government’s ill-conceived legal proceedings.

A threat to take your own life can never translate into a right to interfere with press freedom. But the very fact that Walliams’ lawyers thought this arguable draws attention to how English privacy law has developed to threaten freedom of speech.

Britain, to its discredit, had no protection for privacy until it adopted the European Convention on Human Rights in 1998. The right to “respect” for family life, home and correspondence stopped some press malpractice and served to close the News of the World, but it also provided a basis for oligarchs, tax evaders and wife-beaters to obtain injunctions against the release of information about which they could claim “a reasonable expectation of privacy”.

Judges in our highest court decided that this was an enormously wide field, not only covering physical and mental health but “racial or ethnic characteristics… the generality of personal and family relationships. Information conveyed in the course of personal relationships, a person’s political opinions and affiliations, religious commitments, personal financial and tax related information, past involvement in criminal behaviour…” and so on. Almost anything that a person can find embarrassing can be the subject of a claim for injunction, if the claimant can afford the legal costs (at least £50,000) of an application.

But the real danger in the explosion of privacy law is how it can chill public-interest reporting, especially in coverage of official abuse of power. In the Sir Cliff Richard case, for example, the police, without credible evidence, obtained and executed a search warrant and were obliged – rightfully so – to pay the pop star heavy damages. But he additionally won hundreds of thousands of pounds (and reportedly £1m in costs) from the BBC for televising the raid on his home.

The raid was the result of a warrant that should never have been granted, but the High Court ruled that all police suspects had “a reasonable expectation of privacy” at any stage of the investigation. This seriously handicaps the “watchdog” function of the media which cannot safely report on police dealings, however abusive, with named suspects. It allows the rich to threaten expensive actions against media who wish to expose their questionable commercial or tax dealings and personal affairs no matter how publicly important.

Injunctions are court orders not to publish the information set out in their schedules, on pain of up to two years’ imprisonment. MPs and peers are exempt when they speak under parliamentary privilege – as Lord Hain did when revealing that Sir Philip Green had obtained an injunction to stop The Daily Telegraph reporting allegations that he had sexually harassed and racially abused his staff. Such claims were not regarded by judges in 2018 as of sufficient public interest to override his privacy. But it is to be hoped that their attitudes have now changed.

There is no public list of injunctions that have been granted, and indeed there cannot be for “super injunctions” – the very mention of which is prohibited. In most cases the court will deliver a short public judgment setting out the law and the result and a long secret judgment assessing the facts. What happens to all these secret judgments? Where are they stored and how long must they stay secret? This is unclear.

For a nation that boasts of its “open justice” principle, it is entirely unsatisfactory. As Jeremy Bentham famously said “publicity is the very soul of justice” and courts should not keep secrets. We should at least appoint an “open-justice commissioner” to study and report on injunctions which impact upon public-interest reporting and act as custodian of the secret judgments handed down by our judges and direct their release when appropriate.

As for the damage done to individuals by exposing their private misbehaviour, the media must decide according to its own ethical standards and submit to public judgment. The Guardian was overkind to David Walliams, delaying publication for six months to allow him to make his hopeless case. His publishers, however, threatened to withdraw his popular children’s books, which seems an unnecessary act of censorship (should we really ban Alice in Wonderland because of Lewis Carroll’s alleged proclivities?).

The message of Walliams is clear: injunctions must not be allowed to suppress public interest reporting. And that there is a public interest in allowing women who claim to have been abused by powerful men to tell their stories if they are prepared to attest to the truth. Judges must drop their simplistic distinction between what merely interests the public (in which they find no value) and what is genuinely in the public interest by acknowledging that in the case of victims who want to speak out about sex abuse, it can be both.

Geoffrey Robertson KC founded Doughty Street Chambers and is the author of ‘Lawfare’ and (with Sir Andrew Nichol)‘Media Law’

data.title: Summer heatwaves caused blackouts, admits National Grid
data.description:
Soaring temperatures triggered a rise in energy blackouts during the summer, the National Grid admitted.

The utility giant told investors on Thursday that its network suffered “additional localised outages” in June, July and August, as the heat disrupted the infrastructure distributing power to homes and businesses.

National Grid revealed details of the blackouts in its latest half-year results on Thursday.

“In UK Electricity Distribution, network stability was maintained, but additional localised outages were experienced because of the significant increase in extreme heat during the UK summer period,” the company said.

The admission comes after one of the grid’s toughest summers.

Power networks typically come under heightened pressure during cold, still winter evenings, but multiple heatwaves created a supply pinch this year.

In early August, National Grid Electricity Distribution issued formal alerts and text messages directly to customers across the Midlands and the South, warning that power cuts were increasingly probable.

National Grid’s distribution business is responsible for powering 19 million homes across the East and West Midlands, South Wales and South West England, operating 137,000 miles of lines and cables.

Much of its infrastructure is decades old, leaving it more vulnerable to extreme weather.

Sustained heat prevents underground cables and transformers from cooling overnight, significantly increasing the risk of trips and faults.

Further disruption

The UK’s 14 distribution networks carry power from the high-voltage transmission system to homes and businesses. In England and Wales, the transmission system is owned by National Grid but managed day to day by the National Energy System Operator (Neso).

In June and July, Neso was forced to issue a series of “margin warnings” seeking extra supplies to meet rising demand for air conditioning and other cooling products.

Neso said that no blackouts occurred in July and August, but reports since have highlighted how precarious the situation was.

Whistleblowers from within Neso’s control room alleged that the grid operator underplayed how fragile margins were during the June heatwave, prompting an independent inquiry that raised issues over transparency.

National Grid’s latest admission will heighten concern that the UK is becoming increasingly vulnerable to weather-related disruption.

This is partially because of climate change, but experts also point to a growing reliance on intermittent renewables and the Grid’s ageing infrastructure.

This came to the fore last year when a major fire broke out at National Grid Electricity Transmission’s North Hyde substation in Hayes, west London.

The blaze erupted when an insulating component failed on one of the main transformers, igniting approximately 25,000 litres of cooling oil.

Nearby residents were evacuated as emergency crews tackled the fire, which cut power to 67,000 domestic and commercial customers.

Crucially, the outage severed the primary supply to Heathrow and three major data centres, forcing the airport to shut down for a day.

A subsequent investigation led by Neso, Ofgem and the London Fire Brigade found that the fire was caused by water entering the transformer – a problem detected seven years previously but left unresolved by National Grid.

National Grid said it had “taken further action” to strengthen its operations since the fire, such as carrying out additional risk assessments and retesting the resilience of substations.

A spokesman for the company told The Telegraph: “Our borrowing programme helps reduce our cost of capital and with it, the cost of developing critical infrastructure in the UK. 

“This translates into savings for bill payers. Our business is financially strong. Our UK investment programme is on track, and we have substantially locked in our supply chain, giving us good visibility on costs, delivery and future cash flows. 

“The ratings agencies and financial markets monitor our ability to service our debt, which is reflected in our investment-grade credit ratings.”

data.title: London house prices suffer worst drop since financial crisis
data.description:
Property prices in inner London have suffered the worst drop since the financial crisis as higher mortgage rates slow the capital’s housing market.

A toxic cocktail of soaring borrowing costs, high levels of stamp duty and the looming mansion tax caused central London property prices to slump 7.2pc in the 12 months to September, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

It means the average price of a home in inner London’s 12 boroughs and the City – which includes areas such as Camden, Tower Hamlets, Newham and Lambeth – dropped by just over £48,000 in a year, falling from £669,532 to £621,491.

However, the data revealed there was a significant divide in the areas of the capital where property prices fell. Outer London boroughs recorded just a 0.1pc decline in the price of a home in the 12 months to September.

On average, property prices across the capital dropped 3.5pc in the year to September.

Jonathan Hopper, the chief executive of Garrington Property Finders, said: “This huge divergence reflects the gulf between the buyers typically drawn to the two areas. Demand in outer London comes largely from domestic buyers, and while this has softened over the past year, it has been resilient.”

He warned that in stark contrast “a series of punitive tax increases”, including the looming mansion tax, had dented demand in inner London, with wealthy, international buyers reconsidering whether to purchase property.

Despite the slump, official figures showed that average UK house prices increased by 1.2pc, to £273,000.

London and the South East were the only two regions in the UK to record a drop in annual house prices, the data from the ONS showed.

The capital will be the hardest hit by Labour’s upcoming mansion tax, also known as the high-value property surcharge. The levy will hit properties worth £2m or more with a surcharge of at least £2,500 a year when it comes into effect in April 2028.

Wealthy areas of inner London have also recorded double-digit declines in annual property prices as they grapple with the effect of the scrapping of non-dom status and higher stamp duty rates.

House prices in Kensington and Chelsea declined 15.6pc year on year to an average of £1.17m in September 2026, down from £1.39m, according to Land Registry data.

In Westminster, house prices dropped 18.5pc in the year to September, with the average property costing £861,130, compared to £1.06m in September 2025.

Inner London’s flat market has also experience a significant slowdown, as average flat prices dropped 8.5pc. This compared with a 2.6pc decline in the price of detached properties over the same period.

Despite the fall in property prices in the capital, prospective buyers will still feel the squeeze, as borrowing costs have risen sharply since the outbreak of the Iran war, adding hundreds to mortgage repayments.

Paige Tao, an economist at PwC UK, said: “First time buyers entering the market with smaller deposits are more exposed to higher mortgage rates, while those who have moved out of their childhood home face the added challenge of saving for a deposit.”

data.title: BT races to stop new Grand Theft Auto game crashing the internet
data.description:
BT is racing to prevent the latest instalment of Grand Theft Auto from crashing the internet as gamers rush to get a first taste of the hit title.

The telecoms giant is among the major broadband providers that have increased network capacity ahead of the rollout of the much-delayed GTA VI on Nov 19, which is expected to trigger “unprecedented” demand for data.

Several internet firms are understood to have bought more capacity from major exchanges including the London Internet Exchange (LINX) to handle the spike in traffic.

BT and other companies have also increased their use of caching – where data is temporarily stored in locations closer to the end user – limited scheduled maintenance and stepped up network monitoring.

The release of GTA VI, which is made by developer Rockstar Games, has already broken records for internet demand after fans were given a chance to pre-load the game a week ahead of its launch.

Virgin Media O2 reported its biggest-ever traffic peak and highest-ever daily data volume on Nov 10, with demand surging between midnight and 1am. LINX has recorded its highest ever traffic over the past month at 13.7 terabits per second (Tbps).

The pre-launch was also the second-biggest peak recorded across BT’s broadband network, behind only Arsenal’s Champions League semi-final clash against Atlético Madrid in May.

The eagerly-awaited release has sparked fears of congestion and disruption following similar issues during the launch of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare III in 2023.

While Rockstar has sought to limit the impact by spreading downloads of GTA VI over a week, experts warned this may not be enough to prevent disruption.

William Manzione, at network provider RETN said: “Pre-loading should help reduce the concentration of downloads on launch day, but it does not eliminate the possibility of further traffic increases.

“Players who have not preloaded the game may still download it on release day, while additional patches or updates could create another wave of demand.”

Mr Manzione said the most likely fallout would be slower downloads and localised congestion, rather than widespread outages.

Jeanie York, VMO2’s chief technology officer, said: “GTA VI has already broken broadband records before players have even entered the game, and we’re preparing for another busy day when it launches next week.

“Fans downloading in advance will spread some of that demand, but it’s too early to say whether launch day will set another record.”

A BT spokesman said: “We are building the UK’s digital backbone and connecting and protecting the country like no one else. Our networks are built to support moments of huge national demand like this.

“From the biggest gaming launches to major sporting and cultural events, BT is investing in the scale, capacity and resilience needed to keep millions of customers connected when it matters.”

GTA has been dogged by controversy since its first release in 1997 owing to the game’s graphic depiction of violence, as well as other themes including drugs, prostitution and sex.

But the game, which is largely developed by teams based in Scotland, has enjoyed runaway success. The last title in the series, GTA V, has generated more than $10bn (£7.6bn) in sales since its launch in 2013, making it the third-best-selling video game of all time.

Rockstar, which is owned by US games giant Take-Two Interactive, first unveiled plans for its sixth instalment in late 2023.

The title is rumoured to have a budget of up to $3bn, eclipsing any Hollywood movie, but has been beset by leaks and delays.

In August, Netflix agreed a deal for an exclusive early trailer of the gangland action game. The 25-minute clip racked up 31.1m views in its first four days, jumping to the top of the streaming service’s charts.

data.title: Britain can’t afford any more quangos
data.description:
Who says Andy Burnham doesn’t do anything of significance? In the last few days, his Government has created “water councils” to supervise an industry that is already collapsing under the weight of over-regulation, as well as a “special health authority” to absorb staff from NHS England.

At this rate, we are well on track for a hundred or more new regulatory, supervisory or advisory bodies a year, each one equipped with generously paid staff and swish London offices, plus the obligatory satellite branch in Bolton. 

This is crazy. The British economy can’t afford all the quangos – we should be abolishing them instead.

If you happen to have some spare time on your hands, and feel like a cushy gig, I recommend applying for one of the new water councils.

Apparently there will be eight of them across the country, designed, in the words of Burnham, to give local people “a real say over what they need from their water company”.

Never mind that we already have one water regulator, Ofwat, with an annual budget of £78m, as well as consultative bodies, such as Water Resources East, not to mention the whole series of financial regulators that all the regional water companies have to deal with.

It seems what we need is just one more layer of oversight.

Likewise, most of us might imagine that the answer to the question of “what do we need from our water company” would be pretty straightforward. Clean water, and enough of it that we can use the sprinklers in the garden over a hot summer, with fewer leaks, and lower bills. But, hey, whatever. It seems we don’t need more engineers, or reservoirs, or any of that stuff. We need a “council” where things can be “discussed”.

Similarly, some of us might have imagined that getting rid of NHS England would mean streamlining the health service. But no.

The Special Health Authority is designed to provide jobs for all the people who might otherwise lose them. It will probably be “special” for them, if not for patients.

Meanwhile, back in September, the Government announced the creation of the OneGov Delivery Agency, due for launch next spring, with a budget still to be determined, while Great British Railways has now been formally launched, with Sir John Kingman bringing all his commercial nous as a former permanent secretary to the Treasury to make trains “great” again.

It probably won’t be long before we see the launch of Great British Steel for all the nationalised metal-bashing assets.

The list goes on and on. It seems like a long time since Sir Keir Starmer – if anyone still remembers him – promised a “bonfire of the quangos”. Instead, the Government is launching new ones at an accelerating rate. There doesn’t seem to be any issue that ministers don’t think can be solved by a task force, a council or a special advisory committee.

The trouble is, none of them is actually going to make anything any better.

There are three big problems. To start with, the costs keep adding up. According to figures from the TaxPayer’s Alliance, 438 quangos received total funding of £378bn in the last full financial year.

Between them, they employ almost half a million people. True, some of that is money that the Government would have been spending anyway, except that it has been outsourced to a separate agency.

But each layer adds costs of its own. There are offices to be paid for, and consultants to be hired, and staff, complete with generous pensions, to be added to the payroll. Each one is, without question, more expensive than if the Government were simply doing the work directly.

Next, it means proliferating red tape. As soon as a new council or agency is created it has to keep itself busy. That only means one thing. It has to keep creating new regulations, and targets, followed by reports on their implementation, and fines for anyone who does not follow the rules.

Finally, all quangos expand. They have to build their empires, just like any organisation, and the only way they can do that is by taking on more people, and interfering even more with whatever industry they are meant to be looking after. We can see that very clearly in their budgets.

Why is Ofwat spending 9pc more this year than last year? It is hard to argue the water industry is 9pc better run.

Or why does the Office of Rail and Road need a 5.75pc budget increase, especially given that most of the rail industry has been taken back into state ownership, so it is hard to figure out why we even need it at all.

No quango in human history ever volunteered to close itself down, or for its funding to be reduced, and there is no chance that any Labour minister will ever demand that it does. Instead, they just expand relentlessly.

The British economy is turning into one giant regulatory body with a country attached.

It is crushing growth, stifling genuine entrepreneurship, and running up huge bills that the economy can barely afford. Even by the standards of this Labour Government, two new quangos in a single week is an alarming rate of increase. At best, they will absorb time and money, while making no positive difference to anything.

At worst, they will make each industry they meddle in even more hopelessly inefficient. The only solution is to sweep them all away – but unfortunately there is very little chance of that happening under this Government.

data.title: Ikea scraps investments in Britain because of high taxes
data.description:
Ikea has abandoned plans to invest in Britain after warning that punishing business rates are driving up costs.

The Swedish furniture giant said it had been forced to scrap projects because the UK was becoming increasingly expensive and complex to operate in.

David McCabe, Ikea’s UK chief executive, said Britain had the highest business rates burden of any of the company’s European markets and the third highest worldwide.

He told the Press Association: “Companies like Ikea are looking at incredibly high costs and an increasingly complex operating environment.

“We believe the UK is definitely a market for investment and have recently invested in eight new units in the UK.

“But there are higher costs and complexities here, and it has meant that we have had investment projects in the UK that we have had to abandon, and that is a shame.”

The company did not disclose which projects had been scrapped or how much they would have been worth.

Retailers have faced mounting costs from business rates since April, when a shake-up of the system introduced higher taxes on commercial properties valued at £500,000 or more.

These larger premises now face a tax rate of 50.8pc of their rateable value, compared with 43pc for smaller retail properties. The higher rate was introduced to help fund tax cuts for smaller shops, pubs and restaurants.

The changes coincided with a revaluation of commercial properties, which pushed up bills for some businesses despite reductions in the headline tax rates.

Mr McCabe criticised the Government for failing to tackle the costs facing retailers in last month’s Budget.

He said: “While the Budget avoided adding further costs, it missed an opportunity to back retailers under real pressure, stopping short of addressing the structural challenges holding the sector back.”

Ikea reported that British sales had virtually stalled in the past year, rising just 0.5pc to £2.26bn.

Sales rose 4.7pc in the first four months of its financial year before weakening in the second half as cash-strapped households cut back on furniture purchases.

The retailer has invested £54m in cutting prices on 425 products, including its popular Billy bookcases and Poäng armchairs, with reductions averaging 20pc.

Despite the slowdown, Ikea reported a 14pc jump in kitchen sales as more households sought to improve their existing properties rather than move.

Visits to Ikea’s British stores rose 7pc during the year, boosted by the opening of new outlets.

Online sales, meanwhile, rose just 0.7pc and accounted for more than two fifths of the retailer’s British business.

Ikea has recently opened stores in Brighton, Norwich and York, alongside its flagship on Oxford Street in central London, which opened at the start of last year.

It has also opened a smaller store in Chester and new planning and ordering centres in Dundee and Aberdeen, as it seeks to attract customers beyond its traditional out-of-town warehouses.

data.title: ECB sounds alarm on AI ahead of Anthropic’s $1.5tn listing
data.description:
The AI boom is increasingly mirroring the 2007 global financial crisis, the European Central Bank (ECB) has warned ahead of Anthropic’s $1.49tn (£1.13tn) listing.

The central bank said on Wednesday that it was alarmed at the $500bn borrowing spree among tech companies and data-centre builders, which has raced ahead of some companies’ profits.

It said this had “parallels” with other financial market blow-ups including the dotcom bubble and the financial crash in 2007/08.

Mega-floats of companies such as SpaceX and Anthropic, which is expected to list on the stock market on Thursday, “could be a sign of late-cycle market exuberance”.

Anthropic is set for a valuation $1.49tn (£1.13tn) after the company priced its shares ahead of its blockbuster stock market debut on Thursday.

The Claude maker has valued its stock for its Initial Public Offering (IPO) on the tech-focused Nasdaq at $83 per share.

The stock pricing came in above industry estimates, between $70 and $78, and the initial $1.4tn projected valuation.

The higher-than-expected pricing will give confidence to technology investors and reaffirms the value of the major AI developers, despite fears of a market bubble.

“The rapid shift towards debt finance invokes historical parallels with the dotcom and subprime bubbles,” the ECB said on Wednesday in its latest semi-annual Financial Stability Review.

“Even if AI as a technology successfully transforms the global economy, the credit-driven AI boom may result in overcapacity, capital misallocation and credit losses for investors.”

After SpaceX, it will be the second-largest stock market float in history. OpenAI is expected to launch a similarly gargantuan IPO next year.

But the ECB said investors were already becoming more concerned about the tech giants’ heavy borrowing, their interdependence on each other – known as “circular financing” – and their prospects of profitability.

There are also increasing questions over whether data centre construction can keep pace with what AI firms require.

Alternatively, if AI’s evolution slows then the breakneck build-out could turn to bust.

“The capital spending and technological aspects are reminiscent of the dotcom bubble of the early 2000s, which was characterised by over-investment in infrastructure,” the ECB said.

The sheer volume of IPOs also had echoes in the dotcom era, the ECB said. The total value of shares floated this year is expected to be $225bn, more than five times the $44bn raised last year.

The bank said the AI boom also now resembled the crash of 2007/08, when banks and markets fuelled a credit bubble.

“The rapid acceleration of debt financing raises concerns that the AI build-out might become debt-driven and unsustainable, with further risks added by circular financing, the use of off-balance-sheet transactions and opaqueness in private markets,” the ECB’s review said.

It added: “Such dynamics were evident during the subprime mortgage bubble.”

America’s big tech firms are expected to rack up capital expenditure of as much as $5.5tn by 2030, which would amount to 3pc of US gross domestic product every year.

That would be “considerably larger than the financing of other major innovations in the past”, the ECB said, and was “concentrated among a small group of US firms”.

As cash flow has ebbed at some firms, they are issuing more bonds and also borrowing more against future cash flows. The off-balance-sheet debt topped $4tn in the second quarter.

The ECB said the American AI boom could also be at risk if Chinese open-source models proved cheaper or more popular, or if companies ran into bottlenecks in raw material supplies or grid or data centre capacity.

The review warned that a bust in AI could ripple out into the wider markets and the global economy.

data.title: Europe’s gas shortage could open the door for Putin
data.description:
Donald Trump says he has settled eight wars, but the biggest prize – peace between Russia and Ukraine – still eludes and frustrates him. The president now insists, however, that a “big, beautiful agreement” is on the cards.

His negotiators, Steve Witkoff, the property developer, and Jared Kushner, his son-in-law, will head to Abu Dhabi this week for the first face-to-face peace talks with Russia and Ukraine since February.

This three-way negotiation has squeezed out the other key players with skin in the game: the Europeans. Trump himself said last week that the deal “might involve all of Europe”.

However, Kushner is not worried. “We will consult closely with our European partners on the sidelines,” he said on X last Friday.

Although the Europeans are sidelined, their priority is clear: a peace deal must neutralise the threat of Russian aggression.

But the Americans have muddied the waters. Reports suggest they are pushing for a peace deal that would controversially include the resumption of Russian gas exports to Europe.

The Europeans have spent the past four years painfully weaning themselves off an addiction to Vladimir Putin’s energy bounty. They are now in the final furlong of a legally binding process to shut out Russian gas permanently.

Grounds to reopen Russian pipelines

The plan is to end shipments of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) by New Year’s Day and phase out the last pipeline imports by this time next year.

But if the Americans have their way, they might open the door for Putin to start rebuilding his once-mighty energy leverage over Europe.

Most analysts say there’s little chance that Brussels or Kyiv would countenance any return to relying on the Russians to keep the lights on.

“While there are EU members in the east, like Slovakia, that have always sought to maintain Russian gas flows, the view from Berlin and Paris et al is that the ban on Russian gas from Jan 1 will go ahead,” says Bill Farren-Price, of the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies.

But European households and industries are struggling with soaring energy costs, and countries such as Germany and the Netherlands have not managed to store enough gas this year to be sure of seeing out the winter.

The International Energy Agency warned last week that if Trump doesn’t settle the Iran war soon, and if the winter is long and cold, Europe could be paying elevated prices for gas all the way into next summer.

For every European politician or industrialist who baulks at the Americans’ freewheeling dealmaking with the Kremlin, there might be another who is sorely tempted by the prospect of cheaper gas.

“Although pretty much all the countries around the Baltic Sea would be staunchly against it, Germany would be an interesting case. Germany politically is mostly against it, but German industrialists would probably be quite for it,” said Sergey Vakulenko, of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Centre.

The deal might spur Slovakia and Hungary, which still rely on Russian gas piped through Turkey and the Balkans, to push for a relaxation of the EU-wide ban.

And if Marine Le Pen wins the French presidency next April, she may join their cause. In Germany, the ascendant Alternative für Deutschland party has called for the Russian pipelines to reopen.

A Russian energy renaissance in Europe may still seem far-fetched to many. But as the Americans plan what Kushner calls “an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability”, Putin can dare to dream.

The trickle of reports on the American gas blueprint suggests Kushner and Witkoff have been beavering away at it for several months.

Reuters reported in early October that the pair had proposed marshalling American investors to reopen the Nord Stream pipeline, which used to carry vast amounts of Russian gas to Germany under the Baltic Sea.

Berlin mothballed the pipelines after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, and later that year they were sabotaged in a series of underwater explosions.

Kushner reportedly floated the plan with Kirill Dmitriev, one of Putin’s closest associates. Dmitriev has publicly advocated resuming gas sales to Germany. He has held talks with US energy officials and was in the White House last week to meet Trump himself.

The midterm elections handed control of Congress to the Democrats, who have little appetite to lift US sanctions on Nord Stream. The victors take the reins on Capitol Hill from January, so Trump needs either to strike a deal by Christmas or move to Plan B.

Europe is running out of options

The Wall Street Journal reported last week that Kushner and Witkoff had also proposed selling Russian gas to Europe via a US intermediary to skirt the EU’s ban.

This plan would allow Kyiv to earn transit fees from its pipeline network. And the sales revenue would be held in an escrow account to ensure that Putin could not spend the funds on fighting Ukraine.

Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, said last week that such a deal was not possible now, given “the situation on the ground”. But he did not rule it out.

Vakulenko, of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Centre, doubts this particular plan will fly. “When they start to discuss escrow accounts, that’s a big no-no for Russia. And I also don’t think Trump’s leverage over the Europeans is that strong at the moment,” he says.

Yet surging gas prices are exerting real leverage on Europe, which has almost tripled since the Iran war began in late February.

The EU’s storage tanks are only 74pc full, at least 10 percentage points below the norm for this time of year. Germany’s are only at 60pc capacity.

The Europeans are competing with Asia for expensive cargoes from the US, and banking on the constancy of Norway’s output. This has made the task of weaning the Continent off Russian gas much harder.

Data by think tank Bruegel suggest the EU has been importing about 380 million cubic metres of Russian gas per week recently – exactly the same amount as at this time last year.

The EU still relies on Russia for between 12pc and 15pc of its gas. In August, the bloc bought €756m (£630m) of Russian pipeline gas and €323m of LNG, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

It looks like a tall order, or at least a costly one, to shut out Russian LNG by Jan 1.

The law gives Brussels the power to pause the ban temporarily if energy supplies are under serious threat, but cost alone is not expected to be sufficient grounds.

“Even before the Middle East conflict, there were some people in the market who thought the EU might relax that deadline, push it back until the spring, given the storage situation. We don’t think that will be the case,” says Tom Marzec-Manser, at energy analysis firm Wood Mackenzie.

He adds that even if the Europeans needed Russian gas, they would be conscious of the risk of handing leverage and influence to Putin.

“The moment you do it, you’re put in a position of weakness. You’ve cornered yourself somewhat, from a foreign-policy perspective.”

Dan Jorgensen, the EU’s energy commissioner, is of the same mind. “I certainly would not trust Russia, even if there were peace tomorrow,” he said last month.

But if Trump did, against the odds, deliver peace tomorrow, Russian gas could be back on the table. The Europeans may not trust Putin. The question is whether, faced with the temptation of cheap energy, they can even trust themselves.

data.title: Veterans forced to take 5am rail replacement bus to Remembrance Sunday
data.description:
Veterans have been offered a rail replacement bus at nearly 5am to reach Remembrance Sunday events in London.

Major Christopher McLean, 67, from Wiltshire, said the arrangements were “not good enough” and would prevent fellow veterans attending memorials.

In an email seen by The Telegraph, the Royal British Legion warned Cenotaph Parade ticket-holders that rail engineering works would bring disruption on Nov 8.

The charity advised veterans that South Western Railway and Network Rail Wessex were offering limited one-way bus travel from Winchester and Salisbury railway stations that were departing at 4.45am to arrive at London Waterloo at 8am.

Scheduled replacement bus services are also operating, requiring changes between rail and bus services to arrive in London on time.

Major McLean, who lives outside Salisbury, told The Telegraph that the disruption meant he would have to get up at 3.45am, which was not ideal at his age.

“No one seems to have thought this through,” he told The Telegraph, adding: “If I had planned like that in my Army logistics career, I would have been sacked.”

Veterans forced to ‘make other arrangements’

Major McLean said that veterans would be prevented attending events in the capital because of the disruption.

He said: “Lots of us are in our 70s. What about the implications for people who are infirm? It’s not good enough. Most of the guys I know are going to have to make other arrangements.

“Luckily, I can go up the night before and stay with relatives in Surrey. If I hadn’t had family there, I would have pulled out.

“Others are looking at paying for two nights in a London hotel, which is expensive. The Royal British Legion does a great job getting this all together, but the wider logistics haven’t been considered properly.”

Veterans would have been able to leave closer to 7am if the trains were running. This would still have allowed them enough time to arrive in Whitehall, pass through police security procedures and form up on the Cenotaph for 10.30am.

Major McLean said the rail disruption was the latest woe to be bestowed on veterans.

He said: “Prosecutions of veterans, underfunding of defence – it’s one thing after another, which is really upsetting this community. This is the latest mark of disrespect.”

Veteran’s fiercely oppose Labour’s Northern Ireland Troubles Bill, which is currently in the House of Lords, arguing that it does not adequately protect former service members.

Col Richard Kemp, a retired British Army officer who served from 1977 to 2006, criticised the lack of foresight by the railway operators.

“This is probably the most important day of the year when people can come together and pay respects to the war dead,” he said, adding: “It should be given priority above other events.

“Veterans should be treated with the utmost respect, including by the railway companies. This clearly isn’t good enough.”

Last month, the Government announced that it was extending free railway travel on Remembrance weekend, which currently covers serving military staff, veterans and one next of kin of a service-person who died while serving.

However, networks across the country will be disrupted by engineering work on Nov 7 and 8.

South Western Railway, the first operator to be renationalised by Labour in May 2025, apologised to veterans whose journeys would be affected.

A spokesman said: “South Western Railway is proud of its commitment to the Armed Forces community and this year received the Ministry of Defence Gold Award.

“Unfortunately, long-planned and essential engineering works this weekend mean veterans will need to use a combination of train and rail replacement services to travel to London Waterloo.

“We investigated whether the engineering works could be rescheduled, but this would have meant deferring essential track maintenance to maintain the long-term safety and reliability of the railway.”

A spokesman for the Royal British Legion said: “We’ve worked with the rail authorities to contact veterans affected by planned engineering works so they know a rail replacement service has been arranged.”

data.title: Twelve flights diverted across Europe after bomb threats
data.description:
Twelve flights have been diverted across Europe following a series of bomb threats.

Thursday’s disruption comes days after similar incidents in which eight planes, including three from the UK, were grounded over what Britain dismissed as a “malicious hoax”.

Three of Thursday’s incidents involved flights bound for Italy.

An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to Normandy following a bomb alert, the French prime minister’s office said.

The office of Sébastien Lecornu, the French prime minister, said all 151 passengers and six crew members were safe, and that military bomb defusal teams were examining the plane.

A Finnair flight bound for Helsinki landed in Rome after a threat was reported on board, while a Wizz Air service from Milan Malpensa to Warsaw was diverted to Vienna.

A Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed at Zaventem airport in Belgium after the crew received a “suspicious report concerning a flight to Brussels airport”.

Three more aircraft were forced to land at airports in Bulgaria following bomb threats. 

Two of the planes – travelling from Copenhagen and Madrid respectively – landed in Sofia, the broadcaster bTV, citing the interior minister, reported.

A third aircraft, flying from London, landed in Plovdiv, according to reports. Four planes flying to Prague had been the subject of bomb threats and were preparing to land, according to Czech police. 

A Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest was also targeted, Romanian intelligence services said.

On Thursday morning, Spanish authorities said three flights at Madrid were affected by hoax threats.

None of the threats reported this week have been found to be genuine, despite triggering dozens of unplanned landings as well and escorts by fighter jets.

The EU’s transport commissioner said it was “too early to draw conclusions” on whether Thursday’s spate of bomb threats were linked.

Apostolos Tzitzikostas said in a message posted on LinkedIn that he had asked EU security authorities “to cooperate closely with airport operators, airlines and law enforcement authorities” over the bomb threats.

On Tuesday, at least seven planes were subjected to threats. A flight to Sofia was similarly affected on Monday.

An airport in Warsaw was briefly shut and the Italian air force accompanied one of the flights to Rome. An Israel-bound cruise ship was also searched for bombs in Greece.

A British Government spokesman told The Telegraph that the threats against the UK flights had been a “malicious hoax”, though it was not clear how they had been orchestrated.

Speculation quickly centred on Moscow, with a former MI6 intelligence officer telling The Telegraph that it was his first thought when he learned of the bomb threats, which he said fitted “a pattern of behaviour” by the Kremlin.

The flight disruption follows a week of chaos, with dozens of supermarket fridges across Europe hacked on Monday. The attacks caused large amounts of food to spoil after hackers gained remote access to in-store fridge units and turned up their temperatures, in some cases to as much as 80C.

Hackers also targeted France’s national blood bank, raising the temperature of its cold storage rooms to boiling point.

Facilities at Coolworld were heated to 110C overnight on Sunday after hackers gained access to the temperature settings remotely, Le Canard enchaîné reported. The rooms are normally kept at -30C to preserve donor blood samples.

An on-duty technician detected the unusual rise in temperatures. France’s health ministry said there had been no consequences for patients and no plasma had been destroyed.

The Kremlin said European media accusations of Russian involvement in ‌cyber attacks on supermarkets were not backed up by any evidence.

Dmitry ⁠Peskov, a Kremlin spokesman, told reporters on Thursday: “These are absurd claims. As always, they are backed up by absolutely ‌no reasoning, no evidence whatsoever, and yet here we have ⁠such ⁠baseless accusations against our country, implicating it in everything.”

However, pro-Russian hackers have claimed responsibility for the cyber attacks on fridges.

The pro-Russian hacking collective NoName057(16) claimed to have worked with Z-Pentest, another pro-Russian hacker group, to launch the attack.

A video claiming responsibility for the attack was posted on Telegram, according to the Danish media outlet DR.

In the video, titled Operation Chronicle: Danfoss, the hackers claimed to have “dealt a crushing blow to Danfoss and Dixell XWEB equipment”.

Danfoss and Dixell XWEB were the refrigeration companies targeted in the cyber attack.

“We didn’t even need malware for that. We just exploited the systems’ built-in features,” the hackers said.
